priorities.description:
SEND THE CONCORDIA ACCESS LETTER. Researched and drafted 2026-08-25 -- the full plan, the named people, the four configuration options, the fee schedule and a ready-to-send draft are at project-docs/concordia-access-plan.md. ADDRESSEE: John Richan, Interim Director and University Archivist (also listed as Digital Archivist), via archives@concordia.ca; five-working-day response target. THE ASK IS FOUR THINGS IN ONE LETTER: (1) P0145/12C01 the 1936 Otoreke mixed-camp evaluation, Box HA2315; (2) 12B02, 12B05 and 12B06, the three Kanawana sub-sub-series with no public page; (3) an object list for 12B (t-shirts, badges, ribbons, pennants, film reels); (4) a REST API key plus the REST API added to endpoint_exceptions -- AtoM's own documented configuration for programmatic access, which leaves the JS challenge in force for ordinary traffic. NEEDS MATT: only he can send it. ADDENDUM 2026-08-25 (p_278): add the AV reproduction request to the same letter. Highest value, in order: P0145-11-0193 'Kamp Kanawana - Interview with Woodsman', 24 Aug 1962; P0145-11-0197 'What is God? / Interview of Kamp Kanawana campers and staff', 1963; P0145-11-0191 'Pathfinder evaluation' (bears on the coeducation open question). AV reproduction is $1.00/minute for scholarly use -- these are cheap.

CONSOLIDATED 2026-08-25 — this letter now carries TEN previously separate asks of the same archive, which is why it sits at rank 1: p_275: READ P145/12C01, the file titled 'Evaluation, recommendations re Camp Otoreke as a mixed [gender] camp. - 1936.' This is now the highest-value unread  | p_279: PURSUE P0145/12B06 'CAMPERS' AND 12B05 'STAFF, COUNSELLORS' -- two Kanawana sub-sub-series that have no mirror page and were unknown to this project u | p_280: THE ARCHIVE HOLDS KANAWANA'S MATERIAL CULTURE (f_2267). P0145/12B's physical description lists 'objects (t-shirts, badges, ribbons, pennants)', film r | p_276: RESOLVE THE ACQ FOUNDING-MEMBER CLAIM (f_2215) using P145/12N04, which holds 'Constitution et reglements-Association des Camps du Quebec. - 1979' and  | p_206: Physically inspect Concordia Box HA1874's itemized camp brochures (1950, 1959, [1960s], 1964, 1965, [1968?], [197-], 1978, 1982, 1983, 1997) -- the mo | p_209: Physically consult Concordia's 'Permanent Camp Committee' minute/correspondence files (1895-96, 1899-1901, 1908, 1911-1926, 1921) -- a newly identifie | p_211: Physically consult Concordia sub-series 12L, Box HA2312, 'Director's report (1908)' -- a single, specific dated record from the middle of the undocume | p_213: Physically consult Concordia P0145/12F Box HA1894 to determine why/when the actual 1979-1982 Kanawana-Weredale operational relationship (a signed leas | p_215: Physically consult Concordia P0145/12A for the Camp Perrot 1958 Camp Committee closure decision and reconcile it against the 1959 Cochrane memo and 19 | p_176: Concordia Archives P0145/12B01 — access 1974-1976 camp director correspondence to identify the anonymous 1974-75 director. Also check 1972 Camping and | ADDENDUM 2026-08-25 (p_270): also request the KANAWANA MANUAL OF OPERATIONS described in Canadian Camping, June 1953 -- likely P0145/12B01 or 12B07. See p_285. | ADDENDUM (p_245): request The Lookout Vol.1 Nos.1 and 2 and any 1994 centennial issue -- only Vol.1 No.3 is digitized. | ADDENDUM 2026-08-25: also folds p_049 (P145/12B07 song sheets 1925/1927 and song books 1941-45 -- now more valuable given the Green Triangle read established the motto is ABSENT from the camp's own paper through the 1930s) and p_210 (Gazette, 18 April 1974 -- the 1,200-acre article behind resolved conflict c_026; the operator's own Newspapers.com access reaches it where automated fetch gets 403). | ADDENDUM 2026-08-25 (p_231/p_288): request the 1900 'Seventh Annual Report of the Current Camp Committee' and the six earlier reports in that series -- the digitized 1900 copy is an image-only scan with no OCR layer, and the title dates the series to 1894. ADDENDUM 2026-09-06 (p_326): a SIXTH request has been added to the drafted letter -- P145/12N04, box HA1888, the item "Annuaire 1979, liste des membres. - 1979", plus that box's "Constitution et reglements" (1979) and "Publications, public relations" (1978-1979). The Annuaire is the Quebec association's own annual members directory; the 1979 volume is the earliest copy of the series located anywhere, no volume of it appears in any digitized collection reachable from here, and if it carries directory detail it gives Kanawana's own entry for a period this project is thin on. The letter's opening line now reads 'six requests' -- it had said 'four' while listing five. ADDENDUM 2026-09-06 (p_288): add a SEVENTH request -- the Current Camp Committee report series. The Seventh Annual Report (10 December 1900) has now been read from the Internet Archive scan and it establishes the series ran annually from 1894. Only two of the series are digitized, both from 1900. ASK FOR: the first through sixth reports, 1894-1899; and the replies to the committee's circular letter of 20 October 1900, which asked every member who had been to camp that year for criticisms and suggestions -- about thirty-five were printed in the report, so the letters themselves may have been kept. Concordia's own finding aid records a Permanent Camp Committee with minutes 1895-1896 and correspondence and financial records 1899-1901 (sub-series 12A), which is the same body the 1900 report is addressed to. Those minutes would also settle whether the Dawson who signed as Secretary is Ralph H. Dawson, author of the 1933 history.

priorities.description: The Green Triangle has a 36-year hole in the digitized run: issues exist for 1932-1940 and 1976-1982, with NOTHING between. The 1947 volume would document the Lumbermen-Voyageurs origin contemporaneously rather than through the 1988 retrospective, and the 1940s-50s issues would attack the 1947-1958 director gap.
priorities.notes: 2026-08-25: all 38 DIGITIZED issues downloaded, verified, read in full and cached at sources/cache/green-triangle/. The 36-year hole is CONFIRMED REAL, not a search artefact: the run is dense 1932-1940 (36 issues), then only 1976-09 and 1982-11-15. What remains is the undigitized 1941-1975 material at Concordia -- which is now part of the p_282 letter rather than a separate web-research task.

priorities.description: OPERATOR ACTION: request three folders from Trent University Archives (archives@trentu.ca, 705-748-1011 x7413; access explicitly unrestricted). (2) OCA fonds 78-006, Series F, Box 24, Folder 25 -- a Kanawana brochure c.1970s, filed among 'Y' camps with Pine Crest. (3) 84-019, Box 1, Folder 10 -- 'YMCA - Montreal'. A brochure typically carries fees, session dates, programme, section names and staff.

priorities.description: HEAR THE 1962 AND 1963 CAMPER RECORDINGS. P0145-11-0193 'Kamp Kanawana - Interview with Woodsman' (24 August 1962) and P0145-11-0197 'What is God? / Interview of Kamp Kanawana campers and staff' (1963) are dated oral recordings of campers and staff from a decade this wiki documents almost entirely through annual reports and brochures. They are the closest thing to oral history that exists for the period, and unlike the operator-interview instrument planned under CLAUDE.md's pending priority, they are CONTEMPORANEOUS rather than recalled. Reproduction is $1.00/minute for scholarly use. Also check whether RMA has already posted them to its YouTube channel, as it did with P0145-09-0066 'Canoe Trips' in February 2026. priorities.description: The 1969 camper drowning: find the name and date. Recorded in the Kanawana annual report as "the tragic drowing of one of our campers this Summer" with no further detail. Quebec coroner records, the Montreal Star and Gazette for summer 1969, and Concordia's physical Kanawana holdings are the routes. Handle with care -- a child's death, family very possibly living. Establish the facts; decide publication separately with the operator.
priorities.notes: 2026-08-25: NOT ESTABLISHED. The 1969 annual report line is the only attestation; a full-text sweep of all 634 corpus documents for 'drow*' found every OTHER drowning in the association's record but nothing further on 1969, and the open web has nothing. Remaining routes are the Gazette/Star for summer 1969, Quebec coroner records, and Concordia's physical holdings. Recommend the operator decide whether to pursue a named identification at all before more effort is spent -- see f_2294.

priorities.description: For the ORAL HISTORY INSTRUMENT (p_045 Chopsy). The documentary record on Chopsy is now EXHAUSTED: zero hits across all 634 digitized text items. But two findings reframe the question. (1) "The Cave" in the legend is a real camp building doing exactly what the story says -- the 1987 report has it as the hike-and-trip equipment store. (2) The Haunted House is documented 1928-1940 with its own ghost legend and its own rule (spirits appear only when the wind is from the east and the moon and stars invisible), and stops just before Chopsy's stated 1945 origin. ASK: is Chopsy a successor to, or renaming of, the Haunted House ghost? Also ask about "the deserted village" the 1933 newsletter has campers passing en route.
Collect oral history on 'Chopsy' legend from Matt Aronson — full narrative, origin period, telling context, location ties, jump-scare elements

priorities.description: Confirm or refute the O. N. H. Owens identification behind the Order of Owens. He is documented in Montreal YMCA camping service 1929-1964 -- Chairman of the Kanawana Committee in 1937-38 (named on the camp's own letterhead beside Director W. J. G. Macdiarmid), Chairman of Camp Perrot's Board of Management through the 1940s-50s. A Library and Archives Canada First World War file exists for "OWENS, OWEN NORREYS HARRINGTON" -- initials match, "Norrey" is the natural short form of Norreys -- but the LAC record returns Cloudflare 403 to automated fetch and needs a human or an authenticated route. Also still unknown: what April 13, 1976 commemorates.
priorities.notes: 2026-08-25: THE INTERNAL IDENTIFICATION IS MADE. Norrey Owens = O. N. H. Owens, established by the Quebec Camping Association presidency which both forms of the name hold (QCA President June 1954; O.N.H. Owens on the January 1976 membership roll; 'Norrey Owens' listed among QCA past presidents March 1977). Service span extended 1929-1977. STILL OPEN and now the whole of the task: (a) the LAC First World War file for 'OWENS, OWEN NORREYS HARRINGTON' -- Cloudflare 403 to automated fetch, needs a human or authenticated route; (b) birth and death dates; (c) what 13 April 1976 commemorates -- the corpus sweep found nothing, and the article already establishes it is NOT a death date since Owens presented the award in person that August.

priorities.description: Commission de toponymie du Quebec: settle the lake name changes. The official toponymic record should give (a) the date and rationale of Lac Saint-Louis -> Lac Kanawana, (b) the same for Lac Desjardins -> Lac Wilson, and (c) whether 'Kanawana' has a documented Indigenous-language etymology or is an invented coinage. Surfaced by the p_263 RALPH loop as the highest-value UNFETCHED geographic source in the project. Made sharper by the MIR reconciliation article, which shows genuine Indigenous names and invented pseudo-Indigenous names are equally common in North American camping -- so the question is real, not rhetorical. Also try the Quebec lake registry / RSVL for real bathymetry, since the only area and shoreline figures currently held are from a commercial chart aggregator that disclaims them. WORKED 2026-09-06 -- PARTIALLY ANSWERED, and the answer is that the province does not know either. Route that worked: the Commission's own search form is an ASP.NET postback and returned nothing to a scripted POST, but its FICHE PAGES ANSWER A DIRECT GET on no_seq (https://toponymie.gouv.qc.ca/ct/ToposWeb/fiche.aspx?no_seq=NNNNN), and the no_seq values come from the open datasets at donneesquebec.ca (Toponymes officiels, Toponymes desofficialises, Noms traditionnels autochtones, CKAN API). THAT ROUTE IS REUSABLE FOR ANY OTHER TOPONYMY QUESTION IN THIS QUEUE. (a) and (b): NOT IN THE OFFICIAL RECORD. The desofficialises register (13,951 rows) carries no trace of Lake St. Louis becoming Lac Kanawana or Lac Desjardins becoming Lac Wilson; both changes predate the Commission's file, and the 1968-12-05 date on both fiches is a bulk registration shared by 26,229 toponyms, not a decision about these lakes (f_4876). A DIFFERENT Lac Saint-Louis, at Morin-Heights, became Lac Franc in 1985 -- a near-miss recorded so a later pass does not seize on it (f_4877). (c): the dataset classes Kanawana as ALGONQUIN in origin, but the fiche says the origin and meaning "n'ont pu etre determinees jusqu'a maintenant" and the name is absent from the province's register of traditional Indigenous names (f_4875, f_4878). NEW: Camp Kanawana is itself an official Quebec toponym, entity class Camp, officialised 1985-11-07 (f_4874). Written into indigenous-names-and-land.md with Open Question 1 narrowed. STILL OPEN: the RSVL / lake-registry bathymetry half of this priority was not attempted. SPAWNED p_422. EXTENDED 2026-09-06: with the toponymic datasets already downloaded, the register was queried for the whole Kanawana district and for Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard. THREE RESULTS. (1) ROUND LAKE IS LAC ROND, 45.84582/-74.20147, officialised 1970-02-27 -- the third of Kanawana's three lakes, carried in this wiki on the camp's own word since the beginning with no coordinate and no official name against it. Lac des Becs-Scie is at 45.84855/-74.20959, a few hundred metres west, which is why it keeps being mistaken for one of them. NO ISLAND is registered in any of the three lakes. (2) THREE OTHER CAMPS are official toponyms within a few kilometres -- Camp Olier and Camp de l'Avenir at Sainte-Anne-des-Lacs, NEITHER OF WHICH APPEARS ANYWHERE ELSE IN THIS PROJECT, and Camp Kinkora in the de-officialised register (form change 1984). Camp Tamaracouta is not registered; only its lake is, and that lake's origin is recorded as Algonquin, the same classification given to Kanawana. (3) CAMP JUBILEE'S ISLANDS ARE NOT ON THE OFFICIAL MAP: Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard has 120 official toponyms and exactly one island, Ile Christie; there is no Corbett anything in the Laurentians; so Rock Island and Corbett Island, named in the 1900 report (f_4883), never entered the register. Facts f_4890-f_4892; written into places-and-locations.md (22 -> 23 sources) and camp-otoreke.md (20 -> 21). NEW LEAD: Camp Olier and Camp de l'Avenir should be assessed for the Quebec camp landscape article.

priorities.description: Unmined seams the annual-report sweep identified but did not attempt: (a) the Kanawana balance-sheet property valuations, present in every report from 1925 (e.g. $17,876.39 in 1925, $55,750.30 in 1949, $70,567.80 in 1951) -- a clean book-value series across eighty years, but the columnar OCR is heavily damaged and each figure needs verification against the page image; (b) the World/Foreign Service contribution tables, which carry a Kanawana line every year 1923-1964 from the campers' Sunday collections; (c) the French editions of the 1982-2009 reports, which were spot-checked as translations but not read independently.

Two cataloguing defects to work around and, if possible, report to Concordia/IA: (1) "sgw-ymca-annual-report-1990-1991" and "-1991-1992" hold 1890-91 and 1891-92 content -- misdated by a century, and the 1890-91 one announces W. H. Ball's hiring; (2) the Kanawana orienteering map catalogued as 1974 is internally c.1978-1982 (it shows Katimavik, the sauna and the Grand Portage). Anyone searching that collection by date will miss or misdate these. WORKED 2026-09-06, and the trap is sharper than this priority describes. FOUR cached files carry 1990 or 1991 in their names and TWO ARE NINETEENTH-CENTURY: sgw-ymca-annual-report-1990-1991.txt is the 1890-91 report (Dominion Square building, W. H. Ball's hiring) and -1991-1992.txt is the 41st Annual Report of 1891-92, while sgw-ymca-annual-report-1990.txt IS genuinely 1990 (chairman Claude Lemay, September 1989) and -1991.txt IS genuinely 1991 (the Berlin Wall), each with a French counterpart. All four sit adjacent in the same directory. NOTE THE INTERNET ARCHIVE'S OWN METADATA IS CORRECT -- title 'YMCA Annual Report 1890-1891', date 1891-05-28 -- and only the IDENTIFIER and the inner _djvu.txt filename are wrong, so a fetch of archive.org/metadata/<id> gives the right year and nothing needs reporting to IA on that count. WHAT DID NEED FIXING WAS OURS: three source records carried dates taken from the identifier rather than the document ('1990', '1991-19-92', '1889-18-90') and all three are corrected in place with a note. Fact f_4901. TWO FINDS FELL OUT OF ACTUALLY READING THE FILE. (1) The 1890-91 report states 'THE VOLUNTEER CAMP WORK WAS SUCCESSFULLY CARRIED OUT UNDER THE [affiliation] AND ASSISTANCE OF MR. PATTON' -- the association's own contemporaneous record of camp work in the year of Patton's 1891 camp, which until now was attested only by his 1919 memoir; and 'EARLY LAST SPRING, OUR LEADER MR. PATTON RESIGNED TO ENTER THE SPRINGFIELD SCHOOL', which independently dates him to Springfield from spring 1891 and so into Naismith's December game (f_4902, into t-duncan-patton.md). (2) A CORBETT LEAD for Corbett Island: D. W. Corbett was assistant secretary in charge of boys' work and 'the main-stay of this work' until he left for Honolulu in June 1893, and he appears beside Patton in the 1890-91 report; recorded as a lead, not an answer, since he left a year before the 1894 camp (f_4903, into camp-otoreke.md). THE ORIENTEERING MAP HALF OF THIS PRIORITY IS NOT TOUCHED. MORE, from reading the SECOND misdated file (the 41st Annual Report, 1891-92). Its staff list gives D. A. BUDGE General Secretary, D. W. CORBETT Assistant Secretary, T. DUNCAN PATTON, W. H. BALL Physical Director; and its 'COMMITTEES OF THE BOARD, 1892-93' puts R. L. CHARLTON on TRAINING CLASSES with all four of them. That answers half of rl-charlton.md's Open Question 2 -- he held a documented formal position in the association in the year the camp syndicate formed -- while NOT establishing a camp role, since Training Classes is not a camp committee. It also changes the standing of his 1943 'Notes re Early Days': he was in the committee rooms in 1892, so he wrote as a participant fifty-one years on rather than as a compiler, which raises it among the Concordia asks (f_4904). And Patton is on that staff list AFTER resigning for Springfield in spring 1891, which his own memoir reconciles -- 'During the vacation period of 1891 I RETURNED TO MONTREAL' -- giving a sequence the documents and the memoir agree on and bearing directly on p_286(b), the overlapping Montreal/Winnipeg ranges (f_4905). BOTH ARTICLES UPDATED. THE READ_STATE OF THIS WHOLE CORPUS IS THE REAL LESSON: the pre-1901 annual reports are marked 'skimmed -- full-text-cached-and-keyword-swept-not-read-closely', and two five-minute reads of two of them produced four facts nobody had. Keyword sweeping does not find what you did not think to search for. AND A CORRECTION TO MY OWN FINDING OF AN HOUR EARLIER. Reading the 1893-94 report turned up a section headed MILITARY CAMP: 'The Association placed a tent with full equipment for reading-room, library, games, etc., in the grounds at LAPRAIRIE IN JUNE LAST. MR. T. DUNCAN PATTON HAD CHARGE... The influence of this work FOR MANY YEARS has been most beneficial upon the whole character of the camp life.' So the association ran a tented operation at a militia camp for years before 1894, Patton had charge of it, and the 1890-91 report's 'Volunteer Camp work... under Mr. Patton' MAY WELL BE THAT rather than boys' camping -- which would also dissolve the oddity of 'successfully carried out' beside a memoir about a camp broken up by a drowning. f_1537 had already recorded that in the 1901 Historical Sketch every 'camp' reference is militia. f_4902 is QUALIFIED in place, not superseded, and t-duncan-patton.md now says the phrase is not decided either way and must not be cited as evidence for boys' camping in 1890-91 (f_4906). ALSO: the 1892-93 report contains NO camp content at all, an explicit null in the year the syndicate formed, consistent with the camp starting as a private syndicate rather than association business (f_4907).

priorities.description: The Gas Bag: the digitized "Extra, Vol. 13 No. 1" implies twelve prior volumes, i.e. roughly 1911-1923 of the camp paper. Only two Gas Bag items are digitized. Locating the earlier run would attack the 1902-1920 director gap, the earliest traditions, and the founding period directly.
priorities.result: Completed 2026-08-14 as a NULL on the main question, with three substantive finds from the two issues that DO exist. NULL: only two Gas Bag items are in the digitized fonds -- 1 September 1923 and the 'Extra, Vol. 13 No. 1' (1923). The numbering implies twelve earlier volumes, c.1911 onward, none digitized. They must be sought in Concordia's physical holdings. FINDS from the Extra: (1) THE M. E. WILLIAMS CUPS, a previously undocumented INTER-BRANCH aquatics and athletics competition at Kanawana with a printed winners roll 1917-1922 -- thirty years older than the L&V trophy, and a different format (branch-versus-branch, not two intra-camp teams); (2) the fee was $8.50/week in 1923, extending the documented fee series back four years and showing it unchanged across at least 1923-1929; (3) R. L. Charlton was still working on camp buildings in 1923, arranging a Senior Log Cabin -- placing him at camp between his 1894 committee membership and his 1943 manuscript.

priorities.result: Completed 2026-08-14 for the annual-report half. An agent swept all 114 sgw-ymca-annual-report files that mention Kanawana (1856-2009) for everything except directors. Headline results: the 1894 founding is documented contemporaneously in the 1894-95 report ("our first Summer Camp... 23 workers and boys"), with a clean negative in the preceding year; "Camp Jubilee" appears in NO pre-1921 report; Kanawana's first season is fixed at 1910 by a forward-tense announcement naming W. J. Holliday; nine names now fill most of the former 1902-1920 directorial gap; the association ran TWO anniversary clocks (1894 camping / 1910 site), which is why the 75th was celebrated twice and why 1993 and 1994 both announce a centennial; a 1940 scarlet fever quarantine of four weeks; the 1932 dry wells; and a full year-by-year attendance series 1894-2005. Null results: no fire, storm destruction or death at camp in any of the 114 reports; the 1969 drowning and 1976 meningitis appear only in the camp's own season reports; Camp Weredale and Camp Ouareau appear nowhere.

priorities.description: EDITORIAL DECISION FOR THE OPERATOR: this wiki calls the 1894-1909 camp "Camp Jubilee" across a dozen articles, as though it were the institution's own name. It is not -- every pre-1921 YMCA of Montreal annual report was searched and none uses it; "Jubilee" appears only in the movement's 1844-1894 golden-jubilee sense. The name may still be authentic to camp usage and comes from somewhere (QAHN, the 1951 in-house history, oral tradition). Decide whether to keep it with an attribution, qualify it, or replace it. Renaming a term used across a dozen articles is an editorial call, not a research finding.
priorities.notes: 2026-08-14: evidence assembled and put to the operator. 'Camp Jubilee' appears in exactly ONE of 634 corpus items - the 1988 retrospective - whose 1894 entry is demonstrably wrong in detail (says three islands were PURCHASED in 1894; the 1894-95 report says LEASED, and the 1902 report dates the island auction to 26 Nov 1901). The association's own contemporaneous name was descriptive ('Summer Camp', 'the Summer Camp at Lake St. Joseph'), and the documented proper name for the original site is CAMP OTOREKE, attested from the 1921-22 report. Awaiting the operator's naming decision. MATERIAL UPDATE 2026-08-14: the name is NOT merely a 1988 retrospective coinage -- CONCORDIA'S ARCHIVAL DESCRIPTION of the fonds itself uses it ('P0145/12L - Lac St-Joseph/Camp Jubilee'; 'Season reports of the Junior Camp (Camp Jubilee/Otoreke)'), as does QAHN. It is the received archival/heritage name for the site, with no attestation in the association's own 1894-1909 records. Note also that the camp's own 1935 and 1951 in-house histories do NOT use it. This materially favours KEEPING the name with an attribution over replacing it, since it is the name a researcher would search the Concordia finding aid with. CLOSED 2026-08-14: operator concurs -- keep the name with the explanation. Canonical note added to history/founding-1894.md ('A note on the name'), with short pointers in wiki/README.md, site/camp-otoreke.md and people/billy-ball.md. No articles renamed.

priorities.description: Build the year-by-year attendance series into the wiki. The annual-report sweep produced camper counts and boy-/camper-weeks for roughly 60 seasons between 1894 and 2005, plus fees ($8.50/week 1927-29), staff counts, swim-test totals and Sunday chapel attendances. This is the camp's size over 110 years and belongs in a table, probably in timeline-overview.md or a new meta article. SIX INTERNAL INCONSISTENCIES must be carried as flags, not smoothed: the 289-boy season is attributed to 1919, 1920 AND 1921 across three reports; 1924 boy-weeks 916 vs 906; 1934 boy-weeks 1,017 vs 972; 1932 campers 360 vs 385; 1965 camper-weeks 1,200 vs 1,182; and the 1930 "increase of 432" does not reconcile with its own series.
priorities.result: Completed 2026-08-14. New article meta/attendance-series.md: ~60 seasons of camper counts and camper-weeks, 1894-2023, in three tables (Lac St. Joseph era, Kanawana 1910-1949, Kanawana 1952-2023). All six internal inconsistencies CARRIED AS FLAGS in the tables and explained in their own section -- every one is the association contradicting itself, not a transcription problem. Kept as a separate article rather than bolted onto timeline-overview.md (a source-less hub) so the flags travel with the numbers. Deliberately computes NO aggregate: too many missing years, the 1998-2001 rows count rentals and off-season use, and the two documented lifetime totals (40,000 in 1964, 34,000 in 1984) contradict each other and the series. Marked draft; NOT VERIFY-passed.

priorities.description: Reconcile the scarlet-fever quarantine date. The wiki had 1941 from McMorris; the YMCA annual report describing it is the 1941 report, whose fiscal year ended 31 March, so on the report's own convention the season is 1940. Both are now recorded in wartime-kanawana.md. Reading McMorris's citation would settle it. NOTE THE GENERAL HAZARD: this is the same one-year offset that had the Council Ring rebuild at 1929 when the work was 1928. Every wiki date derived from a YMCA annual report should be checked against the fiscal convention -- year ending 30 April through the 1926 report, 31 March for 1927-1950, calendar year from 1951.
priorities.result: Completed 2026-08-14. Audited every wiki claim citing a YMCA of Montreal annual report against the fiscal convention. THREE genuine offsets found and fixed, all in greig-macdiarmid.md: the MacKinnon succession dated 15 September 1928 is impossible (the 1928 report's fiscal year ends 31 March 1928) and is corrected to 1927; 'entered the Secretaryship 1926' is corrected to 1925-26; and the 1937 report's Protestant Orphans' Home passage described 'that year's' arrangement, reading as 1937, while camp-becsies.md correctly assigns that report to the 1936 season -- the two articles now agree. CONVENTION REFINED: the April-to-March change happens at the 1926 report, not 1927; the 1926 report covers an ELEVEN-MONTH transitional period. Audited clean: camp-becsies, council-ring, the directors-index pre-1921 rows, and all of w-h-spearman. Two forward-looking passages (the 1910 Kanawana announcement, the 1946 Macdiarmid Toronto move) are correct as written and are flagged so they are not 'corrected' later.

priorities.description: FIND THE KANAWANA MANUAL OF OPERATIONS (f_2286). Canadian Camping of June 1953 describes it in detail -- four sections, a statement of camp objectives, sample hike and canoe-trip menus, a seven-page 'Things a new staff member needs to know about Kanawana', per-position staff duties, and the canoeing/rowing/sailing/swimming tests -- and December 1953 reports Roy Locke 'developing a book on the total camp operation'. NO COPY IS KNOWN TO SURVIVE here. It would be the single best document for 1950s camp operation. Most likely home is Concordia P0145/12B01 (General administration) or 12B07 (Program); ADD IT TO THE p_282 LETTER. Also check whether the CCA fonds at Trent holds a copy, since the article was published nationally.

priorities.description: ADVANCE t-duncan-patton.md draft -> R3-verified. TWO OF THE THREE ORIGINAL QUESTIONS ARE ANSWERED (2026-08-25): the 'T.' is THOMAS, born 15 April 1865 Danville QC, died 1 April 1944 Toronto; and his claim to have captained a side in the first basketball game is independently confirmed by the documented roster and by Library and Archives Canada. WHAT REMAINS: (a) locate Jones' Island and any independent record of the 1891 camp or David Louden's death -- a Montreal newspaper of summer 1891 is the obvious route, and Louden's death may also appear in the Montreal YMCA annual report for 1891-92, which this project holds; (b) resolve the overlapping Montreal/Winnipeg date ranges in the player-exhibit timeline against the memoir; (c) find whether Patton ever wrote or spoke about Kanawana after 1919, given he lived until 1944 and stayed in YMCA work until 1926. WORKED 2026-09-06, half of (a) answered. JONES' ISLAND IS LOCATED: Quebec's toponymic register holds exactly one island of the name -- ILE JONES, no_seq 31476, 45.5199/-74.2924, Saint-Andre-d'Argenteuil, "a l'entree de la baie de Carillon... dans l'estuaire de la riviere des Outaouais" -- about 56 km, thirty-five miles, west-north-west of Montreal against Patton's "about 40 miles north-west of Montreal in the Ottawa River". Recorded as an identification BY GEOGRAPHY AND BY THE UNIQUENESS OF THE NAME, not a document: nothing says the camp was pitched there, and two things are unchecked and named (Ontario's own register was not searched, and whether an unregistered island carried the name locally in 1891). The fiche also gives the island's etymology in full -- Martin Jones (1747-1843), a Loyalist who arrived in 1788 with Hannah Brant (1761-1854) and settled at the southeast end of the seigneurie d'Argenteuil -- citing Benjamin N. Wales, 'Memories of old St. Andrews and historical sketches of the seigniory of Argenteuil' (Watchman Press, Lachute, 1934), which is NOT on the Internet Archive and is the obvious next document. Fact f_4889; written into t-duncan-patton.md (13 -> 14 sources), Open Question 3 marked half answered. DAVID LOUDEN'S DROWNING IS STILL UNRECORDED anywhere but Patton's memoir, and the newspaper route named in this priority is now KNOWN CLOSED from this environment: the Gazette's page images are reachable by date but its full text is not searchable here and body text is illegible at the only zoom the archive serves (f_4886, f_4887). The annual-report route was already exhausted at f_2300. Untried: Quebec's civil death registers for 1891, and the Wales history. (b) and (c) not attempted.

priorities.description: GET THE 1900 'SEVENTH ANNUAL REPORT OF THE CURRENT CAMP COMMITTEE' READ. It is digitized (8 pages, archive.org/details/1900-12-10-seventh-annual-report-of-the-current-camp-committee) but has NO OCR layer, so this project holds a 0-byte file for it. Its title dates the camp-committee report series to 1894 -- the founding year -- and only two such reports are digitized at all, both from 1900. TWO ROUTES: (a) run OCR on the existing IA scan, which needs a tesseract-capable environment this session does not have; (b) ask Concordia for the original, and for the six earlier reports in the series, which are not online. ADD TO THE p_282 LETTER. DONE 2026-09-06. Route (a) was never needed and route (b) is only half needed. The item has no OCR layer because THE DOCUMENT IS CURSIVE MANUSCRIPT, not because the scan failed -- no OCR engine was going to read it. The jp2 zip was downloaded from archive.org, the eight page images converted to greyscale and READ BY EYE, and a full transcript written to sources/cache/ymca-montreal-fonds/1900-12-10-seventh-annual-report-current-camp-committee.txt. Leaves 3, 4, 6 and 8 of the scan are inverted 180 degrees. THIS METHOD IS REUSABLE for every other image-only manuscript in the ymca-montreal-fonds collection, and there are others. WHAT IT SAYS: three 1900 parties at LAC ST. JOSEPH (not Kanawana), including a four-day 24 May party of twenty-four senior Association men with the President, Treasurer and four Directors; a fall party of twelve, 21-26 September; the Annual Regatta and eleven prizes at the Ste Agathe Regatta; a dated camper survey of 20 October 1900 with about thirty-five suggestions printed verbatim; and the physical camp named feature by feature -- Rock Island, Corbett Island, High Bluff, Diving Rock, the Rapids, a Lumbermen's Shanty, an unnamed camp island. The attendance figure was LEFT BLANK by the writer. Signed Frank [L.] Benedict, Chairman, and a Dawson, Secretary -- the same two surnames as the 1898 Camp Jubilee photograph, though the Dawson monogram cannot be resolved from this scan. Bergeron and Bergin both appear, independently corroborating the heritage-tour account already in camp-otoreke.md. Facts f_4879-f_4884; f_2322 superseded in place. Written into camp-otoreke.md (18 -> 19 sources, two new open questions). STILL FOR CONCORDIA, added to p_282: the six earlier reports in the series (1894-1899) and the replies to the 20 October 1900 circular.

The 2008 LIT to 2009 JC count came back SIX against the priority's seven, and the priority was right: the index had split Justin Pulfer in two, "Justin 'JT' Pulfer" on the 2008 board and "Justin J. Pulfer" on the 2009 one, because shape() strips a quoted nickname and keeps a middle initial. Merged in scripts/plaque/build_index.py with the reasoning in a comment; both generated files regenerated by their builders; distinct names 1,475 to 1,474 and traced people 160 to 161, progressions unchanged at 69 since LIT to JC is a step between two junior rungs. multi-year-index.md updated in three places and its correction history extended with the seventh split. The priority's other two examples, the Tasses and Lindsay Kertland, are individual careers rather than cohorts and are already carried by multi-year-index.md and f_2357. NO NEW NAMES ARE PRINTED: the section counts cohorts and points at the existing indexes, which keeps it inside the C5 constraint recorded in this article's own research note. Fact f_4932. METHOD WORTH KEEPING: the KB tested the index rather than only consuming it, and that is how the split was found.

priorities.description: Audit the 150-row multi-year index for hidden duplicates and hidden pairs. The merge rules are deliberately conservative: identical normalised forms plus a curated alias list only. That will have SPLIT some people in two (spelling drift across boards) and may have MERGED two people who share a common name. Check the rows with common given-plus-surname combinations first, and check anyone whose trajectory shows an implausible jump.
priorities.notes: Spawned by p_292. The risk runs both ways and neither direction is safe to assume away. STARTED 2026-08-28: three errors already found on the first close reading of the index output -- Ariel McGeary / Ariel McGeary Hall were one person split across two rows (counts fell 150->149 traced, 44->43 progressions), and 'Sally Waff' / 'Matt Iviott' were displaying plaque misreadings this project had already resolved elsewhere. A PREFERRED display map was added to build_index.py for cases where the plaques disagree and one reading is settled. THE REMAINING RISK RUNS TOWARD SPLITTING, not merging: the rules are conservative, so the true traced count is likely a little below 149 and the true progression count a little above 43. ADVANCED 2026-08-28: two systematic splits found and fixed (staff-column keys f_2335; Knights Sir/Lady titles f_2355). 30 probable same-person pairs remain as CANDIDATES needing human judgement -- NOT to be auto-merged; the matcher wrongly paired David/Dave Paltiel, a merge this project had already declined on reasoning, and collapsed Elissa with Melissa Sukosd, who are more likely sisters. | ADVANCED 2026-09-02. The candidate list is now GENERATED with evidence (scripts/plaque/candidate_pairs.py -> kb/plaque-audit/candidate-pairs.json), not held in a session. 39 pairs; three mechanical tests reduce the ones needing a person to 33, and name the six that have evidence. Chasing them turned up f_2369: 16 of 78 curated alias entries could never match, so three pairs on the list had ALREADY been decided. Remaining work is genuinely operator-dependent.

priorities.description: Confirm or rule out the fourteen sibling-shaped pairs recorded as observations in f_2341 (Rotman, Bracken, Anders, Brzezinski, Azofra, Shatani, Lerikos, Braide, Gillett, Fincham, Burman, Snabl and others). Only the Bollhorns and Pungartniks are confirmed. Operator or alumni knowledge is the realistic route; do not assert a family relationship from a shared surname.
priorities.notes: Spawned by p_292. ADVANCED 2026-08-28: surname clustering across all 1,483 indexed names produced a tiered candidate list (f_2354) -- 3 confirmed, 27 strong (same board or same year), 63 plausible, 73 weak. The strong tier is the one worth putting to alumni.

priorities.description: Two site questions raised by the plaque vocabulary and answerable only by someone who was there: (1) What was THE SANCTUM, and what happened to it in 2007? A single Senior Boys board records both its name and its epitaph, 'May the Sanctum R.I.P.' (2) Where was THE SUEZ BRIDGE, named on a 1987 board, and does it survive? The Knights charter's fifth challenge asks candidates to contribute 'a substantial part of a totem pole, or a bridge', so camper-built named bridges are plausible. Also: who was RAKU (f_2349), and were there other camp animals?
priorities.notes: Spawned by p_295/p_296. Operator or alumni knowledge; no documentary route identified. RESOLVED 2026-08-28 by operator, all three: THE SANCTUM was the Senior Boys section cabin, mid-1990s to its 2007 demolition -- which explains the epitaph on the board that names its last occupants, and is an architectural exception since Senior sections are otherwise platform tents. THE SUEZ BRIDGE crosses the narrow channel between Lake Kanawana and Lake Wilson, the same point as the dam that is ceremonially opened each season and the route of the 1998 5 km swim. RAKU was Director Joanna A.A. Hoad dog, which CONFIRMS the inference drawn from the boards bone shape and paw print (f_2349) and dates to her first season as on-site Director.

priorities.description: Add an INTERNAL-CONSISTENCY check to scripts/verify/verify_harness.py. Three of the four live defects found by p_227 were a claim in prose disagreeing with a table in the SAME FILE -- a year listed as open in a summary that the article's own table fills, a count asserted in text that the rows beneath it do not support, a title given twice with different values. A citation checker cannot catch these because both halves are properly cited. Start with the two mechanical cases: (a) a stated count against the number of table rows it refers to, (b) a year or year-range asserted as a gap that a table row in the same file covers.
priorities.notes: Spawned by p_227. This is the gap that let ten defects sit inside top-status articles until draft articles inherited them. | 2026-09-02: PARTLY SUPERSEDED IN ONE DIRECTION. The VERIFY pass on the six plaque articles added the wide versions of checks A1 and G (duplicate/skipped source NUMBERS) to the harness, and widened them to ALL statuses -- that is the second mechanical case above, done. The (a) case, a stated count against the data behind it, is still open and is now the highest-value one: it was the ENTIRE defect class in that pass (see f_2360). The counts to check are not table rows but numbers computed from kb/plaque-audit/person-index.json, so the check likely wants a small registry of 'this number in this article comes from this expression' rather than a general parser. | COMPLETED 2026-09-02. scripts/verify/consistency.py: 7 DERIVED rules plus a general TABLE check, both verified by reintroducing the real defects and watching them fire. See f_2368.

priorities.description: Clear the backlog the widened harness checks just exposed. Twelve articles have a '*Sources: N*' header that disagrees with the number of entries beneath it, SEVEN of them at E1-reviewed or R3-verified: a-ross-seaman (7 vs 9), camp-otoreke (16 vs 18), indigenous-names-and-land (12 vs 14), kanawana-in-media (19 vs 20), lv-games (9 vs 10), notable-alumni (40 vs 42), plus the drafts geoff-anderson, james-h-turner, leo-robitaille, order-of-owens, roy-locke and t-duncan-patton (whose header is HIGHER than its entry count, a different and worse shape). Four more skip source numbers entirely: council-ring and lv-games have Sources sections that mix a bullet list with numbered entries starting at 8, da-budge starts at 5, billy-ball skips 8. Fix the numbering, then the headers, then re-run.
priorities.notes: Every one of these predates 2026-09-02 and none was visible while checks A1 and G ran on drafts only. The direction of the error is the tell: eleven of twelve headers are LOW, i.e. sources were appended to finished articles and the header was never touched -- which is exactly the life-cycle stage the draft-only scope could not see. See f_2365. | COMPLETED 2026-09-02. All sixteen articles fixed; every whole-wiki check now reports zero. Four shapes, recorded at f_2366 -- header drift, entries stranded below the '## Research Notes' heading, bullets mixed with numbers, and orphan label markers. Tool written: scripts/verify/renumber_sources.py (dry-run by default).

priorities.description: Merge the duplicate SOURCE RECORDS in sources.json. One QAHN article on the YMCA camp at Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard is held under three ids (src_qahn_howard, src_qahn_ymca_camp, src_qahn_ymca_camp_saint_adolphe) -- see f_2367. Check K separately reports twenty source_ids each held by more than one RECORD, including src_flickr_kanawana x6 and src_cca_history x3. Both directions break the same thing: a [src_] citation stops naming one object. Pick a canonical id per source, repoint facts and articles, and delete the rest. NOTE 2026-09-06 (p_220): three of that campaign's remaps had to pick between duplicate twins holding the same URL -- src_westmount_mag_mclean vs src_westmountmag_mclean, src_ymca_pip_sharpe vs src_ymca_pip_sharpe_2018, src_youtube_kanawana_silent vs src_youtube_kanawana_1960s_silent_film. Which way each went is recorded in project-docs/source-id-remap-2026-09-06.md, so this cleanup should fold the losing twin into the winner rather than the other way round. The duplicate count is unchanged at 20.
priorities.notes: Spawned by p_302. The QAHN case was found only because a FOURTH id, src_qahn_kanawana, was cited by an article and existed nowhere -- check D caught the phantom and the triple turned up while resolving it.

priorities.description: RE-READ EVERY SOURCE WHOSE read_state_basis IS 'derived:cited-by-fact'. The 1951 Kamp Kanawana History was marked extracted on that basis, with no cached text, and nine facts quoted it. Reading it end to end on 2026-09-02 produced four new facts, one correction, and the answer to an Open Question rated CRITICAL in lake-wilson.md -- an article that named two archive-only documents as 'the most likely sources' while the answer sat in this one. 'Extracted' means somebody took what they went looking for; it does not mean anyone read the document. Work the list in order of how many articles depend on the source, cache the full text every time, and record read_state_basis 'direct'.
priorities.notes: See f_2376. The verify harness's provenance pass (check H) already counts read_state values -- it can produce the worklist. Note that 724 sources currently read 'extracted'; the subset with basis 'derived:cited-by-fact' AND no cache_path is the priority. | MEASURED 2026-09-02: 616 of 1,310 source records -- 47% -- are marked read only because a fact cites them and hold no cached text. That is the size of the exposure, not an estimate. | RESCOPED 2026-09-02 after measuring the cache. No fresh OCR is needed for most of the corpus: 40.3 MB of OCR'd text was already on disk. But 300 of 904 cached files belonged to NO source record -- 25.8 MB, ~6.5M tokens, including 164 issues of Canadian Camping Magazine 1949-1988 against 18 records for the run. 251 non-duplicate files are now catalogued with read_state 'unread' (scripts/reread/catalog_orphans.py). The queue is 1,447 documents: 857 with cached text, 537 URL-only, 53 with neither. See f_2382, f_2383.

priorities.description: OPERATOR ACTION, Concordia Archives -- three item requests surfaced by the re-read, in priority order. (1) 'Kamp Kanawana: Report of First Year of Camp, 1910' (P0145/12B01): the camp's own report on its first season at Saint-Sauveur. (2) The SIX MICROFICHES 'Junior Camp Opening Roster, 1924-1939' (P0145/12B01): sixteen consecutive years of camper names, by far the largest body of named people in the archive and the obvious complement to the plaque index, which holds almost nothing before 1956. (3) 'Winter ski camp records, 1945-1947' (P0145/12B07), which contradict this wiki's 'summer-only until the 1970s' framing -- see f_2379. Fold into the existing Concordia access letter (p_282) rather than sending separately.
priorities.notes: From the first hours of the p_304 full re-read. All three are item TITLES the finding aid gives plainly; none had ever been recorded here. See f_2380.

priorities.description: OPERATOR DECISION: the repository is PUBLIC, and sources/cache/ is committed to it. That corpus includes the raw OCR of internal camp documents -- among them the 1973 director's report whose Recommendations section names five seasonal staff with negative personal assessments (registered as r_0001). This was committed in an earlier session, not by the p_304 re-read, and it is in git history, so removal means rewriting history and force-pushing, not a delete commit. THREE OPTIONS, all the operator's call: (a) leave it -- the same documents are already public on Internet Archive and the indexed layer is clean, which is where the harm would be; (b) remove sources/cache/ from the repo and history, keeping it locally and in Drive, which costs the reproducibility of every cached citation; (c) make the repository private, which protects the corpus but also takes the wiki off the open web. Recommend (a) plus a note in the repo README explaining what sources/cache/ is, unless the wiki is intended to be a published site, in which case revisit.
priorities.notes: Raised while building the restricted register at the operator's request. The register itself is content-free and safe to publish; this priority is about the raw corpus underneath it, which predates the register. | RESOLVED 2026-09-03 by operator decision: option (a), leave it. 'The archive itself is publicly accessible, having the names in a public git is fine. It's pushing them to an unrestricted section of the wiki when the wiki goes up that is questionable.' The design was rebuilt around this: restricted material is now HELD in kb/facts.json with a publication block and gated at the wiki boundary, rather than kept out of the KB altogether.

priorities.description:
Retrospective sweep for material withheld before the register existed. The p_304 re-read passed over sensitive passages in at least one document before kb/restricted/register.jsonl was created, and the earlier plaque audit and Phase 2 research passes almost certainly did the same without recording it. Re-check the reading ledger (kb/reread/ledger.jsonl) and the research log for anything marked withheld, omitted or 'not extracted', and register each one. Going forward every withholding gets a register entry at the moment it is made.

CONTEXT ESTABLISHED (extraction pass, issues 115-116). The full documentary cycle a 1970s Canadian camp staff record sat inside is now described in the association's own pages, which is the context the embargo policy asks for around r_0001. Barry Lowes, Director of Camp Timberlane and a CCA Task Force member, October 1977: unit or section heads evaluate all staff; a formal sit-down at the end of the first few days; a counsellor self-evaluation at mid-summer on the same form the unit head will use; a final evaluation at the end; and the directors 'collate all of these reports. From them develop lists of repairs, items to be purchased, staff to be rehired, programs to change.' The December 1977 newsletter adds the front end: a STAFF INTERVIEW EVALUATION chart rated one to ten on Appearance, Composure, Maturity, Self-Confidence, Frankness, Leadership Potential and Experience with Children, with the autobiography kept on file. So Robitaille's rehire list is the last step of a nationally recommended procedure, written four years before Lowes set it out. Lowes also states the safeguards that were supposed to come with it -- 'You must be sure to let staff know who will have access to the evaluations. Confidentiality is vital!' and that a subject has 'a right to discuss the report with the person doing them. It is a basic human right and also a sound evaluation technique.' Nothing in the Kanawana document shows whether the people named were ever told.
priorities.notes: The point of the register is that a later pass can see what an earlier one decided not to write down. Entries created retrospectively are worth less than entries created at the time, but they are worth more than nothing.

priorities.description: WIKI UI: decide how embargoed passages are surfaced. The data layer is settled -- embargoed material is held in full in kb/facts.json and written into articles inside <!-- embargo:r_NNNN --> blocks, with kb/restricted/register.jsonl giving the kind, basis and review date for each. What is NOT decided, and should be decided once at the UI layer rather than repeatedly at the collection layer, is what a published edition does with a block: redact the names and keep the passage, replace it with a placeholder naming the register entry and review date, gate it behind a login for researchers, or publish it because the embargo has lapsed. Whichever is chosen, the builder should read the register rather than hard-code dates, so that an embargo lapsing changes the site without changing the articles.
priorities.notes: Reframed 2026-09-03 from a build hook to a design decision, per the operator: 'We need to make surface publication policy decisions at the wiki UI design level, not here.' scripts/build-content.ts is still the boilerplate scaffold it shipped as and is not pointed at wiki/; whatever policy is chosen gets implemented there.

priorities.description: Formal RALPH cycle on derek-walsh (spawned 2026-09-04 as a stub from the Canadian Camping run). He directed Kanawana 1974-Feb 1979 while serving as CCA Vice-President 1974-1981 and president of the QCA's English section, wrote the association's promotion pamphlet in both languages, and ran its magazine feasibility study -- and none of it is in any Kanawana record. Needed: birth/death, education, occupation outside camping, and above all where he went after February 1979 (a Derek Walsh appears at Camp Thunderbird, Victoria B.C. in May 1979, but the CCA calls him 'of Montreal' in December 1980; see f_2470). Search obituaries, the Gazette via Google Books, CCA and OCA records, and Camp Thunderbird BC directly.
priorities.notes: Enters at stub on the Part 5 precedent: clears the structural draft bar, has had no RALPH cycle.

priorities.description: Sampling read of whole Canadian Camping issues, to test what the term list missed. The p_304 pass indexed all 164 issues mechanically and read 664 extracted passages, but the extraction is a term list, and a term list finds only what someone thought to look for -- the failure mode of f_2335 and f_2378. Read six to ten complete issues chosen across the run (early 1950s, mid 1960s, mid 1970s, late 1980s) and record whether anything relevant appears that the terms did not catch. If the sample is clean, the extraction method is validated for the rest of the corpus; if it is not, the term list needs widening and re-running.
priorities.notes: This is the honest complement to a method that traded completeness for tractability, and it is what makes that trade checkable rather than merely asserted.

priorities.description:
The 1972 CCA national songbook. In Fall 1972 Canadian Camping asked every camp in Canada to send in 'the words and list the tune of your camp song so that it can be shared across Canada' for a songbook to be made available to all camps (issue 96 of the word-for-word read). Kanawana was an accredited Quebec camp and a member camp; if it replied, the words AND the tune of a Kanawana camp song were recorded in 1972 -- in the window between the 1941-1945 song books and the modern Marching Song, and the only likely source outside Concordia for a tune attribution. TWO ACTIONS: (1) read forward through the 1973-1976 issues of this run for any announcement, contents list or advertisement for the songbook, and note it in the findings file when found; (2) search externally for a published Canadian Camping Association songbook of the 1970s (Internet Archive, Library and Archives Canada, WorldCat, AbeBooks, Trent University Archives). A SECOND, REAL CANADIAN CAMP SONGBOOK EXISTS AND IS DATED (added 2026-09-04, issue 123). Paul Potter's report on the Nova Scotia Camping Association's 1978 summer project: 'May and June also saw the development of a song book. Although some camps had been working on their own song book, none was large enough to hold all of the songs from every camp. Therefore a PROVINCIAL SONG BOOK WITH MORE THAN FIVE HUNDRED SONGS was published. Since its publication, the book has been in constant demand and may soon require a second printing. The cost is $3.00 and it is available from: Nova Scotia Camping Association, Box 696, Halifax, Nova Scotia B3J 3H5.' This is a findable object: a 1978 provincial camp songbook of 500+ songs, compiled from the repertoires of many camps, published by a CCA member association. Even though it is Nova Scotian rather than Quebec, the Canadian camp song repertoire is largely shared, and a 500-song collection is the best available comparator for identifying which Kanawana songs are house compositions and which are movement-wide. WHERE TO LOOK: the Nova Scotia Camping Association's successor body; Nova Scotia provincial and university libraries; Library and Archives Canada; and Trent (p_312), which collected member-association publications. Note also that the CCA president reported in December 1978 that the NSCA planned to 'put to music' the songbook it had produced. A THIRD SONGBOOK, WITH MUSIC (added 2026-09-04, issue 131): 'Sing with Jack', the first Camp Tawingo Publication, announced in May 1980 -- 'the words and music to 37 favorite camp songs, plus notes for actions by the leader', $4.00 through the CCA Publications Service, by Jack Pearse, then immediate past president of the CCA. Two sequels were announced: 'Campfire Programs with Jack Pearse' and 'Sing (One More Time) with Jack Pearse'. Unlike the Nova Scotia collection this one carries MUSIC as well as words, which makes it the better comparator for identifying tunes. Camp Tawingo still operates, so its own publications office is the first place to ask. BOTH SONGBOOKS NOW HAVE FULL CATALOGUE ENTRIES (added 2026-09-04, issue 134). The CCA's own bilingual publications catalogue of December 1980 lists them: (1) '*COME ON ... LET'S SING* -- Nova Scotia Camping Association, 156p, 1979, $3.75. Words to 583 favorite camp songs compiled by the N.S.C.A.' -- a title, publisher, year, page count, price and song count for the provincial collection first reported at issue 123, and 583 songs rather than the 'more than five hundred' of the original notice. Search library catalogues for 'Come On Let's Sing' with the NSCA as author. (2) '*SING WITH JACK PEARSE* -- J. Pearse, 37p, Camp Tawingo Publications, 1980, $4.00. 31 songs with music, delightfully illustrated, many actions included' -- so 37 PAGES and 31 SONGS, correcting the May 1980 announcement's '37 songs'. A sequel, 'Sing (One More Time) with Jack Pearse', was due early 1981. Also in the catalogue: 'Sing!', ed. ACA Publications Committee, 95p, World Around Songs, revised 1978, words and music; 'Tent and Trail Songs', 80p, World Around Songs, 1966, 116 songs to supplement Sing!; and J. Tobitt's 'A Counselor's Guide to Camp Singing', ACA 1971. Between them these five books are the printed repertoire a Canadian camp of 1980 could buy, and the comparison set for deciding which Kanawana songs are house compositions.

AMENDMENT (extraction pass, issue 123): A REAL CANADIAN CAMP SONGBOOK EXISTS, DATED AND ADDRESSED. Paul Potter's report on the Nova Scotia Camping Association's 1978 summer project: 'a provincial song book with more than five hundred songs was published. Since its publication, the book has been in constant demand and may soon require a second printing. The cost is $3.00 and it is available from: Nova Scotia Camping Association, Box 696, Halifax, Nova Scotia B3J 3H5.' Five hundred songs compiled from the repertoires of every camp in a province. It is Nova Scotian rather than Quebec, but the Canadian camp song repertoire is largely shared, and a collection that size is the best available instrument for deciding which Kanawana songs are house compositions and which are movement-wide -- the question traditions/camp-songs-cheers.md cannot currently answer. Ask the NSCA's successor body, Nova Scotian public and university libraries, LAC and Trent. Two related items from the same years: the CCA's Skill School Project planned a national SONGLEADING instructors' school for 1979, and Tolbitt's Counsellor's Guide to Camp Singing (44 pp.) was in the CCA catalogue from 1975.

THE NOVA SCOTIA BOOK NOW HAS A TITLE (extraction pass, issue 134). The CCA's December 1980 catalogue lists it: 'COME ON ... LET'S SING -- Nova Scotia Camping Association, 156p, 1979, $3.75. Words to 583 favorite camp songs compiled by the N.S.C.A.' Searchable in library catalogues by that title. The same catalogue corrects the Tawingo book: 'SING WITH JACK PEARSE -- J. Pearse, 37p, Camp Tawingo Publications, 1980 -- 31 songs WITH MUSIC.' Words only in the Nova Scotia book, tunes in the Tawingo one, so both are wanted for different reasons. The full 1980 printed repertoire also includes Sing! (ACA/World Around Songs, revised 1978, words and music), Tent and Trail Songs (116 songs, 1966) and Tobitt's A Counselor's Guide to Camp Singing.
priorities.notes: Feeds p_045-adjacent song threads and p_048 directly. Source: Canadian Camping Vol. 25 No. 1 (Fall 1972), p. 3. Nova Scotia songbook recorded at issue 123 (Canadian Camping Vol. 31 No. 1, February 1979, p. 6) and issue 122.

priorities.description:
[ANSWERED 2026-09-04 -- destination confirmed as TRENT, superseding the earlier Waterloo note] Locate the C.C.A. Archives. The Fall 1972 notice asked every camp director to send the CCA office 'two copies of your camp brochure -- they are needed for the C.C.A. Archives and for display at the February Conference at Geneva Park.' The Summer 1973 issue reported that a new ARCHIVES committee was to gather material 'to be housed at THE UNIVERSITY OF WATERLOO' -- but that was the 1973 plan, not the outcome. Adele Ebbs, chairman of the CCA Archives Committee, writing in October 1976: 'In 1967 official collecting and sorting of camping records was started by a small group... We have been fortunate in finding a home for our Canadian Camping Archives at Trent University in Peterborough. Their Department of Canadian Studies is very supportive of our efforts... Such national papers belong at Trent.' Material was to be sent to 'Mr Kenneth Johnson, Archivist, Trent University, Peterborough, Ontario K9J 7B8', with the CCA paying delivery costs. The founding deposit was F.M. Van Wagner's own papers ('The first and very valuable contribution of papers came from F.M. Van Wagner who was C.C.A. President 1958-60'). The Archives Committee was constituted with a representative from each provincial association. NEXT ACTION: query Trent University Archives for the Canadian Camping Association fonds and for camp brochures collected from member camps in the 1970s -- a Kanawana brochure of the early 1970s is exactly the kind of item the 1972 solicitation was designed to collect. Trent already holds the OCA deposit (22 October 1970) and the Mary S. Edgar fonds, so one enquiry covers three collections. RESIDUAL CHECK ONLY: ask Waterloo Special Collections whether a first tranche was deposited there in 1973-75 and never transferred. ALSO ASK TRENT FOR (added 2026-09-04, issue 111): Sharon Brown's CCA bibliography of 'all books, catalogues, papers, magazines etc. which would be of any interest to anyone in the camping and related fields', announced in February 1977 as due mid-April 1977. If it survives it is a finding aid for the whole field, compiled by the association whose archive is at Trent. Ask also for the CCA Publications Committee records of Punch Jackson's book service of the same period. TWO NAMED CONFERENCE REPORTS TO ASK FOR (added 2026-09-04, issue 124): the CCA stated in March 1979 that 'the content of each Conference is gathered together and each of these reports may be obtained through the Publications Committee at the National Office', naming the FRENCH LANGUAGE CAMPING CONFERENCE (1976) -- the first in Canada, chaired by Abbe Paul Belanger at the Montmorency Forest -- and the OUTDOOR EDUCATION CONFERENCE (1974). Both were purchasable documents in 1979 and are exactly the sort of association publication the archive collected. Ask also for the Woodsmanship Instructor's Manual (bilingual, in preparation 1979) and the reports of the Geneva Park national conferences. NOTE the Archives chairmanship passed from Adele Ebbs to HELEN STEWART by March 1979 -- a second name to cite when writing to Trent. PROVENANCE NOTE (added 2026-09-04, issue 131): the scanned copies this project is reading came from Trent itself. The mailing label on the back page of the May 1980 issue reads 'Trent University, Archives Dept., Peterborough, Attention: K. Johnson' -- the archivist Adele Ebbs named in 1976. The Internet Archive run of Canadian Camping is Trent's own deposit copy, which both corroborates the Trent story and means the association's other publications very likely went to the same address by the same route.

AMENDMENT (extraction pass, issue 109): THE ARCHIVIST IS NAMED. Adele Ebbs gives the address to write to -- 'Mr Kenneth Johnson, Archivist, Trent University, Peterborough, Ontario K9J 7B8' -- says the Canadian Camping Archives Committee was established in 1975 with representatives from each province, dates the start of official collecting to 1967, and states that 'The Archives at Trent are National'. The founding deposit was F. M. Van Wagner's papers (see p_317).

TWO MORE ITEMS FOR THE SAME ENQUIRY (extraction pass, issues 111 and 113). (a) Sharon Brown was compiling for the CCA, due mid-April 1977, 'a complete bibliography of all books, catalogues, papers, magazines etc. which would be of any interest to anyone in the camping and related fields' -- a finding aid for this whole field if it survives. (b) The 1977 Task Force report on the CCA's future, chaired by John Latimer, was distributed so that 'the full report along with all of the background material is available in every Provincial Association office,' which means a copy went to the Quebec office. Ask Trent for both by name.

THREE MORE NAMED PUBLICATIONS FOR THE SAME ENQUIRY (extraction pass, issues 124 and 127). (a) The reports of the FRENCH LANGUAGE CAMPING CONFERENCE (1976) and the OUTDOOR EDUCATION CONFERENCE (1974), which the March 1979 issue says 'may be obtained through the Publications Committee at the National Office' -- the 1976 one being the first French-language camping conference in Canada. (b) Kirk Wipper's WOODSMANSHIP LEADERS' GUIDE (CCA, 1979, 155 pp., $6.00, loose-leaf), translated into French by Rosaire Corbin. Also note that ARCHIVES passed from Adele Ebbs to HELEN STEWART for 1978-79, so Stewart is a second name to ask Trent about.

PROVENANCE NOTE (extraction pass, issue 131): THE SCANS THIS PROJECT READS CAME FROM TRENT. The mailing label on the back page of Vol. 32 No. 3 (May 1980) reads 'Trent University, Archives Dept., Peterborough, Attention: K. Johnson' -- the archivist Adele Ebbs named in October 1976. The Internet Archive run of Canadian Camping is Trent's own deposit copy, addressed to the man who received the Canadian Camping Archives. That corroborates the Trent story from the physical object, and means the association's OTHER publications very likely reached the same address by the same route -- the conference reports, the Woodsmanship Leaders' Guide, the tabulated tripping survey, the songbooks. Ask for the whole accession, not for titles one at a time.
priorities.notes: Sources: Canadian Camping Vol. 25 No. 1 (Fall 1972), p. 3; Vol. 25 No. 4 (Summer 1973), p. 2; Adele Ebbs, 'Canadian Camping Archives', Canadian Camping Vol. 28 No. 4 (October 1976). Found by the word-for-word read, issues 96, 99 and 109. The Waterloo destination recorded at issue 99 was superseded by the Trent statement at issue 109; block 99 of cc_findings.md has been patched in place to say so.

priorities.description: Jack Pearse's national camping history committee, 1972. Canadian Camping Fall 1972 reports that 'Jack Pearse is working on the establishment of a committee to investigate ways and means of gathering together material which can be compiled into a master document on the history of the camping movement in Canada.' Whatever that committee produced -- or failed to produce -- is the natural place for a national account in which Kanawana, as one of the oldest camps in Canada, would appear. Track it forward through the run, then search externally for any resulting publication.
priorities.notes: Source: Canadian Camping Vol. 25 No. 1 (Fall 1972), 'Have You Heard? Do You Know?', p. 13.

priorities.description: THE ANNUAL QUEBEC ACCREDITATION REPORTS ON KANAWANA. John Hasell, chairman of the CCA National Standards Committee, states in the January 1975 Directory Issue that 'some provinces requir[e] a visit every two or three years, but Quebec has developed its programme to the point where every camp is re-accredited annually' -- printed in both languages. Kanawana was an accredited Quebec camp; Alta Kahn dates Quebec accreditation to the pioneer years of 1959-60. So what is missing is not one report but A SERIES: an annual, itemised, externally written assessment of Kanawana's administration, personnel practices, site, programme, health and safety, running from about 1960. Hasell lists what each visitation examined; Madelene Allen of Camp Ouareau (issue 101) describes a visitation in practice, including a written MARKING SCHEME. WHERE TO ASK, in order: (1) the QCA English Section's own Archives -- the same directory names Mr. Joseph A. Hood as Archives committee chairman in 1975; (2) the successor body, the Association des camps du Quebec, at its Montreal office; (3) Concordia's YMCA of Montreal fonds, since the camp would have kept its own copies; (4) BAnQ, for a body incorporated under Quebec law. ASK TRENT FIRST (added 2026-09-04, issue 118). The project already knows of a QUEBEC CAMPING ASSOCIATION FONDS AT TRENT UNIVERSITY, 85-013, covering 1948-1982 -- cited as source 23 of connections/related-camps/quebec-camp-landscape.md and never queried for accreditation records. That date range covers the entire accreditation era this priority is about, and Adele Ebbs confirms Trent is where the national and provincial camping papers were being gathered (p_312). The word-for-word read has since shown exactly what that fonds should contain: the QCA English Section executive met monthly at the MONTREAL YMCA (13 February, 13 March, 10 April, 8 May, 12 June 1978), held general meetings, an annual conference, a Counsellor Conference and a STANDARDS MEETING (7 June 1978), and the joint ACQ-QCA Provincial Council met separately. Minutes of the QCA Standards Committee are the specific target. NOTE ALSO a corroborating detail from Eanswythe Flynn's May 1978 director's checklist -- 'Find out from your provincial camping association whether or not THIS IS YOUR YEAR for a Standards Visitation' -- which is written for an Ontario readership on a multi-year cycle and independently confirms that Quebec's annual re-accreditation was exceptional, not the norm. ONE MORE ACQ DOCUMENT TO ASK FOR (added 2026-09-04, issue 129): the ACQ's 'formateurs-multiplicateurs' Director Education Program, prepared February 1976 and serialised in Canadian Camping from February 1980, refers to a standard interview sheet -- 'un formulaire est necessaire pour obtenir les renseignements utiles... (cf. feuille A.C.Q.)'. A provincial association's own staff-selection form, dated to the exact period of Kanawana's thinnest records, and issued to its member camps. Ask the ACQ successor body and Trent for the programme and the form together.
priorities.notes: Sources: Canadian Camping Vol. 27 No. 2 (January 1975), Hasell 'Standards for Camps' pp. 20-21 and QCA English Section officer list; Vol. 26 No. 1 (Fall 1973) for Kahn; Vol. 26 No. 2 (Winter/Spring 1974) for Allen. Word-for-word read, issues 100, 101, 103. Extended at issue 118 (Canadian Camping Vol. 30 No. 2, April 1978) and issue 117 (Vol. 30 No. 1, February 1978, the 1978 calendar). The Trent QCA fonds 85-013 pointer comes from the project's own existing source list, not from the magazine.

priorities.description: THE NATIONAL YMCA CAMP DIRECTORY, c.1975. The back page of the January 1975 Canadian Camping Directory Issue advertises a 'DIRECTORY OF YMCA/YM-YWCA/YWCA RESIDENCE CAMPS IN CANADA -- to be available soon at all Y's', from the National Council, YMCA of Canada, 2160 Yonge Street, Toronto M4S 2A9, and the YWCA of Canada, 571 Jarvis Street, Toronto M4Y 2J1. A national directory of YMCA residence camps, published about 1975, in which Kanawana would necessarily appear -- a separate publication from the CCA's. ACTIONS: search Library and Archives Canada, the YMCA Canada national archives, University of Minnesota's Kautz Family YMCA Archives (which holds Canadian material), WorldCat and the Internet Archive for a mid-1970s YMCA of Canada camp directory. A YMCA-published entry would give the camp's own description of itself rather than the association's summary.
priorities.notes: Source: Canadian Camping Vol. 27 No. 2 (January 1975), back page advertisement. Word-for-word read, issue 103.

priorities.description: KANAWANA'S 1975 SEASON AND FEES, recoverable from the page image. The Quebec table in the January 1975 Directory Issue carries a SEASON/FEES column, but the cached OCR renders it as a floating block of dates and prices detached from their rows, so Kanawana's season dates and fee CANNOT be safely attributed from the text. They are on the printed page. ACTION: fetch the page images for this issue from the Internet Archive item and read the Kanawana row directly. The same fetch would settle the three single-character column codes ('X X C') whose headers the OCR mangles, and recover the fee for Les Voyageurs de la Verendrye. Low effort, high certainty.
priorities.notes: Source: Canadian Camping Vol. 27 No. 2 (January 1975), Quebec accredited member camps table. Word-for-word read, issue 103.

priorities.description:
FIND VAN WAGNER'S 1955 MANUAL OF STANDARDS. The April 1975 tribute to F.M. Van Wagner states that 'In 1955 he formulated and first introduced a Manual of Standards for children's summer camps in the Province of Quebec.' That is the origin document of the standards Kanawana was accredited against, with an author and a year. The sequence is now continuous: manual 1955 -> accreditation 'in the pioneer stage' 1959-60 under Alta Kahn -> provincial incorporation 23 January 1961 -> annual re-accreditation of every Quebec camp by 1975. WHERE TO LOOK -- FIRST: the F.M. VAN WAGNER PAPERS AT TRENT. Adele Ebbs (October 1976) reports that Van Wagner's own papers were the founding deposit of the Canadian Camping Archives at Trent University, Department of Canadian Studies -- 'from these papers we have many records of the early days of our Association.' A manual he authored is precisely the kind of document that would travel with his papers, and this is now the single most likely location. THEN: the QCA/ACQ successor body; the Camp Nominingue archive (Van Wagner founded and ran it 1925 onward, and Nominingue is still operating); BAnQ; Concordia's YMCA of Montreal fonds, since an accredited camp would hold a copy; and Trent, alongside the OCA deposit. Note also that Van Wagner was CCA president 'with Office in Montreal from 1958 to 1961' -- the national office was in Montreal for three years, and its records of that period are a separate target.

AMENDMENT (extraction pass, issue 109): LOOK IN THE VAN WAGNER PAPERS AT TRENT FIRST. Adele Ebbs, writing as chairman of the CCA Archives Committee in October 1976: 'The first and very valuable contribution of papers came from F.M. Van Wagner who was C.C.A. President 1958-60. From these papers we have many records of the early days of our Association.' Van Wagner founded the Quebec Camping Association in 1937 and was its first president, wrote the 1955 Manual, and was CCA president with the national office in Montreal. His own papers were the founding deposit of the national camping archive at Trent, so the Manual and early QCA records are more likely to be there than anywhere else this project has considered. Ask Trent for the Van Wagner papers by name, alongside the OCA deposit of October 1970 and the Mary S. Edgar fonds -- three separate camping deposits at one institution.
priorities.notes: Source: Frances M. Kelly, 'A Tribute to Q.C.A.'s Mr. Van', Canadian Camping Vol. 27 No. 3 (April 1975), p. 11-12. Word-for-word read, issue 104. Feeds p_314. Sharpened 2026-09-04 at issue 109: Van Wagner's papers are the founding deposit of the CCA archive at Trent, so p_317 and p_312 should be pursued in the same enquiry.

priorities.description: FIND COUSINEAU'S 'HEBERTISME' BOOKLET (1975). The November 1975 Canadian Camping newsletter advertises: 'HEBERTISME -- a new booklet written by Claude Cousineau and published by the Ontario Ministry of Culture and Recreation. 50 cents each from: Ontario Government Publications Service, 3 B-7 Macdonald Block, Queen's Park, Toronto.' This is the document that would settle the open conflict on Hebert's own dates: Cousineau (issue 82) has a pre-war methode naturelle demonstrated in 1913, brought to Quebec after the Second World War by Father Raoul Cloutier and Georges Gauvreau; Walter Mingie (issue 94) has Hebert training the French navy DURING the First World War. Cousineau wrote one side of that conflict and here sets it out at length for a government publisher. SEARCH: Ontario government publications 1975, Library and Archives Canada, University of Ottawa (where Cousineau taught in the School of Physical Education and Recreation / Departement de Recreologie), WorldCat, and the Ontario Ministry of Culture and Recreation's publication lists. Bears on wiki/traditions/programs-activities.md, which carries the hebertisme paragraph. SECOND DOCUMENT ADDED 2026-09-04 (issue 110): the Alberta Camping Association announced a 'Practical Guide to Hebertism', produced out of the experience of three Alberta camps funded in 1976 by the provincial Department of Recreation and Parks to set up hebertisme courses. As a government-funded provincial publication it may be easier to locate than Cousineau's booklet -- try the Alberta Camping Association successor body, Alberta provincial government publication catalogues, and university libraries in Alberta. New Brunswick reported in October 1976 that hebertisme 'continues to grow in many camps... due to the tremendous influence of Claude Cousineau's book on the subject', so the method was demonstrably travelling across the country within a year of publication. DATING NOTE (added 2026-09-04, issue 120): the CCA's June 1978 publications catalogue lists the Alberta Camping Association's 'Director's Guide for Counsellor Training' at $3.00 as a published Canadian book, but does NOT list the 'Practical Guide to Hebertism'. So as of June 1978 the hebertisme guide had not yet appeared -- do not assume a 1977 imprint when searching library catalogues; look from 1978 onward.
priorities.notes: Source: Canadian Camping Vol. 28 No. 1 (November 1975), p. 4 notice. Word-for-word read, issue 106. Extended at issue 110 (Canadian Camping Vol. 28 No. 5, December 1976, p. 4).

priorities.description:
TRACE THE 1976 NATIONAL ORAL-BIOGRAPHY PROJECT -- and check whether a Quebec tape covers Kanawana. Adele Ebbs, October 1976: 'At the Quebec Board meeting last spring a long list of camp pioneers was drawn up and agreement was reached by the Provincial Presidents that their associations would start taping oral biographies of those people.' Tapes were to go to Trent, where 'The Trent Archivist will make a copy and return the original.' This means (a) a list of Canadian camp pioneers was compiled at a CCA board meeting held in Quebec in spring 1976, and (b) the Quebec Camping Association undertook to tape its own pioneers. Anyone who ran or shaped Kanawana before 1976 -- and F.M. Van Wagner, who wrote Quebec's standards -- is a candidate to be on that list or on a tape. NEXT ACTION: ask Trent Archives for the CCA oral history tapes, the pioneer list itself, and any accession from the Quebec/ACQ association; ask the QCA successor body whether its tapes survive locally, since only copies went to Trent. A recording of a Quebec camp pioneer speaking in 1976-77 would be the earliest oral-history material this project could reach. SECONDARY VALUE: this is a direct 1976 precedent for the project's own pending DRAFT_ORAL_HISTORY_INSTRUMENT -- if the CCA's interview guidance survives with the tapes, it is worth reading before drafting ours. THE PROJECT HAD A NAMED CHAIRMAN (added 2026-09-04, issue 116): the CCA's list of committees and projects for 1977-78 includes 'PROJECTS -- Oral History -- Jay Haddad -- Ontario'. So the taping agreed at the Quebec board meeting in spring 1976 became a standing national project with a chairman by the winter of 1977-78. Haddad also sat on the CCA Task Force that reported in April 1977. ASK FOR: Haddad's oral history project files, correspondence and tape list, at Trent alongside the CCA fonds; and search for Jay Haddad himself (Ontario camping, 1970s) for a personal deposit or an obituary naming the project. A SECOND TAPE SERIES EXISTS (added 2026-09-04, issue 119): the CCA sold audio cassettes of its National Leadership Development Conference at Geneva Park, 19-22 January 1978 -- eighteen sessions at $3.50 each, ordered from M. Lee, R.R. No. 1, Port Sydney, Ontario.
