The published titles and speakers are: Selecting a Site (Ruth Mowat); Finance and Legislation (Ron Johnstone); Effective Administration (Ken Willis); Conserve Society (Craig Copeland); Maintenance and Building (Wilf Jackson, of Catholic Community Services Montreal); There's More to P.R. (Punch Jackson); Help a Child Grow (Gordon Jasper); Expectations (Bruno Morawetz); To Whom Directors Answer (Shanley Parkinson); Human Climate in Camp (Jean Funk); Will Staff Return (Bob Slingerland); Needs of Children (Patterson and Owen); High A.Q. Programs (Mayotte and Delainey); Program Models (Elaine King); Developing a Nature Program (Bob Cameron); Developing Programme Goals (Lorne Bowering); Year Around Programme Ideals (Ted Yard); New Program Ideas (Austin Matthews). This is a dated, itemised 1978 recording of Canadian camp directors talking about their work -- distinct from the pioneer oral biographies, and worth asking Trent for by conference name. THE PROJECT WAS FOLDED INTO ARCHIVES (added 2026-09-04, issue 129). By February 1980 the CCA's committee list reads 'Archives and Oral History -- Miss Helen Stewart': the separate Oral History project under Jay Haddad has been merged with the Archives committee under a single chairman. That simplifies the search -- the tapes and the pioneer list should be wherever the Archives committee's material went, which Adele Ebbs states was Trent (p_312). Ask Trent for the Archives committee's accessions of 1976-1980 as one body, under Ebbs, Stewart and Haddad's names together, rather than for an oral history collection by that name. THE ARCHIVE HAS A NAMED ARCHIVIST AND A PUBLISHED INVITATION (added 2026-09-04, issue 140): Canadian Camping Vol. 33 No. 6 (Winter 1982), p. 5, prints the association's own notice -- 'The CCA/ACC Archives are located at Trent University. The Oral History Interview Tapes reflect the efforts of many volunteers to record the history of the camping movement in Canada. Anyone wishing further information on the CCA/ACC Archives should communicate his specific area of interest to: Mr. Ken Johnson, Archivist, Thomas J. Bata Library, Trent University, Peterborough, Ontario K9J 7B8, (705) 748-1413.' That is the same K. Johnson to whom the May 1980 issue in this run was addressed (issue 131), which also confirms that the scans being read are Trent's own deposit copies. The association's instruction is to write in with a SPECIFIC AREA OF INTEREST, so the request should name Quebec, the Association des Camps du Quebec, the Quebec Camping Association English Section, the YMCA of Montreal, and Kanawana. CRITICALLY: the Charles Plewman interview printed in that same issue (Jay Haddad, 15 August 1976) is an EXCERPT -- 'the following are excerpts from that interview'. So the tape series holds full interviews of which the magazine printed only parts, and the request must ask for the recordings and any transcripts, not only for what was printed. Also ask whether the association's minutes are in the same fonds, since they bear on conflict c_029 (the Ottawa/Toronto disagreement about where the CCA was founded). THREE NAMED DOCUMENTS TO ASK FOR (added 2026-09-04, issue 142). The CCA/ACC Archives Committee's annual report for 1981-82 (Canadian Camping Vol. 34 No. 2, Summer 1982, p. 9; the chairman named three months earlier is Eileen Mayotte of Saskatchewan) records that it circulated three things to every provincial association, Quebec included: (1) a SAMPLE QUESTIONNAIRE ON CAMP ARCHIVES, sent to all provincial presidents in May 1981, which several provinces used -- this is the form on which a Quebec answer would have been written; (2) the oral-history taping 'GUIDELINES FOR INTERVIEWS', DEVELOPED BY THE OCA ARCHIVES COMMITTEE -- exactly the instrument this priority says should be read before the project drafts its own oral-history interview instrument, and it may be easier to obtain from the Ontario Camping Association's successor than from Trent; and (3) the 'FINDING AID FOR CCA/ACC ARCHIVES' stored at Trent University, forwarded to each province -- so a catalogue of the Trent holdings exists in multiple copies and should be requested by that title before any blind enquiry. Ask Trent for all three, and ask the OCA separately for the interview guidelines. AND ASK FOR THE 1982 'CATCH UP WITH YOUR PAST' RETURNS (added 2026-09-04, issue 143). Canadian Camping Vol. 34 No. 3 (Autumn 1982), p. 9, prints a boxed appeal over Ken Johnson's name at Trent: 'Children's camping is older than most of us realize. In time for the coming International Camping Congress and for our own information, we need to know WHO OPENED THE FIRST CAMP IN CANADA. As well, we would like to co-ordinate A LIST OF CAMPS IN CANADA WHICH WERE OPENED PRIOR TO 1900, 1910, AND 1920. Please dig into provincial government departments (education, health, land titles/surveys) as well as those of Church, YWCA, YMCA, Boy Scouts, Girl Guides, CGIT, and private records. This kind of information has never been researched in detail.' KANAWANA DATES ITSELF FROM 1894 AND BELONGS ON THE PRE-1900 LIST, so if the Quebec association or the YMCA of Montreal answered, an independent 1982 statement of the camp's founding date went to Trent -- and the compilation, gathered for the January 1983 Congress, would sit with the Congress papers in the same fonds. ASK FOR: the returns, any compiled list, and any correspondence with Quebec. Note also that the search list the CCA gave its members is a good checklist for Kanawana's own pre-1900 record in its own right: provincial education, health, and land titles/survey departments. UPDATE 2026-09-04 (issue 147, the 1982 Annual Report insert): the Archives Committee report for 1982-83, signed BRUNO MORAWETZ, Ph.D. -- a new chairman's name, and the same Bruno Morawetz who directed Camp Ponacka and wrote the 1975 'annual Hoax' article -- is the fullest account of CCA archival practice this read has found, and it changes where to look. (1) Provincial associations were told in the plainest terms to 'send all materials relating to the business of the Provincial Association to the CCA office for DEPOSIT AT TRENT UNIVERSITY', so anything the Quebec association or the ACQ sent after January 1983 is at Trent and not in Quebec -- ask Trent for Quebec provincial association material by name. (2) BERNADINE DODGE is named alongside Helen Stewart and Ken Johnston [Johnson] as having built the Congress Archives Room display; add her to the Trent enquiry. (3) A PHOTOGRAPHIC RECORD OF ALL FORMER CCA PRESIDENTS was prepared in January 1983, 'consisting of two frames with empty spaces for the next five CCA Presidents' -- a discrete, findable object that should be in the fonds and that would picture the Quebec presidents. (4) The Archives Room also held exhibits from the KANAWA MUSEUM provided by Professor Kirk Wipper, assisted by EANSWYTHE FLYNN -- a second new name. (5) Explicit null: six provincial associations sent slide carousels of camp scenes (Newfoundland, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Ontario, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia); QUEBEC IS NOT AMONG THEM, nor Alberta nor B.C. (6) Separately, Janet Adamson's Ontario report states that 1983 was the OCA's 50th anniversary and that 'the Archives Committee is publishing a booklet of the OCA's history to commemorate this anniversary. This will be available in the Autumn.' A 1983 OCA HISTORY BOOKLET therefore exists -- written by the association whose own 1930-33 founding date this project has three competing versions of, and by the archives committee that would know. Find it: Trent, the OCA itself, Ontario library catalogues, AMICUS/Voila, WorldCat. UPDATE 2026-09-04 (issue 148): THE TRENT ARCHIVIST IS NAMED WITH AN ADDRESS. Bruno Morawetz's Archives Update in Autumn 1983: 'We have a new archivist working on our collection at Trent University. Congratulations to Mrs. BERNADINE DODGE on her recent appointment at Trent. Interested members may contact Bernadine Dodge at: BATA LIBRARY, TRENT UNIVERSITY, PETERBOROUGH, ONTARIO K9L 7B8.' So the CCA fonds had a named professional custodian from 1983; any finding aid for the collection was made under her; and her own later career at Trent is traceable, which is a way into the collection's history if the fonds description is thin. Morawetz also renews the deposit instruction in a narrower and more useful form -- 'now is the time to send copies of last year's CONFERENCE PROGRAMS to the CCA Archives c/o the National Office' -- so provincial and camp conference programmes, Quebec's included, were actively solicited into the fonds in 1983-84. And Cliff Labbett, Immediate Past President, was in autumn 1983 'canvassing all the CCA Past Presidents for ideas to celebrate CCA's 50th Anniversary in 1986', which means (a) a 1986 anniversary publication or event may exist and be findable, and (b) correspondence with every living past president was generated in 1983-84 and should be in the fonds. UPDATE 2026-09-05 (issue 150): THE OCA HISTORY IS PUBLISHED AND NAMED. It is 'BLUE LAKE AND ROCKY SHORE', 112 pages, illustrated, written by a committee of OCA executive members, published by NATURAL HERITAGE of Toronto ((416) 694-7907 in 1984), launched at the OCA annual conference at the Inn On The Park, Toronto, 23-25 February 1984, and sold through the CCA Bookstore at $8.95. Order it or find it: Natural Heritage / Natural Heritage Books (later an imprint of Dundurn), Ontario library catalogues, AMICUS/Voila, WorldCat, abebooks. The magazine reviewed it as the first history of Canadian children's camping ever written, covering the turn of the century onward, so it is a secondary source on the whole movement and not only on Ontario -- and it is ten years earlier than any Kanawana centennial material. Note for the founding-date question: the review says only that the OCA was 'founded in the early Thirties', which does not discriminate between 1930, 1932 and 1933. ALSO from this issue: the NEATHERN TRUST is now sized and dated -- a $10,000 grant to the CCA announced spring 1984, instigated by Dr. Mary L. Northway, principal and interest to be expended after ten years, for simple outdoor living, understanding of the natural world, and conservation/energy education. Its projects therefore run 1984-1994. Northway's own camp biography is given: camper then staff at Glen Bernard Camp, Sundridge, 1922-1939; co-founder with Flora Morrison of Windy Pine, a tripping camp near Minden, in 1940. Her papers and the trust's records are worth the same enquiry as the CCA fonds. UPDATE 2026-09-05 (issue 151): TRENT HOLDS TRANSCRIBED ORAL HISTORIES -- stated outright for the first time in this run. Adele and Harry Ebbs's 1984 tribute to C. R. 'Blackie' Blackstock prints several hundred words of his speech and says: 'The following quotes are excerpts from the CAMPING ARCHIVES AT TRENT UNIVERSITY.' So the collection contains interview transcripts, not only institutional paper, and the Jay Haddad interview series this project has relied on (Plewman 1976, May Brown 1976, Latimer 1982, Booth 1982) may survive there in fuller form than the edited magazine versions. ASK TRENT FOR THE INTERVIEW/ORAL HISTORY SERIES BY NAME. Also: Bruno Morawetz's 1983 archives report describes HOW provincial material arrives -- 'each Provincial Association was sent a large brown envelope marked "Archives"... for mailing at a later date when the envelope is about to burst' -- so Quebec deposits, if any, arrive as irregular bulk envelopes rather than ordered transfers, and may be uncatalogued. Archivist address restated as Bernadine Dodge, Trent University, Peterborough K9J 7B8 (issue 148 gave K9L 7B8; OCR variance, check both). And Clifford Labbett's 50th Anniversary Task Force lists five candidate 1986 activities -- kite flying across Canada; participation in the July 1st celebrations in Ottawa; a National Camping Day tie-in with private-industry sponsorship; official UNESCO recognition for camping's contribution to environmental protection; and across-Canada campfires -- any of which would have generated 1986 paper reaching member camps. UPDATE 2026-09-05 (issue 152): A NATIONAL TAPING INSTRUCTION, AND A CALL FOR PROVINCIAL HISTORIES. Bruno Morawetz's 'Are You Taping Your Leaders?' (Autumn 1984), crediting the inspiration of HELEN STEWART, the Ontario Archives Chairman, tells every provincial association: 'make use of TAPE RECORDERS to tape interviews with individual Camp Directors and to tape addresses that are given at conferences and workshops... send copies to the CCA Archives at Trent University, Peterborough, if it is of national importance.' Taken with issue 151's statement that the Blackstock quotations are 'excerpts from the Camping Archives at Trent University', it is near-certain the Trent collection holds SOUND RECORDINGS as well as paper, accumulating from 1984 onward. ASK TRENT FOR AUDIO / ORAL HISTORY RECORDINGS BY THAT DESCRIPTION, not only for files. Second: 'The Ontario Archives Committee has just finished writing the history of the Ontario Camping Association... and IT IS HOPED THAT OTHER PROVINCES WILL START THINKING ABOUT THE WRITING OF THEIR OWN HISTORIES.' So provincial associations were formally urged in 1984 to write their own histories -- ASK WHETHER THE ACQ OR THE QUEBEC CAMPING ASSOCIATION EVER DID, and if so when and by whom; a Quebec equivalent of Blue Lake and Rocky Shore would be a major secondary source for Kanawana. Also from the same issue: the editor's own list of the complete interview series he published -- CHARLES PLEWMAN, JUNE LABBETT, MAY BROWN, JOHN LATIMER, MARJORIE BOOTH and LEO BUSCAGLIA -- which is the exact set to ask Trent for in unedited form. UPDATE 2026-09-05 (issue 153): 1985 IS THE YEAR TO LOOK FOR KANAWANA HERITAGE MATERIAL. Three separate national prompts to Canadian camps to write down their own history all land in 1985: (a) the CCA's International Youth Year 'National Celebration Event' of August 1985, for which every member camp was to receive programme kits on fitness, environment, PEACE and HISTORICAL ROOTS (issue 151); (b) Bruno Morawetz's instruction to provincial associations to tape interviews with camp directors and conference addresses for deposit at Trent (issue 152); and (c) HERITAGE YEAR 1985, marking a century since land was set aside near Banff, for which the Winter 1985 issue printed seventy-plus bilingual suggestions including 'RECORD THE ORAL HISTORY OF YOUR COMMUNITY ON AUDIO OR VIDEO TAPE by interviewing senior citizens and local historians', 'produce an historical atlas of your community', 'produce an historic newspaper', and 'compare the local natural environment with various periods in the past, using archives, oral histories, wildlife and bird counts'. If Kanawana ever generated heritage or oral-history material outside its annual reports, 1985 is the single most likely year, and it falls squarely inside the 1980-1986 period for which no Kanawana season report survives. ALSO from this issue, and important for the project's own record-keeping: Fitness Canada withdrew funding for the CCA executive director's post at the end of November 1984 and cut all management support by 33-1/3% a year to terminate in 1988 -- which is why Canadian Camping stops in 1988. That belongs in meta/sources-index.md as the explanation of this source's end date. UPDATE 2026-09-05 (issue 154) -- THE SINGLE MOST CONCRETE 1980s ASK. The International Youth Year kit was not a vague plan: 'The Canadian Camping Association will provide each member camp with a kit of program material... The kit will be DIRECTLY MAILED TO EACH CAMP IN EARLY MAY [1985].' Its contents are credited by author, and the first is 'HISTORICAL ROOTS ACTIVITIES - DR. BRUNO MORAWETZ, CAMP PONACKA' -- written by the CCA's own archives chairman. Others: Environmental Activities (Mike Walters, Camp Chief Hector); Fitness Activities (Fitness Canada); Peace Activities (Canadian Peace Congress); IYY Campfire Program (Jack Pearse, Jane McCutcheon, John Jorgenson, Camp Tawingo). The National Celebration Event was WEDNESDAY 24 JULY 1985 and every camp was asked at minimum to run the common campfire programme. ASK TRENT FOR THE 1985 IYY KIT BY NAME, and for Morawetz's Historical Roots Activities specifically -- it is a named document by a named author, mailed to Kanawana, inside the 1980-1986 window for which no Kanawana season report survives. The national co-ordinator was Ian Fowler, 100 Westmorland Street, Moncton, N.B.; the Quebec member of the task force was PETER GODDARD OF MONTREAL. UPDATE 2026-09-05 (issue 157): A SECOND NATIONAL HISTORY PROMPT, AND THIS ONE LEAVES OBJECTS. 'CELEBRATE CCA's 50th BIRTHDAY WITH AN ADVENTURE INTO THE PAST - 1936-1986. 1986 is the CCA's fiftieth birthday. Your camp can take part in the celebration this summer! All across the country camps will participate by including one or all of the following activities in their programs: HISTORICAL JOURNEYS; RE-ENACTMENT OF EARLY CAMPING LIFESTYLES; CEREMONIES AND THEME EVENTS. Each participating camp will be recognized with A WALL CERTIFICATE and those camps pre-registering will receive CARDS FOR EACH OF THEIR CAMPERS.' Registration forms went through the provincial associations, so the ACQ held the Quebec list. TWO THINGS TO LOOK FOR: a KANAWANA WALL CERTIFICATE dated 1986 (dining-hall walls and photographs), and a camper's card from summer 1986. Ask Trent and the ACQ for the registration lists -- those would say directly whether Kanawana took part. Together with the May 1985 IYY 'historical roots' kit this makes TWO SUCCESSIVE SUMMERS in which every member camp in Canada was asked to research and perform its own history, both inside the 1980-1986 window for which no Kanawana season report survives. UPDATE 2026-09-05 (issue 158): THE PRE-FOUNDING MINUTES MAY EXIST. Adele Ebbs, Taylor Statten's daughter, describing the supper club of six private camp directors that preceded the CCA -- Mary S. Edgar (Glen Bernard), Mary G. Hamilton (Tanamakoon), Ferna Halliday (Oconto), Ernie Chapman (Kagawong), A. L. Cochrane (Temagami) and Statten, meeting four or five times a year in each other's homes in the early 1930s -- says: 'I was secretary, I FINALLY STARTED TO TAKE NOTES SOMETIME BEFORE I GOT MARRIED, AND THAT WAS 1935.' Minutes of the pre-founding meetings therefore exist from about 1934-35, kept by Ebbs, who was later Archives chairman for both the CCA and the OCA. ASK TRENT FOR THEM BY THAT DESCRIPTION -- they would settle the 1936/1938/c.1947 founding-date question outright. Also from the same interview: the early CCA presidential sequence is given as Taylor Statten, Dais Gass, Anne Vail, TED YARD, Irv Haladner, F. M. Van Wagner -- placing Ted Yard, the Camp Pine Crest director whose ceremony text this read recorded at issue 145, among the association's first presidents. ||| ADDED 2026-09-05 (issue 159, Canadian Camping Vol. 38 No. 2, Fall 1986). (1) *** THE STRONGEST NEW LEAD IN THIS READ: A NATIONAL YMCA COSTING SURVEY THAT SHOULD NAME KANAWANA. *** Shirley Yard, interviewed about her husband W. E. (Ted) Yard: 'There was a project of the Boys' Work Committee of the National Council YMCA. It is a survey of costs and factors in Canadian YMCA Camps. This is probably what he did his thesis on when he completed his Master's degree at George Williams College in 1958/59.' A national YMCA camp costing survey of 1958-59 is very unlikely to have omitted the YMCA of Montreal's own resident camp, and it would report Kanawana FROM OUTSIDE the Montreal association's files -- precisely what is missing for 1947-1967, since the Montreal annual reports of those years name no paid camp director and give Kanawana no separate accounting. WHERE TO LOOK: George Williams College thesis holdings (the college's records went to Aurora University, Illinois); the Kautz Family YMCA Archives at the University of Minnesota, which hold National Council material of this period; and the YMCA Canada national office records. Search terms: Yard, W. E. / Ted Yard; 'costs and factors'; Boys' Work Committee; George Williams College MS thesis 1958 or 1959. Written into wiki/history/postwar-gap.md as a lead, explicitly not as evidence that Kanawana appears in it. (2) The Ted Yard CAMP DIRECTOR'S CALENDAR, compiled 1959 at George Williams College and still in circulation in 1986 -- a month-by-month administrative calendar; useful as a period benchmark for what a camp director's year contained. (3) REPERTOIRE DE L'INVENTAIRE DES CAMPS D'EXPRESSION FRANCAISE (INCEF), second edition launched autumn 1986, data gathered by M. Jean-Luc Cote of the Conseil de la Vie francaise en Amerique, 59 rue d'Auteuil, Quebec G1R 4C2. Would map every French-language camp in Canada as of 1986. Ask the Conseil's successor and the ACQ. (4) *** ASK THE ACQ ABOUT THE SUMMER OF 1986 BEFORE ASKING WHAT IT HOLDS. *** Its 1986 report records that Employment and Immigration Canada funded a three-person team that spent that summer RECLASSIFYING ALL OF THE ACQ'S ARCHIVES AND CAMP DOSSIERS. The present arrangement of the ACQ's own records dates from that project; a request should be framed in its terms (camp dossiers, by camp) rather than in pre-1986 terms. The same report names the three accreditation consultants of 1986 -- Leo Venditti, Yves Legault, Louis Jean -- who between them visited 76 camps; Kanawana changed director inside FY1986 and by the ACQ's own stated rule should be among them. (5) 400 slides shot at Quebec camps in summer 1986 by Jean-Marc Amyot of the R.L.Q. audio-visual service for a bilingual slide show -- a dated photographic survey of Quebec camps that may include Kanawana; ask the ACQ and BAnQ. ||| ADDED 2026-09-05 (issue 160, Canadian Camping Vol. 38 No. 3, Winter 1987). (1) *** THE 50TH ANNIVERSARY OF QUEBEC CAMPING, 1988. *** Ken Willis, CCA/ACC Vice-President (Quebec Region): 'The organized camping movement in Quebec was born in 1938. TONY SHORGUN, who has been involved in camping during many of the intervening years, is already at work laying plans for the 50th Anniversary of this birth which, obviously, will be held next year.' If the event happened it produced a programme, press coverage or a commemorative publication assembled by a participant -- a history of Quebec camping in which Kanawana, a member camp throughout, would appear. Shorgun is a name new to this project: search obituaries, ACQ records, La Presse and the Gazette for 1988, and ask the ACQ directly. Note the run itself stops in 1988, so the magazine may not have covered it -- the last four issues should be watched for it. (2) BIG COVE YMCA CAMP now has three founding dates -- 1889 (encyclopaedic), 1890 (Jack Pearse, 1979), 1891 (Kelley Byrne, the camp's own director and president of the Nova Scotia association, 1987). Kanawana's second-oldest position is unaffected by all three, but if the wiki keeps asserting a date for Canada's oldest camp it should be sourced from a Nova Scotia primary record, not from any of these. Ask the Camping Association of Nova Scotia and the Halifax YMCA. (3) PROVINCIAL ASSOCIATION ARCHIVES. Bruno Morawetz, 1987: 'Some Provincial Associations have their own archives where they collect printed material about their member camps.' With the ACQ's summer-1986 archive reclassification (issue 159), that is two independent reasons to ask the QUEBEC association what it holds on Kanawana rather than only Trent. (4) Mary S. Edgar's memoir 'Turn of the Century for Suzanne Marie' remains the lead recorded earlier; the 1987 interview adds that her fonds came to Trent through John and Barb Gilchrist, who are the people to ask about anything Edgar kept from her Oolahwan years (1915-1919) -- the Quebec YWCA camp that visited Kanawana. ||| ADDED 2026-09-05 (issue 161, Canadian Camping Vol. 38 No. 4, Spring 1987). (1) A LETTER WENT TO THE QUEBEC ASSOCIATION IN FEBRUARY 1987 asking it to gather records AND to tape people. Bruno Morawetz: 'In February of this year a letter was sent to all Provincial Archives Chairmen, or to the Provincial President... I would urge your member camps to collect as much written material as possible and have it lodged in your own provincial archives... One of the ways of collecting archival material is to interview persons who are playing important roles in camping -- these too can be lodged and catalogued in an archival collection.' With the ACQ's summer-1986 archive reclassification (issue 159) and Morawetz's note that some provincial associations already held their own archives (issue 160), that is a THIRD prompt inside eighteen months for Quebec camping records to be assembled somewhere other than Trent. Ask the ACQ specifically whether it holds tapes or transcripts made after February 1987. (2) INCEF '87, the second edition of the repertoire des camps d'expression francaise hors Quebec, was PUBLISHED at the end of January 1987 with funding from the Conseil de la Vie francaise en Amerique and the Ministre des Affaires Intergouvernementales, copies held at the CCA office in Toronto. A dated, findable document. (3) EILEEN MAYOTTE was alive and donating to the CCA Patrons' Fund in 1987 -- the latest fixed point this project has for her, and a reason to look for an obituary from 1987 or later rather than earlier. She was QCA secretary in the 1940s and later president of the Saskatchewan association; a stub is warranted. (4) PAGE 7 OF THIS ISSUE ('Between the Covers', by Nancy Barker) produced no machine-readable text in the Internet Archive scan and has NOT been read. If a clean copy is ever obtained, that page is outstanding. ||| ADDED 2026-09-05 (issue 162, Canadian Camping Vol. 39 No. 1, Summer 1987). (1) A DATED TAPE IN THE CCA FONDS AT TRENT. Jocelyn Palm, writing Mary Northway's memorial: 'In 1981, I interviewed Dr. Northway in order that the tape could be added to the CCA Archives. I have just listened to that tape.' So a Palm-Northway interview tape existed in the Trent fonds and was playable in 1987. Northway 'engineered the collection and organization of the OCA and CCA Archives now at Trent University' -- she is the reason the collection this project depends on exists, and the tape is a specific, findable item. She died 26 February 1987. (2) THE OLDEST-CAMP QUESTION (see c_031): ask the YMCA-YWCA of Winnipeg and Manitoba provincial archives what the 1891 'Lake of the Woods Institute' actually was, and whether Camp Stephens's 1991 centenary produced a published history; ask the Camping Association of Nova Scotia and the Halifax YMCA for a primary record of Big Cove's first season. Kanawana's national ranking depends on both answers. (3) The CCA/ACC held its Board of Management and President's Council ANNUAL MEETING IN QUEBEC CITY, 1-3 May 1987, hosted by the ACQ, with visits to Camp Keno (Marist Fathers, chemin Saint-Louis) and Camp Oasis Notre-Dame (lac Simon, Portneuf). Pere Paul Belanger, a FORMER CCA VICE-PRESIDENT, received the council -- a Quebec name new to this project and worth researching. Minutes of that meeting would be in the Trent 'brown bag' accession for 1987. ||| ADDED 2026-09-05 (issue 163, Canadian Camping Vol. 39 No. 2, Fall 1987). (1) *** A DEMOGRAPHIC SURVEY OF QUEBEC CAMP CLIENTELE. *** ACQ president Henri Chalifoux, autumn 1987: a study 'to identify our summer camp clientele', funded by the ministere des Loisirs, de la Chasse et de la Peche (M.L.C.P.), renewing user research first done in 1982. If either the 1982 study or its 1987-88 renewal survives it would describe the population Kanawana drew from -- the only such source this read has encountered. Ask the ACQ and BAnQ; the M.L.C.P.'s successor ministry holds the funding records. (2) HENRI CHALIFOUX, ACQ president in 1987 and Quebec's national representative, is a name new to this project. So is the fact that FIVE consultants visited over 80 Quebec camps in summer 1987, ten of them applying for first-time ACQ membership. Kanawana was a member throughout; a 1987 visitation report should exist. (3) MATERIAL SENT TO THE MAGAZINE MAY NOT BE AT TRENT. The 'Jackpot!' notice states that the magazine forwarded donated memorabilia 'to the Canadian Camping Association Archives at Trent University OR to the appropriate provincial camping association archives in the camp's home province'. Third statement in three consecutive issues that provincial associations held their own archives. Quebec material from 1986-88 may be with the ACQ. (4) EILEEN MAYOTTE was on the Commission des camps d'expression francaise for 1987-88 (as Saskatchewan's member) AND donated to the Patrons' Fund that year -- two independent fixed points in 1987 for the QCA's 1940s secretary. KEN WILLIS stayed on as the committee's Quebec member after retiring as vice-president. (5) INCEF 1988 was planned, to carry a review ('bilan') of the three French-language camp inventories made since 1985 -- the single most useful of the INCEF documents if it was published, and the run stops in 1988. (6) PARC completed a NATIONAL SURVEY of physical activity programmes at Canadian camps in 1987 with a high response rate; the summary was promised for the next issue, which is the last one the magazine published. Watch issue 164. ||| ADDED 2026-09-05 (issue 164, Canadian Camping Vol. 39 No. 3, Winter 1988 -- THE LAST ISSUE; the word-for-word read of all 164 issues is now complete). (1) *** A. ROSS SEAMAN DIED 23 OCTOBER 1987. *** Exact date, from the memorial fund notice. This narrows an obituary search to the last week of October and the first weeks of November 1987 -- The Review (Vankleek Hill), the Montreal Gazette, and Concordia's own newsletters. The A. Ross Seaman Leadership Development Fund was founded by family, friends and colleagues meeting in EARLY NOVEMBER 1987, with a minimum goal of $25,000, interest only, administered by Universite Concordia, Bureau des finances AD 130. CONCORDIA'S OWN FINANCE AND ADVANCEMENT RECORDS for that fund are a documented, named, findable file about a Kanawana director -- ask for the fund's establishing file and its founding donor list, which will name the family, friends and colleagues who met in November 1987. (2) THE ACQ'S FOIRE DES CAMPS at the COMPLEXE DESJARDINS, MONTREAL, early 1988, with the ACQ as maitre d'oeuvre. A public camp fair in downtown Montreal that Kanawana as a member camp had every reason to attend; it would have produced press coverage (La Presse, Le Devoir, the Gazette, January-March 1988) and a printed programme listing exhibitors. (3) MADELENE ALLEN, director of Camp Ouareau, joined the ACQ's Conseil d'administration at the start of 1988, replacing Ken Willis. (4) The PARC national survey report -- a fuller summary was to be MAILED TO ALL CCA MEMBER CAMPS early in 1988. Kanawana was a member camp; a copy may be in the YMCA of Montreal fonds. 197 of ~600 camps responded (33%): 70 religious, 52 private, 50 agency, 14 special-needs, 11 other. (5) The magazine's own last words on its finances: 'There is no money left in the budget to produce this very C.C.A./A.C.C. Magazine you now hold in your hands.' Camp Tawingo underwrote the entire production cost of the final issue. A third International Congress for Toronto, a 1989 Directors' Institute at Bolton (9-12 November) and a 1989 national conference were all planned; whether any happened is outside this corpus and worth one search each.

AMENDMENT (extraction pass, issue 116): THE PROJECT HAS A NAMED CHAIRMAN. The CCA's list of committees and projects for 1977-78 gives ORAL HISTORY as a standing national project under JAY HADDAD of Ontario, who also sat on the Task Force that reported in April 1977 and who later edited the magazine (mid-1981 to Winter 1986). So the taping agreed at the Quebec board meeting in spring 1976 was institutionalised within eighteen months. Ask Trent for Haddad's oral history project files, correspondence and tape list by name alongside the CCA fonds, and search for Haddad himself for a personal deposit or an obituary naming the project. This is the most promising lead the read has produced for reaching recorded voices of Canadian camping in the 1970s, and Quebec was a participating association.

SECOND TAPE SERIES, ITEMISED (extraction pass, issue 119). Distinct from the pioneer oral biographies this priority was created for, the CCA sold cassettes of EIGHTEEN sessions from the Geneva Park national conference of 19-22 January 1978 at $3.50 each, ordered from M. Lee, R.R. No. 1, Port Sydney, Ontario. Named sessions include 'Maintenance and Building' (Wilf Jackson, Catholic Community Services Montreal), 'Expectations' (Bruno Morawetz), 'Will Staff Return' (Bob Slingerland), 'High A.Q. Programs' (Mayotte and Delainey), 'Finance and Legislation' (Ron Johnstone), 'Effective Administration' (Ken Willis, later QCA president) and 'To Whom Directors Answer' (Shanley Parkinson). Cassettes of the January 1975 conference were sold the same way. Ask Trent for both series by conference name and date.

THE ADDRESS, IN THE ASSOCIATION'S OWN WORDS (extraction pass, issue 140). Canadian Camping, Winter 1982, at the foot of the Plewman interview: 'The CCA/ACC Archives are located at Trent University. The Oral History Interview Tapes reflect the efforts of many volunteers to record the history of the camping movement in Canada. Anyone wishing further information on the CCA/ACC Archives should communicate his specific area of interest to: Mr. Ken Johnson, Archivist, Thomas J. Bata Library, Trent University, Peterborough, Ontario K9J 7B8, (705) 748-1413.' The Plewman interview printed there IS one of those tapes -- Jay Haddad recorded it on 15 August 1976 at Plewman's Haliburton rest home and the magazine printed excerpts after Plewman's death in December 1981. So the series holds full interviews of which the magazine printed only parts, and the request should ask for RECORDINGS AND TRANSCRIPTS, not the printed text. The association's own instruction is to write in with a specific area of interest: ask for anything Quebec, Montreal, YMCA or Laurentian.

THREE NAMED DOCUMENTS TO ASK FOR (extraction pass, issue 142). The CCA Archives Committee's 1981-82 report names them: (a) the 'FINDING AID FOR CCA/ACC ARCHIVES' stored at Trent, forwarded to every provincial association -- so a catalogue exists and a copy went to Quebec; (b) the oral history taping 'GUIDELINES FOR INTERVIEWS', developed by the OCA Archives Committee and circulated to each provincial archives contact, which is exactly the instrument to read before this project drafts its own oral history interview document; and (c) a SAMPLE QUESTIONNAIRE ON CAMP ARCHIVES circulated to all provincial presidents in May 1981, which is the form a Quebec answer would have been written on. The report adds 'We still lack contacts for Archives Chairmen in some provinces', so Quebec may or may not have had one. Also worth asking for: the CCA National Photo Contest collection from 1982 onward, since all submitted photographs became association property.

A FOURTH THING TO ASK TRENT FOR (extraction pass, issue 143): THE 1982 'CATCH UP WITH YOUR PAST' RETURNS. Canadian Camping, Autumn 1982, over the Trent archivist's name: 'we need to know who opened the first camp in Canada. As well, we would like to co-ordinate a list of camps in Canada which were opened prior to 1900, 1910, and 1920... This kind of information has never been researched in detail.' KANAWANA DATES ITSELF FROM 1894 AND WOULD BELONG ON THE PRIOR-TO-1900 LIST. The returns were being gathered in time for the January 1983 Congress and went to Ken Johnson at Trent, so any compilation sits in the CCA/ACC fonds beside the Congress papers. A Quebec answer naming Kanawana would be the earliest independent statement of its founding date outside the YMCA's own papers. The notice's own list of where to look is also a checklist for Kanawana's pre-1900 record: provincial education, health and land titles/surveys departments, alongside Church, YWCA, YMCA, Scout, Guide and CGIT records.

A NAMED PROFESSIONAL CUSTODIAN, AND TWO MORE ITEMS (extraction pass, issues 147-148). Bruno Morawetz, Autumn 1983: 'We have a new archivist working on our collection at Trent University. Congratulations to Mrs. Bernadine Dodge on her recent appointment at Trent. Interested members may contact Bernadine Dodge at: Bata Library, Trent University.' So the CCA fonds had a named professional custodian from 1983, the finding aid was made under her, and her own later career at Trent is traceable. Also to ask for: the PHOTOGRAPHIC RECORD OF ALL FORMER CCA PRESIDENTS assembled for the January 1983 Congress Archives Room, and the CONFERENCE PROGRAMMES actively solicited into the fonds in 1983-84 -- provincial and camp programmes both, which would include any Quebec ones. And the deposit instruction is explicit: PROVINCIAL ASSOCIATION BUSINESS RECORDS WENT THROUGH THE CCA OFFICE TO TRENT, so anything the Quebec association sent is at Trent and not in Quebec. Add the Ontario association's own 1983 fiftieth-anniversary history booklet to the same request.
priorities.notes: Source: Adele Ebbs, 'Canadian Camping Archives', Canadian Camping Vol. 28 No. 4 (October 1976). Word-for-word read, issue 109. Pursue in the same enquiry as p_312 and p_317. Chairman identified at issue 116 (Canadian Camping Vol. 29 No. 6, December 1977, p. 10). Second tape series recorded at issue 119 (Canadian Camping Vol. 30 No. 3, May 1978, p. 11). Merger recorded at issue 129 (Canadian Camping Vol. 32 No. 1, February 1980, p. 2).

priorities.description:
SEARCH MONTREAL MEDIA FOR QUEBEC 'CAMP WEEK', 5-11 MARCH 1977. The Canadian Camping Association's February 1977 newsletter reports a province-wide promotional campaign run by the ACQ-QCA with provincial support: 'Some of the upcoming events in Quebec include "Camp Week" (March 5-11)... promotional spots on radio and television; advertisements and public service announcements in every newspaper; buttons, posters, badges etc. will all be used to make everyone in Quebec more aware of camping opportunities for children and young people in that Province.' This is a dated, one-week, province-wide advertising campaign on behalf of every accredited Quebec camp -- Kanawana among them. WHERE TO LOOK: the Montreal Gazette and Montreal Star for 5-11 March 1977 (BAnQ numerique for the Star; Gazette via Google News Archive and Newspapers.com), La Presse and Le Devoir for the same week via BAnQ, and Laurentian local papers; look for camp directory advertisements, public service announcements, and any listing that names member camps. A camp-by-camp advertisement would give Kanawana's 1977 fees, dates and age ranges in a single place, and the campaign material (buttons, posters, badges) is collectible ephemera that may surface on eBay or WorthPoint. RELATED: the same column reports $300,000 of provincial money for the association's spring training programme, so a Quebec government grant record for fiscal 1977 should name the programme. CAMP WEEK WAS ANNUAL (added 2026-09-04, issue 116): the CCA's bilingual Calendar of Events for 1978 lists '2-9 March -- ACQ-QCA semaine de Camps', so the March 1977 campaign was not a one-off. Search the same Montreal and Quebec papers for the first full week of March in 1977, 1978 and the years either side. The same calendar also shows the Quebec association's monthly Montreal souper-causerie series with published themes -- 'Plein air: publicite, depliants' (30 January 1978), 'Recrutement: mode de selection' (23 February 1978), 'formulaires: Mecanismes de controle' (16 March 1978) -- and a seminaire des directeurs de camps on 7-9 April 1978. Kanawana's director was the English section's president through this period, so any minutes or attendance records of these meetings would place him and name his camp.

AMENDMENT (extraction pass, issue 116): CAMP WEEK WAS ANNUAL, NOT A ONE-OFF. The bilingual 1978 calendar printed in the December 1977 newsletter carries '2-9 March 1978, ACQ-QCA semaine de Camps' -- so the provincial promotion week recurred, and the search should cover early March in successive years rather than one week in 1977. The same calendar gives the Montreal souper-causerie themes, which are worth searching alongside it: 'Plein air -- publicite, depliants' (30 January 1978), 'Recrutement -- mode de selection' (22-23 February) and 'formulaires -- Mecanismes de controle' (15-16 March).
priorities.notes: Source: 'News and Views from Across Canada' (Quebec), Canadian Camping Vol. 29 No. 1 (February 1977), p. 2. Word-for-word read, issue 111. Extended at issue 116 (Canadian Camping Vol. 29 No. 6, December 1977, p. 8).

priorities.description: FIND MARVIN GRANEK'S THESIS AND ITS RAW DATA. 'An Investigation Into the Attitudes of Resident Camp Administration Towards Critical Problems in Resident Camping', MA in Recreation, University of Waterloo, c. 1977-78, summarised by the author in Canadian Camping Vol. 30 No. 5 (October 1978). It surveyed Canadian resident-camp administrators on 33 attitude statements across eight areas and analysed the results by thirteen background characteristics including camp type and REGION, reporting Quebec results separately: Quebec camps were having more difficulty filling their camper quota than any other region, were (with agency camps) most in favour of CCA research investment, and resident camping in Quebec and Ontario 'may have peaked'. Kanawana was an accredited Quebec agency camp of exactly the kind surveyed, and its director was the province's English-section president in the survey period, so it is a strong candidate to be among the respondents. WHERE TO LOOK: the University of Waterloo's institutional repository UWSpace and its library catalogue; Theses Canada / Library and Archives Canada; ProQuest Dissertations; and the CCA archive at Trent (p_312), since the association printed the findings and Granek invited correspondence care of the CCA office. WHAT TO EXTRACT: the regional breakdown for Quebec in full, the questionnaire instrument itself, and any list of responding camps or administrators. The study is a partial replication of an American Camping Association-sponsored study, which should also be identified.
priorities.notes: Source: Marvin Granek, 'Report on the Findings of a Survey of Camp Directors', Canadian Camping Vol. 30 No. 5 (October 1978), pp. 6-10. Word-for-word read, issue 121. Feeds between-centennials.md and the coeducation/enrolment thread.

priorities.description:
IDENTIFY THE 1978 QUEBEC WILDERNESS-TRIP TRAGEDY, AND WHAT THE QUEBEC ASSOCIATION DID ABOUT IT. The Canadian Camping Association's December 1978 editorial: 'The tragedy at the beginning of the wilderness trip attempted recently in Quebec brought camping people up short. We have become somewhat complacent during the past ten or twelve years assuming our performance standards are satisfactory... A review of this incident indicates this is not so. Even government regulations are not broadly known nor publicized well enough.' No camp, party, date or water is named. DO NOT ASSUME AN IDENTIFICATION. One candidate to test, and only to test, is the Lake Temiskaming drowning of 11 June 1978, in which twelve boys and one master of St. John's School of Ontario died -- Lake Temiskaming lies on the Ontario-Quebec boundary, which could account for 'in Quebec', but the party was Ontarian and the editorial's phrase 'at the beginning of the wilderness trip attempted recently in Quebec' may equally describe a separate, smaller and less remembered incident. Establish which before citing anything. WHERE TO LOOK: Montreal Gazette, Montreal Star, La Presse and Le Devoir for summer 1978; Quebec coroner's inquest records; the CCA and QCA records at Trent (p_312, p_314) for the review the editorial calls for; and the following issues of this newsletter, which should report what the association actually did. WHY IT MATTERS FOR KANAWANA: Les Voyageurs de la Verendrye was a separately accredited Quebec wilderness tripping camp operating in exactly these years under exactly this association, so any provincial tightening of tripping standards in 1979 applied to it. ALSO WORTH ESTABLISHING: the 1920s Balsam Lake incident the editorial cites as precedent, credited with producing both the slogan 'Hang on to the canoe -- for three days and three nights' and the standardisation of canoe strokes in Canadian camping. A NAMED BODY WAS ALREADY RESEARCHING IT (added 2026-09-04, issue 125). C. R. Blackstock's obituary, May 1979: 'He gave input to the CURRENT RESEARCH BEING DONE BY THE SOCIETY OF CAMP DIRECTORS, of which he was a Founding Fellow, when he alleged that canoe trippers should be trained to handle risk and to anticipate it.' So within months of the 1978 tragedy the Society of Camp Directors -- a body distinct from the CCA and the provincial associations, whose inaugural dinner date is itself an open conflict in this project -- had research under way on canoe tripping risk, and was taking evidence from the Canadian Red Cross's former Director of Water Safety. FIND THAT RESEARCH: ask Trent for Society of Camp Directors records alongside the CCA fonds; ask the OCA, with which the Society overlapped heavily (Ron Johnstone held both presidencies in 1973). Blackstock's own stated position is worth recording either way -- on lifejackets he 'believed that sufficiently trained persons would know under what conditions they should be worn', which is the argument the November 1975 federal regulation had just overridden. THE REVIEW IS FOUND, IN PART (added 2026-09-04, issue 131). The May 1980 issue prints the free-text answers to question 139 of the SOCIETY OF CAMP DIRECTORS' TRIPPING QUESTIONNAIRE -- 'Do you have any thoughts or concerns on the matter of canoe tripping in camps?' -- unattributed and unedited, about fifty of them. So the questionnaire ran to at least 139 questions and its results were tabulated. FIND THE FULL INSTRUMENT AND ITS RESULTS: ask Trent and the Ontario Camping Association successor for Society of Camp Directors records c. 1979-1981. The same issue prints the OCA's emergency procedures and a reporting policy 'adopted as policy of the O.C.A. effective February 1980' requiring a member camp to telephone the president within 24 hours of a serious accident or death and file a written report within 20 days. ASK WHETHER QUEBEC ADOPTED AN EQUIVALENT -- if the ACQ did, its files would contain camp incident reports, which is a second reason to pursue p_314. Note that the questionnaire responses still do not name the 1978 incident, so the identification question remains open. THE FULL REPORT IS FOUND (added 2026-09-04, issue 132). The June 1980 issue carries Michael Hoyer's write-up of the whole survey with five tables: about 120 questionnaires sent, about 60 returned, mostly resident camps, majority Ontario members but eight provinces represented. Hoyer was assistant camp director of Camp Oconto; the work was funded and supported by MARY NORTHWAY and the NEATHERN TRUST. His closing note says 'the questionnaire and the tabulated responses can be obtained from the C.C.A. office', so a full data set once existed on paper -- ASK TRENT FOR IT by that description, and ask for the Neathern Trust's records, since a funder's file may hold the instrument even where the association's does not. Northway's own papers are a third route. STILL OPEN: neither the report nor the free-text answers names the 1978 Quebec incident, so the identification question is untouched.

AMENDMENT (extraction pass, issues 131-132): THE SOCIETY OF CAMP DIRECTORS' SURVEY IS THE RESEARCH, AND IT IS PARTLY PRINTED. Canadian Camping printed about fifty unedited free-text answers to QUESTION 139 in May 1980 and Michael Hoyer's full report with Tables I to V in June 1980. Method: about 120 questionnaires to resident, agency, church, private and outdoor-education camps and tripping businesses, about 60 responses, eight provinces. Hoyer's opening explains the whole 1979-80 exercise and enlarges the picture: 'Following A NUMBER OF TRAGIC CANOEING AND TRIPPING ACCIDENTS in Canada, the Society of Camp Directors became alarmed to hear of the number of organizations and associations which initiated plans to establish yet more sets of standards and rules' -- plural, so the December 1978 Quebec incident was not the only one. His closing note says 'the questionnaire and the tabulated responses can be obtained from the C.C.A. office', so a full data set once existed on paper. Ask Trent for it by that description; try also the NEATHERN TRUST and MARY NORTHWAY's own papers, since a funder's file may hold an instrument the association's does not. Still open: nothing printed names the 1978 incident.
priorities.notes: Source: editorial, Canadian Camping Vol. 30 No. 6 (December 1978), p. 3. Word-for-word read, issue 122. Watch the 1979 issues for the follow-up as the read continues. Questionnaire responses found at issue 131 (Canadian Camping Vol. 32 No. 3, May 1980, pp. 1-4).

priorities.description:
ASK FOR KANAWANA'S RECORDS BY THE NINE STANDARD FORM NAMES. The Ontario Camping Association sold a kit of 'Suggested Camp Forms' at $3.30 a set in March 1980, printed on 8.5x11 paper and explicitly designed to be copied or adapted by any camp. The nine forms are: CAMPER APPLICATION FORM; CAMP STAFF APPLICATION FORM; STAFF HEALTH CERTIFICATE; CAMPER'S HEALTH CERTIFICATE; STAFF CONTRACT LETTER; STAFF REFERENCE FORM; COUNSELLOR EVALUATION FORM; CAMPER EVALUATION REPORT FORM; ACCIDENT REPORT FORM. Every document class this project has been reconstructing piecemeal from the camping press turns out to have existed as a standardised purchasable set. ACTION: when next writing to Concordia (YMCA of Montreal fonds P0145) and to Trent, ask for Kanawana material under these exact names rather than in general terms, and ask the Ontario Camping Association's successor body whether a copy of the 1980 kit survives, since it would show what a camp's blank forms looked like even where the completed ones are lost. ALSO ASK the ACQ successor body for the Quebec equivalents -- the ACQ's own 'feuille A.C.Q.' interview sheet is named in its 1976 director education programme (p_314). NOTE for the embargo register: the Counsellor Evaluation Form and Staff Reference Form are the instruments behind r_0001-type material, and the Camper's Health Certificate carries medical and, for girls, menarche information -- any such Kanawana documents that surface are sensitive on their face and should be registered before extraction. TWO MORE FORM NAMES (added 2026-09-04, issue 134): the CCA's December 1980 catalogue sells ACA health forms individually at 5c each, marked 'These forms are not to be reproduced by any other agency', and the list adds GIRL'S HEALTH EXAMINATION CARD and BOY'S HEALTH EXAMINATION CARD to the Ontario set, alongside Accident Report Form, Health Record Card, Camp Health Record Form, Camp Health Examination Form and Camp Staff Application. Ask under these names too. Note also that the ACA forms were NOT to be copied, unlike the Ontario kit, so a camp using them would have bought printed stock -- which may survive as blanks. AND ASK FOR THE STAFF MANUAL, WHICH HOLDS THE REST (added 2026-09-04, issue 135). The association printed a full specification of a camp staff manual in February 1981: bound 'in a stiff loose-leaf cover' with 'different coloured pages for different sections', and containing, among seven parts, a directional map and site sketch showing trails, programme areas and buildings; 'a brief historical sketch of the camp'; an explanation of the role camping plays in the sponsoring organization's total programme; personnel policies including 'employment and dismissal procedures' and salary scales; SAMPLE FORMS USED AT CAMP -- 'test sheets (swimming, canoeing, camp crafts); TRIPPING REPORTS; PARENT REPORTS, REPORTS TO SECTION HEADS; COUNSELLOR EVALUATION'; and JOB ANALYSES for programme director, section head, specialist, activity counsellor, cabin counsellor and the CIT programme. A single surviving Kanawana staff manual would therefore carry the camp's own historical sketch, its site map, its dismissal procedures, its pay scales, its blank forms and its job descriptions together. ASK CONCORDIA FOR IT BY NAME -- 'staff manual', 'camp manual', 'counsellor manual' -- and note the project already holds one document of the family, the 1951 'Kamp Kanawana History' presented at a staff training course, which is exactly the 'brief historical sketch' the specification prescribes. AND FIND WILKINSON (added 2026-09-04, issue 137). Robert E. Wilkinson, 'Camps, Their Planning and Management', C.V. Mosby, Toronto, 1981, 291 pp., hardcover -- by a professor in McGill's Department of Physical Education who was a CCA member THROUGH THE ASSOCIATION DES CAMPS DU QUEBEC and associated with Camp Nominingue. Its reviewer, Eanswythe Flynn, says it carries 'scores of charts, sketches, plans and SPECIMENS OF EVERY KIND OF BUSINESS FORM ANY CAMP RECORDS WOULD REQUIRE', with 52 sketches and charts by Mrs Wilkinson, and the publisher says it 'includes national code of ethics for Canadian Camping Association'. A copy would show what Quebec camp paperwork of the period looked like, from a Quebec-affiliated author, and would supply the CCA code of ethics in full. Widely held academic title -- try McGill, Concordia, BAnQ and interlibrary loan before any archive. AND ASK FOR THE JANUARY 1983 NATIONAL STANDARDS WORKSHOP PAPERS (added 2026-09-04, issue 142). Brian Law's CCA Standards Task Force report for 1981-82 says Fitness Canada agreed to fund a workshop in January 1983 'to examine the national picture on standards and recommended practices for member camps', and lists the questions it would put to every provincial association: a provincial comparison of written standards as they stood in the summer of 1981; then, by province, who has mandatory standards, who uses a scoring or percentage system, whether there is a pass/fail system, the question of authority as it relates to provincial legislation, informal or formal ties to provincial licensing bodies, and whether accreditation and visitation is annual, biennial or triennial; and then the composition of visitation and accreditation teams -- who qualifies to accredit a camp, what qualifications are required, what training is required yearly, and who gives that group its credibility and authority. If the workshop produced a written comparison it would contain the fullest description of the ACQ's accreditation process this project could obtain, and would say exactly what a Kanawana accreditation visit involved and what record it generated. Ask Trent (CCA/ACC fonds) for the workshop papers, and the ACQ successor body for its own submission. TWO MORE OBJECTS TO ASK FOR BY NAME (added 2026-09-04, issue 146). (1) THE CCA/ACC MEMBER CAMP CERTIFICATE. The magazine's advice column describes the system: 'there is one for camps accredited by the provincial standards committee and another for member camps who are not accredited. Once the camp receives the member camp certificate, the CCA/ACC forwards the year stickers to all the provincial presidents. These are sent to each camp to keep the certificate up to date.' A Kanawana certificate would have hung in the camp office, and ITS YEAR STICKERS WOULD DATE THE CAMP'S MEMBERSHIP YEAR BY YEAR -- ask former staff and the Concordia fonds for the object, not just the paperwork. (2) THE CCA CIT MANUAL, 'a practical manual for counsellor-in-training programs, with handy instructor insert notes', published by the Canadian Camping Association and available 1 May 1983 -- the manual begun by Jean Funk's committee and redrafted under Dinny Biggs; relevant to traditions/cit-lit-program.md. UPDATE 2026-09-04 (issue 147): Brian Law's Standards Task Force report confirms the document exists and names it. The National Standards Workshop of 25-26 January 1983 had as its first objective to 'update the EXISTING COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF PROVINCIAL STANDARDS for organized camping', and delegates prepared their provincial comparisons IN ADVANCE of the workshop -- so a written, updated, province-by-province comparison of camp standards including Quebec's was compiled in January 1983, and the earlier edition it updated predates it. Its second objective was to 'review and document extensively the visitation process', which would describe how a camp like Kanawana was actually inspected. The task force was extended eighteen months with a further workshop set for 1985. Ask Trent for Standards Task Force / National Standards Workshop files 1982-1985. Note also the workshop's conclusion, now written into canadian-camping-movement.md: 'CCA/ACC should not accredit camps but should promote good camping practices through education of camp directors.' UPDATE 2026-09-05 (issue 151): a SECOND edition is planned. Brian Law's Standards Task Force report for 1983 sets as objectives for the autumn of 1984 'a new provincial comparison of existing practices, the education of visitors, and an examination of the process of accreditation'. So there are now at least three generations of this document to ask Trent for: the pre-1983 original, the January 1983 update prepared for the National Standards Workshop, and the autumn 1984 revision. Law also notes requests for standards information reaching the CCA from Mexico, the USA and South America.

EXTENDED (extraction pass, issue 132): A FOURTH RECORD CLASS. The Society of Camp Directors' 1980 tripping survey records that at Canadian camps 'Logs are kept for future occasions, evaluations of campers for post camp evaluations, staff evaluations for future reference, are all carried on in some form or other.' So the request should name TRIP LOGS and the camper and staff evaluations written FROM trips, alongside the nine standard OCA forms. And for Quebec specifically, ask the ACQ successor for the 'feuille A.C.Q.' -- the standard staff interview sheet the association issued to member camps, named in its own 1976 Director Education Program.

THREE MORE ROUTES TO THE BLANK FORMS (extraction pass, issues 134-137). (a) The ACA health forms the CCA sold at 5 cents each in 1980, named individually: Accident Report Form, Health Record Card, Camp Health Record Form, Girl's Health Examination Card, Boy's Health Examination Card, Camp Health Examination Form, Camp Staff Application. (b) ROBERT E. WILKINSON, 'Camps, Their Planning and Management' (C.V. Mosby, Toronto, 1981, 291 pp.) -- written by a McGill professor who was a CCA member THROUGH THE ASSOCIATION DES CAMPS DU QUEBEC and Camp Nominingue, and which Eanswythe Flynn's review says carries 'specimens of every kind of business form any camp records would require', plus the CCA's national code of ethics in full. A widely held academic title: try McGill, Concordia, BAnQ and interlibrary loan before any archive, and ask under 1978 as well as 1981, since Chapman's April 1981 article cites a 1978 C.V. Mosby edition. (c) The February 1981 STAFF MANUAL specification, which lists what a camp's own binder should contain -- historical sketch, site sketch with 'special problems which site gives rise to', dismissal procedures, salary scales, job analyses and the blank forms themselves.
priorities.notes: Source: 'Suggested Camp Forms', Canadian Camping Vol. 32 No. 2 (March 1980), p. 6, with the Camper's Health Certificate reproduced in full. Word-for-word read, issue 130. Feeds p_312, p_314 and the retrospective embargo sweep p_307.

priorities.description:
RECOVER THE COLUMN HEADINGS OF THE 1980-81 NATIONAL CAMPING STATISTICS TABLE. Canadian Camping Vol. 33 No. 5 (October 1981), p. 23, prints a table of figures for 1980-81 for all nine provinces beneath Rosaire Corbin's special report. The numbers are clean in the Internet Archive scan; THE COLUMN HEADINGS ARE SET IN ROTATED TYPE AND ARE COMPLETELY ILLEGIBLE. Quebec's row is 125 / 63,243 / 5,694 / 40; the national totals are 574 / 313,953 / 37,690 / 228. Columns 2 and 3 are almost certainly campers and staff, since their totals track the association's own 1976 projections of 260,000 campers and 32,000 staff, and column 1 reads as the number of camps -- but that is inference, and column 4 (all round numbers, summing to 228) is not identifiable at all. ACTION: obtain a clean copy of that single page -- try the Internet Archive item's page images at higher resolution or a different derivative, Trent University Archives (which holds the CCA fonds and whose deposit copies are the source of much of this run), and the ACQ successor body, which printed the French original. Do not label the columns in any wiki article until the headings are read. NOTE ALSO, from the same catalogue: Mary I. Casey's The Nurse and the Health Program at Camp is described in October 1981 as 'a revised and expanded edition of the 1979 manual' and attributed to Camp Tawingo Publications, while this project holds a CCA-published item of the same title at $2.00 by 1977 -- three dates and two publishers, possibly two different books. Resolve when a copy of either is seen. COLUMNS 1-3 ARE NOW EFFECTIVELY IDENTIFIED (added 2026-09-04, issue 142). The Summer 1982 issue prints a LABELLED national statistics table for 1980 and 1981, compiled by Marjorie Booth in March 1982. Its 1980 volunteer staff (18,405) plus paid staff (19,282) is 37,687 -- three away from the illegible table's third-column total of 37,690, which identifies COLUMN 3 AS TOTAL STAFF. Its accredited member camps (590 in 1980; 533 plus 44 non-accredited in 1981) bracket the 574 of column 1, identifying COLUMN 1 AS CAMPS. Column 2's 313,953 is consistent with a head count of campers rather than camper/days (which was 3,962,848). COLUMN 4 IS STILL UNIDENTIFIED: its values are 10, 18, 15, 40, 60, 15, 20, 40, 10, summing to 228; it is not day camps (126 nationally), not extended-season camps (7), and not a subset of column 1 (Saskatchewan's 20 exceeds its 19 camps). A clean copy is still needed for column 4 and for confirmation of 1-3. SECOND TABLE TO RECOVER FROM THE SAME CAMPAIGN: the FOREIGN CAMP COUNSELLORS table (CCDO 2333-126, source Canada Manpower & Immigration) in Vol. 34 No. 2 (Summer 1982), p. 10 -- national totals of 828 (1980) and 820 (1981) are legible but the provincial columns are not, so the Quebec figure for foreign counsellors admitted with and without Manpower clearance is recoverable but not yet read. THIRD RECOVERY TARGET, AND THE MOST URGENT (added 2026-09-04, issue 145): EVERY PAGE OF CANADIAN CAMPING VOL. 34 NO. 4 (WINTER 1983) WAS SCANNED 180 DEGREES ROTATED and machine-read upside down, so the cached OCR text is unusable as it stands. The issue was read by way of scripts/reread/unrotate.py, a decoder written for this project that reverses each line and maps rotated glyphs back; the recovery is roughly 80% clean but LOSSY AND AMBIGUOUS (rotated 'b' and rotated 'q' both arrive as 'b'; rotated 'a' arrives as 'e', 'B' or 'q'). Findings block 145 and the wiki passages drawn from it are flagged accordingly. WHAT A CLEAN COPY WOULD SETTLE: (1) the exact wording and the figure in Marjorie Booth's statement that only about 10-12% of Canadian camps belonged to their provincial association -- the single most important number this read has produced about the association's coverage; (2) the acreage (160) and the 60% French / 40% English camper split she gives for Camp Oolahwan in 1977; (3) THE YEAR OF THE CCA CONFERENCE DIGEST from which Bruno Morawetz's 'The Importance of the Unimportant' is reprinted -- the attribution line appears only in this printing and the digits are consistent with 1961 or 1971, which matters because the essay has been quoted in this wiki from the 1975 and 1977 printings and its true origin is earlier than either; (4) the '600,000 Canadian children every year' figure and how it reconciles with the 313,953 campers reported by member camps; (5) the surname of the letter-writer whose objection to the beer editorial describes the camp labour market. ACTION: request a re-scan or a photographic copy of Vol. 34 No. 4 from the Internet Archive item, from Trent University Archives (which holds the CCA/ACC fonds and deposited much of this run), or from any library holding the bound volume. UPDATE 2026-09-04 (issue 147): LARGELY ANSWERED for the categories. The 1982 Annual Report prints 'CCA/ACC STATISTICS 1982 - SUMMER' by province with EVERY HEADING LEGIBLE -- member camps total/accredited/non-accredited, day/resident/other, 4-season and 3-season, camper-beds, individual campers, camper-days, foreign campers and camper-days, volunteer and paid staff, staff-days, foreign staff, student staff, $ food, $ wages, $ foreign staff wages, $ foreign camper fees, and % return per province. That is the same family of headings as the illegible October 1981 table, and it is consistent with the identification made at issue 142 (camps, campers, total staff). STILL OPEN: column 4 of the 1981 table (10, 18, 15, 40, 60, 15, 20, 40, 10) matches no 1982 row and remains unidentified -- a clean scan of Vol. 34 No. 1 (October 1981) is still wanted for it, as is the rotated Vol. 34 No. 4 scan. Quebec 1982 for the record: 129 member camps, all 129 accredited, 117 resident and 10 day camps, 15,791 camper-beds, 52,977 individual campers, 820,812 camper-days, 4,618 paid staff against 790 volunteers, $5.371M wages, $3.208M food, 48% return rate.

WHAT THE TABLE SAYS, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT (extraction pass, issue 139). The figures themselves are clean and are now in kb/facts.json: NFLD 29 / 12,974 / 353; NS 37 / 7,704 / 1,078; NB 21 / 35,764 / 4,497; QUE 125 / 63,243 / 5,694; ONT 197 / 91,281 / 13,339; MAN 33 / 10,047 / 2,228; SASK 19 / 3,677 / 422; ALTA 62 / 60,804 / 8,356; BC 51 / 19,459 / 1,723; TOTAL 574 / 313,953 / 37,690, with a fourth column of round numbers summing to 228 that is not identifiable at all. Columns 2 and 3 total in line with the association's 1976 figures of 260,000 campers and 32,000 staff, so campers and staff is the natural reading -- an inference from the totals, not a heading. TWO CAUTIONS MUST TRAVEL WITH ANY NUMBER TAKEN FROM IT. Rosaire Corbin's accompanying text says the figures 'ont la valeur objective de savants calculs d'extrapolation effectues afin de remedier aux 45% des non-repondants' -- extrapolations covering a 45% non-response rate. And the headings are rotated type illegible in this scan, which is a defect of the copy, not an absence in the source: get a clean page image before labelling the columns anywhere.

THREE OF FOUR COLUMNS DECODED (extraction pass, issue 142). Marjorie Booth's labelled national table of March 1982 gives 1980 volunteer staff 18,405 and paid staff 19,282, totalling 37,687 -- three away from the provincial table's column-3 total of 37,690, which is as close as two separately compiled tables get. So COLUMN 3 IS TOTAL STAFF. COLUMN 1 IS CAMPS: 574 against 590 accredited member camps in 1980 and 533 + 44 = 577 member camps in 1981. COLUMN 2 IS CAMPERS as a head count, not camper/days, consistent with the 1976 projection of 260,000. COLUMN 4 IS STILL UNIDENTIFIED: values 10, 18, 15, 40, 60, 15, 20, 40, 10; not day camps (126 nationally), not accredited camps as a subset (Saskatchewan's 20 exceeds its 19 camps), not extended-season camps. A SECOND TABLE TO RECOVER FROM THE SAME CLEAN COPY: Barry Lowes's 'FOREIGN CAMP COUNSELLORS (CCDO 2333-126)' from Canada Manpower & Immigration, 1980 and 1981 by province, with and without Manpower clearance -- national totals 828 and 820, Ontario 709 and 654, and a Quebec row the OCR cannot read.

SUBSTANTIALLY ANSWERED (extraction pass, issue 147). The 1982 annual report prints 'CCA/ACC STATISTICS 1982 - SUMMER' by province WITH EVERY HEADING LEGIBLE, and the categories confirm the identification made from Booth's national table. Quebec's column and the national totals are now in kb/facts.json, including a '% Return/Province' row that gives Quebec 48% -- the per-province response rate this project needed, printed beside the numbers. TWO THINGS STILL OUTSTANDING: column 4 of the illegible October 1981 table (10, 18, 15, 40, 60, 15, 20, 40, 10) matches no row in the 1982 table and is still unidentified; and Barry Lowes's 'FOREIGN CAMP COUNSELLORS' table by province remains unreadable in the Summer 1982 scan. A clean copy of Vol. 34 No. 4 (Winter 1983) is a third recovery target, since that whole issue is scanned 180 degrees rotated.

priorities.description:
OBTAIN THE PROGRAMME AND DELEGATE LIST OF THE FIRST INTERNATIONAL CAMPING CONGRESS, TORONTO, 26-29 JANUARY 1983. Canadian Camping Vol. 33 No. 6 (Winter 1982), p. 10, advertises it in both languages -- 'Bienvenu a Toronto pour notre premier congres international des camps', Sheraton Centre, full registration $160 ($125 before 20 December 1982), slogan 'ENSEMBLE ON EST PLUS FORT' -- and the Central Region report calls it 'the CCA/ACC's biggest event ever', with leaders in camping from all over the world invited as speakers or delegates and a National Workshop on Promotion timed to coincide, chaired by Marnie Ellis, an active A.C.Q. member. WHY THIS MATTERS HERE: connections/institutional-lineage/sgw-concordia-connection.md already records that Raye Kass -- Concordia Assistant Professor of Applied Human Sciences, Program Director of the Centre for Human Relations and Community Studies, and Hedley Dimock's collaborator -- 'presented on camp leadership at the International Camping Congress', undated and sourced only to Wikipedia. The CCA's 1983 Toronto congress was the first of its name in Canada and is a strong candidate for the one she spoke at, but international camping congresses were also held elsewhere, so NOTHING IS ASSERTED IN THAT ARTICLE until the programme is seen. ACTION: ask Trent University Archives (Thomas J. Bata Library, which holds the CCA/ACC fonds) for the 1983 Congress programme, proceedings, delegate list and any published papers; check them for Raye Kass, for the Association des Camps du Quebec, and for any YMCA of Montreal or Kanawana name. If Kass is on the programme it dates and places a documented link between Concordia's human-relations centre and the national camping movement, three years before the period this project's Kanawana record thins out. A PARTIAL SPEAKER LIST IS NOW IN HAND (added 2026-09-04, issue 141): John Latimer's Congress update in Canadian Camping Vol. 34 No. 1 (Spring 1982), p. 13, names those committed as of that spring -- Sir Edmund Hillary (opening session, 26 January), Dr. Leo Buscaglia (closing banquet, 29 January), and as session leaders Bruce Werber (Colorado Outdoor Education Center for the Handicapped), Barbara Hertell (Youth Programmes, Alberta Forest Service), Bryce Taylor ('one of Canada's most significant authorities on Indian Lore and Culture'), DR. HEDLEY DIMOCK, Steve Van Matre, Dr. Betty van der Smissen (President, ACA), Chuck Kujawa (incoming ACA President), Nelson Weiters, Ron Johnstone, Barry Lowes, Bruno Morawetz, Brian Law, Kirk Wipper, Ken Low, Bill Mason and Richard Underwood (NASA), plus one speaker from Tokyo and one from New Delhi. Raye Kass is NOT on this list, but the list is explicitly incomplete ('there are so many more from whom we have yet to hear') and her closest collaborator, Dimock, IS on it. TWO FURTHER REASONS TO GET THE PRINTED PROGRAMME: (a) the fund-raising appeal signed by Al Goodman promised that 'every member who makes a donation... will be acknowledged in our printed programme material', so the programme carries a DONOR LIST in which any Quebec or Montreal camp that gave will be named; (b) the Department of External Affairs circulated 32 countries and the Society of Camp Directors gave $1,500 with members asked to match at $19.83 each, so the finances and the international invitation list are documented somewhere in the same fonds. The Congress was co-sponsored by the Ontario Camping Association, so OCA records are a second place to ask. PRE-CONGRESS PROGRAMME NOW KNOWN (added 2026-09-04, issue 143). Canadian Camping Vol. 34 No. 3 (Autumn 1982), p. 9, prints the pre-Congress schedule. The CCA/ACC Board met 24-25 January 1983; three CCA workshops ran 25-26 January -- Promotions (Marnie Ellis, Quebec), Standards (Brian Law) and Education (Dorothy Walter) -- and Jocelyn Palm's President's Perspective states that EACH PROVINCIAL ASSOCIATION HAD FOUR REPRESENTATIVES WHOSE TRAVEL WAS PAID BY THE CCA AND FITNESS CANADA, so the Association des Camps du Quebec sent four named people to Toronto in January 1983 at national expense and the names should be in the CCA's records. Six KINDRED GROUPS met beforehand at the Sheraton Centre, and one of them is A YMCA GROUP, coordinated by Rob Fleming c/o Camp Wanakita, Hamilton YMCA, meeting 25 January 9 a.m. to 26 January noon -- THE MOST LIKELY SINGLE OCCASION FOR A YMCA OF MONTREAL OR KANAWANA REPRESENTATIVE TO HAVE BEEN PRESENT, and worth asking about by name. The other kindred groups were Christian Camping International, Brethren Assemblies Camps, Private Christian Science Camps, Day Camp (Larry Bell), and 'Career Preparation for University Students in the Outdoor Field' convened by Claude Cousineau of the Department of Recreology, University of Ottawa. The Canadian Recreational Canoeing Association held six committee meetings on 28-29 January including a joint executive with the American Canoe Association. Kirsty Griffiths, seconded by the Ontario March of Dimes, co-ordinated the entire Congress programme; Al Goodman chaired fund-raising and Jack Zoubie handled External Affairs publicity in over 30 countries. DONOR LISTS: donors' names were to be printed BOTH in the programme material and on the BANQUET PROGRAM. THE CONGRESS WAS RECORDED AND SOLD ON CASSETTE (added 2026-09-04, issue 146). The back page of Canadian Camping Vol. 35 No. 1 (Spring 1983) advertises 'Audio Cassettes Available -- Recorded live at the International Camping Congress Conference, Sheraton Centre, Toronto, January 26-29, 1983', sold by AUDIO ARCHIVES OF CANADA, 1140 Victoria Park Avenue, Markham, Ontario L3R 1B2, at $9 a cassette with a six-cassette binder free on every order of six, and PRINTS THE FULL SESSION LIST WITH CODES AND SPEAKERS. Sessions include 'Camping Is For Everyone' (Hillary), 'Camp Leadership - The State of the Art', 'Legal Liability of Organized Camps & Youth Organizations' (van der Smissen, two parts), 'CAMPER SAFETY AND THE LAW' (DR. R. E. WILKINSON OF McGILL, MONTREAL), 'Good Grief!' (John Saynor), 'Cults: A Threat to Campers and Staff', 'Safe Whitewater Canoeing at Camp', 'Wilderness Medicine', 'Third World Camping', 'Camping with Persons with a Disability', 'The Underprivileged: from Camp to Group Home', 'Tapping Your Greatest Natural Resource: Your Staff!', 'Environmental & Outdoor Education in the UK', 'Outdoor Education in South Australia', 'Who Are We? Leadership Training in the Sugar Bush', and Buscaglia's closing address. THIS IS THE MOST DIRECT ROUTE TO WHAT WAS ACTUALLY SAID: try Audio Archives of Canada or its successor, Trent (CCA/ACC fonds), and the Ontario Camping Association's successor. CONFIRMED FROM THE DELIVERED PROGRAMME: over 1000 delegates from Japan, England, New Zealand, the USA, Australia, Norway and Canada; over 90 sessions; 1,100 at the closing banquet; four years in planning; the next congress planned for 1987 in Washington, D.C. RAYE KASS IS ABSENT FROM A THIRD LIST -- recorded as a repeated null, not a conclusion, since all three lists are partial and none is the printed programme. A CONGRESS PHOTO COMPETITION was also held, with winners named in Canadian, United States and International categories, so a set of prize-winning 1983 camp photographs was held by the association.

TWO MORE REASONS TO GET THE PROGRAMME (extraction pass, issue 141). (a) HEDLEY DIMOCK IS ON THE SPEAKER LIST. John Latimer's Spring 1982 update names the session leaders committed so far, including 'Dr. Hedley Dimock' -- the Concordia professor who did the 1960-61 counsellor-effectiveness research AT KANAWANA and gave the CCA's 1967 keynote. Raye Kass is not on the preliminary list, but it is explicitly incomplete ('there are so many more from whom we have yet to hear') and her closest collaborator is on it, which strengthens the case that the congress she presented at was this one. Also on the list: Sir Edmund Hillary at the opening session, Leo Buscaglia at the closing banquet, and 'Bryce Taylor, one of Canada's most significant authorities on Indian Lore and Culture' -- a new name for site/indigenous-names-and-land.md. (b) THE PROGRAMME CARRIES A DONOR LIST. The fund-raising appeal promised that 'every member who makes a donation... will be acknowledged in our printed programme material', so any Quebec or Montreal camp that gave will be named in it.

A YMCA KINDRED-GROUP MEETING AT THE CONGRESS (extraction pass, issue 143). Six kindred groups met before the 1983 Congress, among them YMCA, coordinated by Rob Fleming, c/o Camp Wanakita, Hamilton YMCA, from 25 January 9 a.m. to 26 January noon. That is the most likely single occasion in the whole run for a Kanawana or YMCA of Montreal representative to have been present, and it should be asked about by name alongside the main programme. The Promotions, Standards and Education workshops of 25-26 January each took FOUR REPRESENTATIVES PER PROVINCIAL ASSOCIATION with travel paid by the CCA and Fitness Canada -- so the ACQ sent four people to Toronto at national expense and their names are in the CCA's records. Also convening: Claude Cousineau of the University of Ottawa's Department of Recreology, on career preparation for university students in the outdoor field.

THE CONGRESS HAPPENED, AND IT IS ON TAPE (extraction pass, issue 146). Over 1000 delegates from Japan, England, New Zealand, the United States, Australia, Norway and Canada, over 90 sessions, 1,100 at the closing banquet, 26-29 January 1983 at the Sheraton Centre, Toronto. EVERY SESSION WAS RECORDED AND SOLD: 'Audio Cassettes Available -- Recorded live at the International Camping Congress', from AUDIO ARCHIVES OF CANADA, 1140 Victoria Park Avenue, Markham, Ontario L3R 1B2, $9 a cassette, with the full session list and speakers printed. That is a commercial artefact set and a direct route to what was actually said -- try Audio Archives' successor, Trent, and the OCA. CONFIRMED DELIVERED: Dr. Robert E. Wilkinson of McGill ran 'Camper Safety and the Law', so the Montreal presence is real and not merely announced. Raye Kass is absent from this speaker list too -- a third null, recorded as that and no more, since these lists are partial. Derek Walsh received his CCA Certificate of Appreciation at the reception before the Congress banquet on 29 January 1983.
