priorities.description: FIND THE ACQ'S ANNUAIRE 82 -- a published 1982 directory of Quebec camps that would list Kanawana. The Association des Camps du Quebec's own annual report for 1981-82, printed in French in Canadian Camping Vol. 34 No. 2 (Summer 1982), p. 7 and signed CLAIRE MENARD, says the association spent the year affirming 'sa representation et l'image des camps du Quebec par la publication de l'Annuaire 82, par une Semaine des camps intensive, par une presence de plus en plus incitante aupres des media et du publique.' Kanawana was an accredited Quebec camp and a member of the ACQ, so it would be listed -- with, on the pattern of the 1975 and 1976 directories this read has already used, its address, director, capacity, ages served and session structure. That is a direct answer to several of this project's thinnest questions about the early 1980s. WHERE TO LOOK: the ACQ's successor body (Association des camps du Quebec, camps.qc.ca) and its own archives; BAnQ, which receives Quebec legal deposit and should hold a published annuaire; the CCA/ACC fonds at Trent, which received provincial directories; Concordia's YMCA of Montreal fonds, since a member camp would have been sent one; and university libraries in Montreal. ALSO ASK for the other years of the series -- an Annuaire published annually would give a run of Kanawana entries through the 1980s. RELATED: the same report names the ACQ's 1982 Congress, held in March at Laval under the theme 'Les Vacances, Facteur de Croissance', and an intensive 'Semaine des camps'; conference programmes and Camp Week material are worth asking for in the same request. CLAIRE MENARD is a new name for the Quebec association's officers and should be added to the people index and assessed for a stub. ALSO ASK ABOUT NATIONAL CAMPING DAY, 1 APRIL 1983 (added 2026-09-04, issue 145): the CCA's Executive Director said in November 1982 that the pre-Congress promotion workshop, chaired by Marnie Ellis of the Quebec association, would produce 'a National Camping Day which will be focusing on the value of the camp counsellor's contribution to the children of this country. This will be happening on April 1st', with two trained delegates per province to carry it home and the hope it would become annual. A dated national publicity event run through a Quebec chairman should have left traces in the Quebec press and in the ACQ's own records, and if Kanawana took part it would be one of the few dated public appearances of the camp in the early 1980s. Ask the ACQ successor body, and search La Presse, Le Devoir and the Gazette for late March and early April 1983. UPDATE 2026-09-04 (issue 147): the ACQ's 1982-83 annual report, again signed CLAIRE MENARD, adds three more Quebec documents to look for alongside the Annuaire 82. (1) An ETUDE DE MARCHE -- a market study of Quebec camp clientele 'realisee cette annee', reporting a high rate of client satisfaction: the only known survey of what Quebec camp families thought of their camps in this period. (2) A GUIDE D'EVALUATION DES SERVICES 'actuellement en phase de realisation'. (3) The rebuilt accreditation programme itself -- 'un renouvellement important' reorienting it toward member self-evaluation, universal standards and a code of ethics, so the ACQ CODE D'ETHIQUE and the revised standards are separate findable documents, and a Kanawana accreditation file from before and after 1982-83 would be assessed on different terms. On the Semaine des camps: it had been running 'depuis plus de cinq ans' by 1983, i.e. from about 1977, through exhibition halls, shopping centres, radio and television, and newspaper and magazine articles -- a five-year run of Quebec press coverage with Kanawana a member camp throughout. In 1983 it was deliberately moved 'to coincide with April 14th and featured a media blitz', so BAnQ for the week of 14 April 1983 is the single highest-yield date to search. Add also the ACQ colloquium for directors, senior staff and counsellors of 13-15 MAY 1983. UPDATE 2026-09-04 (issue 148): the 1984 National Camping Day was devolved to the provinces -- posters went to the PROVINCIAL offices in early November 1983 with a letter to each Director and an inquiry form, and 'each province should have a list of all its member camps ready to send out to those filling in the inquiry form'. So the ACQ held a ready list of its Quebec member camps in the winter of 1983-84: another form of the Quebec camp directory this priority is chasing, and one that was mailed to the public on request. Second National Camping Day: 21 March 1984, theme 'Don't Wait for Summer - Think Camping Now!'. UPDATE 2026-09-05 (issue 151, the ACQ's 1983 annual report signed Claire Menard): FOUR NEW QUEBEC LEADS. (1) LA SEMAINE DES CAMPS 23-28 APRIL 1984, the ACQ's principal spring promotion, run with a special project in collaboration with the MINISTERE DU LOISIR, DE LA CHASSE ET DE LA PECHE that paid for a 'message radio' during the week -- an exactly dated week of Quebec camp promotion in press and on air; search BAnQ and broadcast archives for 23-28 April 1984, and the MLCP's own files for the project. (2) THE ACQ SOUGHT AN EXEMPTION FOR SUMMER CAMPS FROM QUEBEC'S LOI SUR LA PROTECTION DU CONSOMMATEUR, through 'plusieurs rencontres avec differents intervenants' in 1983-84. This governed how camp fees, contracts and refunds with parents worked and applied directly to Kanawana; trail runs through the Office de la protection du consommateur and the National Assembly record. (3) An ACQ QUESTIONNAIRE was sent to all member camps in the AUTUMN OF 1983 asking what they needed and what services they expected from the association -- Kanawana very likely answered one, and the compiled results would describe the Quebec camp sector from the inside. (4) ACQ thematic days on 'La gestion par informatique', 'Les nouveaux jeux' and 'La place des parents au camp'. Also for the record: the ACQ could not use its national Consultant/Advisor in 1983-84 'due to insufficient registration for their Winter Conference', and the CCA's French Language Committee was founded in the AUTUMN OF 1974 and held a SPRING 1976 CONGRESS of French-language camp directors from every province on the theme 'L'activite pedagogique du camp de vacances' -- proceedings or a programme may survive. UPDATE 2026-09-05 (issue 157): TWO FRENCH-LANGUAGE DOCUMENT SETS ENTER THE CCA CATALOGUE, both worth finding. (1) The SERIE 'UN CAMP A FAIRE' -- an eight-part French camp-management curriculum: Manuel de gestion volumes on 'Aspects generaux de l'administration', 'Gestion des ressources humaines', 'Gestion des programmes', 'Gestion des equipements' and 'Gestion financiere', plus 'Evaluation du rendement', 'Les objectifs et le programme' and 'La planification des ressources humaines et selection du personnel'. Almost certainly ACQ or Quebec-government work rather than CCA work, though the catalogue does not say. This is the management doctrine a Quebec camp director of the later 1980s was being sold. (2) 'LES COLONIES DE VACANCES D'EXPRESSION FRANCAISE EN BELGIQUE (COMMUNAUTE WALLONIE-BRUXELLES) ET LES CAMPS DE VACANCES AU QUEBEC' -- a comparative study setting Quebec's camps beside francophone Belgium's, sold nationally in 1986. An outside description of the Quebec camp sector, which is rarer than an inside one. Neither author nor publisher is given; try the ACQ, BAnQ, Voila/AMICUS and Belgian holiday-camp federation records. UPDATE 2026-09-05 (issue 158): A KANAWANA ACCREDITATION VISIT SHOULD HAVE HAPPENED IN 1986, AND THE ACQ SAYS WHY. Its 1986 report: 'quatre consultants visiteront pres de soixante (60) camps de vacances. Ce programme exige que LES CAMPS ACCREDITES SOIENT VISITES TOUS LES DEUX ANS. Les camps de vacances qui ont connu des changements majeurs au cours de l'annee (LE CHANGEMENT DE DIRECTEUR, PAR EXEMPLE) sont egalement visites.' Kanawana's directorship passed from Peter Goddard to Jay Netherwood inside the YMCA's FY1986, so on the ACQ's own stated rule Kanawana was visited in 1986 on account of the change, and a VISITATION REPORT should exist. Ask the ACQ and Trent for 1986 Quebec visitation records. Note also the shift from the annual visitation of 1975 to a TWO-YEAR CYCLE by 1986, worked by four consultants over about sixty camps. TWO MORE QUEBEC DOCUMENTS from the same issue: a NEW ACQ PARENTS' GUIDE AND DIRECTORY in members' hands in 1986; and a 1985 REPERTOIRE DES CAMPS FRANCOPHONES HORS QUEBEC, published by the CCA's French Language Committee with the CONSEIL DE LA VIE FRANCAISE EN AMERIQUE, twenty-four camps in its first edition -- available in limited numbers from provincial associations or the CCA national secretary. And the ACQ dated its own 25th anniversary to JANUARY 1961, the amalgamation of the French and English sections, rather than to the 1937 founding of the English Section. UPDATE 2026-09-06 (searched, and the result is an ACCESS FAILURE not a null): the four catalogue surfaces that would locate a copy were all unusable from this environment on 2026-09-06 -- iris.banq.qc.ca and voila.bac-lac.gc.ca were both refused at the network gateway (CONNECT answered 502, logged as a policy denial), search.worldcat.org returned HTTP 429, and the Google Books API returned HTTP 429 for quota exhaustion, so its three null queries mean nothing. Internet Archive full-text DID run and is genuinely empty: "Association des camps du Quebec" numFound 0, title:(annuaire) AND (camps OR colonies) three hits all irrelevant. BAnQ numerique's own record for the ACQ's "Rapport annuel" (notice 52327/3671752) shows the run COMMENCING WITH 2012/2013 and consultable only from terminals inside BAnQ buildings, so BAnQ numerique does not reach the 1980s. See f_4871, f_4872. WHAT THE SEARCH DID PRODUCE: the nearest surviving volume of the series was already in this project's own notes and had never been connected to this priority -- Concordia P145/12N04, box HA1888, "Annuaire 1979, liste des membres. - 1979" (f_2262). The request for it has been ADDED TO THE CONCORDIA LETTER (p_282, request 6) along with the same box's constitution and 1978-79 publications. Also established: "Annuaire" names a genre in this movement, not one publication -- the Ontario association's Annuaire des Membres et Associes (quoted January 1975) and the CCA's own "Annuaire National des Camps 1976" -- and the 1979 ACQ volume's own title calls it a liste des membres, so the assumption that an ACQ Annuaire carried directory detail is UNTESTED (f_4873). Written into canadian-camping-movement.md. STILL OPEN, and now blocked on routes a person must walk: BAnQ's IRIS catalogue and legal-deposit register, the Trent CCA fonds, the ACQ itself, and Montreal university libraries.

priorities.description: CORRECT THE CITATION IN greig-macdiarmid.md AND REWRITE ITS OPEN QUESTION 1. That article attributes the Toronto General Secretaryship, the Pine Crest/Norval/Wangoma expansions, the twenty-three day camps, the Camp Illahee sentence word for word, the 21 May 1962 death and the heading form "J. G. 'Greig' Macdiarmid" to footnote 10, Grace McMorris's 2023 Concordia MA thesis. McMorris was quoting an obituary, and the read has now found it: Canadian Camping Vol. 15 No. 1 (December 1962), p. 18. Cite the primary. Open Question 1 currently says "A Toronto obituary of May 1962 is now a dated, findable target" -- but the obituary the article is quoting is this one, in the national camping magazine, and it is read in full; rewrite the question so a later pass does not hunt for a document the project already has. A Toronto NEWSPAPER obituary may still exist and may still expand his first two initials; say that instead. Also add the two new details: the wartime title "Senior Officer Overseas of Canadian YMCA War Services" (a third form, alongside the two from the Montreal annual reports, to be recorded beside them rather than collapsed into them) and the epithet "To those who knew him, he was truly 'THE CHIEF'". | COMPLETED 2026-09-05. The obituary was read in the original (Canadian Camping Vol. 15 No. 1, December 1962, p. 17-18) and everything the article had been attributing to McMorris's thesis is now cited to it as source 11: the Toronto General Secretaryship, the Pine Crest, Norval and Wangoma expansions, the twenty-three day camps, the Camp Illahee sentence, the 21 May 1962 death and the 'J. G. "Greig"' heading. Both new details added in a paragraph of their own: the wartime title 'Senior Officer Overseas of Canadian YMCA War Services', recorded BESIDE the two forms the Montreal annual reports give rather than merged with them, and the closing line 'To those who knew him, he was truly "THE CHIEF"'. Open Question 1 rewritten so no later pass hunts for a document this project already holds: what is outstanding is a TORONTO NEWSPAPER obituary of late May 1962 (Globe and Mail, Toronto Daily Star), the kind of notice that prints full given names. FINDING NOTE recorded in f_4853: the OCR renders the surname 'Macdiarniid' throughout the notice, so searching the correct spelling returns nothing in that issue -- the passage is found on 'Wangoma', 'Illahee' or 'CHIEF'.

priorities.description: RESOLVE A. ROSS SEAMAN'S 1962 SECRETARYSHIP -- national or provincial? wiki/people/a-ross-seaman.md says "He is QCA Secretary again in the 1962 and 1963 officer lists." The masthead of Canadian Camping Vol. 14 No. 2 (February 1962), under the heading "CANADIAN CAMPING ASSOCIATION, 2233 Belgrave Avenue, Montreal 28, Quebec," reads "Secretary -- Mr. A. Ross Seaman, 4140 Jean Renou, Lachine, Que.", and the same masthead stands unchanged in June 1962. He replaced Agnes Mutchler, who had held it as CCA Corresponding Secretary in December 1961. So either the article has conflated the national and provincial bodies or Seaman held both posts. Either way the article is missing a substantial fact: the serving director of Kamp Kanawana was national secretary of the Canadian Camping Association in 1962. Check the 1963 masthead and the QCA officer lists before revising.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 41-56, converted to KB facts
priorities.resolution: NATIONAL, not provincial. The 1962-63 officer list naming Seaman Secretary at 4140 Jean Renou, Lachine is the Canadian Camping Association masthead -- headed 'CANADIAN CAMPING ASSOCIATION, 2233 Belgrave Avenue, Montreal 28, Quebec', the national body, whose head office was in Montreal through Kenneth H. Murray's presidency. He is there in February 1962, June 1962 and February 1963; Agnes Mutchler held the post as Corresponding Secretary in December 1961; and by the April 1963 masthead the office has moved to Calgary with Eleanor Logan of the Edmonton YMCA as Secretary under a new president, Dr Don Smith. No Quebec Camping Association officer list appears in any cached issue between December 1961 and June 1963 -- 'Quebec Camping Association' occurs once in those eight issues, in the notice of the joint CCA/QCA/ACQ convention of 22-24 March 1962 -- and April 1962 and December 1962 carry no masthead page in the digitized text at all, so those two months can be read neither way. The article conflated the two bodies; corrected in place in wiki/people/a-ross-seaman.md, with the erroneous sentence quoted so the mistake is traceable. Whether he ALSO held the provincial post is unproven rather than disproven, and that is written into the article. See f_4928; f_2471 carries a [CORRECTED 2026-09-06] note.

priorities.description: FIND THE SUPREME COURT OF QUEBEC'S 1961-62 DROWNING JUDGMENT AGAINST A CHILDREN'S CAMP. Clifford Labbett, Canadian Camping Vol. 14 No. 3 (April 1962), p. 118: "The Supreme Court of Quebec recently handed down a 4 to 1 decision against a children's summer camp when a suit for damages was brought against the camp because a boy drowned last summer. The boy disobeyed a camp rule but the camp was still held responsible." Neither camp nor boy is named. Name them and find the citation: Quebec law reports (Rapports judiciaires de Quebec / Quebec Official Reports, Queen's Bench 1961-62), the Montreal Gazette and La Presse for summer 1961 and early 1962 via BAnQ, and CanLII's historical Quebec collection. WHY IT MATTERS: this judgment set the liability standard every Quebec camp, Kanawana included, then operated under -- a camp is liable even where the child broke a camp rule -- and it gives eight years of context to Kanawana's own 1969 drowning, attested only in the camp's own season report (p_248).

priorities.description: TRACE THE MIMEOGRAPHED PREDECESSOR OF CANADIAN CAMPING, c. 1936-1948. Anne I. Vail's tribute to Mary Edgar, Canadian Camping Vol. 12 No. 4 (June 1960), p. 167: "We are proud that she was the first editor of Canadian Camping magazine and, with her Committee, changed it from a mimeographed bulletin to a creditable printed magazine." The printed run this project has read word for word begins at Vol. 1 No. 1, February 1949. A CCA bulletin therefore circulated before that, edited by Edgar, covering roughly the years from the association's founding to 1948 -- for Kanawana, the interwar-to-postwar gap the wiki has least for. Charles Plewman's February 1957 profile independently calls the OCA's "stencilled news bulletin" begun in his presidency from 1945 "the forerunner of the present periodical." WHERE TO LOOK: the Canadian Camping Association / Ontario Camping Association fonds at Trent University Archives; Mary S. Edgar's own papers; Glen Bernard Camp.

priorities.description: CHASE THE YMCA'S OWN CAMP APPRAISAL RECORDS FOR KANAWANA. "Towards Better Practices and Higher Standards," commissioned by the National Committee on Youth Programme of the YMCA's of Canada, Canadian Camping Vol. 13 No. 4 (June 1961), p. 180, names three things: (1) "as early as 1922 an extensive system of grading YMCA camps was inaugurated by the Ontario and Quebec Boys' Work Committee," giving points for sanitation, site, equipment, programme, organization and administration, conservation, and printed reports -- that committee is Kanawana's own jurisdiction, so surviving gradings would be per-camp assessments of Kanawana from the 1920s; (2) "a major camping consultation" in 1947; and (3) "The self-evaluation form and the visitors' appraisal form now used by Canadian YMCA camps have been in use (with modifications and developments) since 1953." WHERE TO LOOK: YMCA Canada's national records; the YMCA of Montreal fonds at Concordia; the National Council of YMCAs of Canada fonds.

priorities.description: CHASE THE QCA'S 1960-61 CAMP VISITATION RETURNS. Two sources establish that Quebec camps were being visited and appraised in exactly the years Kanawana was an accredited QCA member camp in the association's own city. Canadian Camping Vol. 12 No. 4 (June 1960), p. 207: "It was agreed by Q.C.A. members that camp visiting should continue in that province, to follow the experimental lead of the Ontario group." And Alta Kahn's Quebec report, Vol. 13 No. 4 (June 1961): the QCA's goals for 1961 were a government charter incorporating the French and English sections, granted March 1961, and "To visit and appraise all camps in 1961," with a Manual of Desirable Practices two years in visitors' hands and "a committee ... working on a marking process that will ensure confidentiality." The December 1962 "Camp Director's Bookshelf" lists "Camp Visitation Forms for Alberta, Ontario, Quebec -- apply to provincial associations," so the instrument was printed and distributable. The confidentiality machinery explains why such a record was never published, and is a reason to expect it survives in an association file rather than in print. WHERE TO LOOK: Association des camps du Quebec; the CCA fonds at Trent; the CCA's Montreal office records (the office at 2233 Belgrave Avenue, Montreal, 1958-1963, whose fate is itself an open lead).

priorities.description:
SPAWN A STUB FOR POWTER'S CAMP / CAMP SANS EGAL, AND USE IT ON THE FOUNDING QUESTION. N. B. Powter, "Sixty Years Ago," Canadian Camping Vol. 14 No. 2 (February 1962), pp. 54-57, 67, is the only source found in the whole 164-issue read that dates Kanawana's predecessor camp from outside the YMCA's own paperwork: C. B. Powter "also directed the Y.M.C.A. camp at Lac St. Joseph which had been founded in 1893." C. B. Powter was Springfield-trained, on the Montreal Y staff, captain of the first basketball team to play in Canada, then Instructor of Physical Training at the High School of Montreal; he founded Camp Sans Egal on the same lake in June 1902 with 50 Montreal boys, claimed as "the first private camp in Quebec." Camp Sans Egal appears nowhere in this repo. The article also carries a full operating description (tent-group Leader system, Officer of the Day, the 1915 two-miles-to-the-inch camp map still in use in 1962, the Honour Roll of lakes visited). This belongs in connections/related-camps/, and the 1893 sentence belongs in founding-1894.md recorded as an INDEPENDENT recollection -- not folded into the pile of YMCA retrospectives, and not treated as contemporary either, since the author was an infant in 1902 and writing seventy years after the fact.

AMENDMENT (extraction pass, issue 91): THE FAMILY WAS STILL RUNNING THE CAMP IN 1971. Canadian Camping Vol. 23 No. 4 (Summer 1971) prints a visiting-policy statement signed C. B. Powter for "Powter's Camp for Boys, St. Donat de Montcalm, Quebec." The run therefore documents the Powter camp across at least 1893 to 1971, at a later site than the Lac St. Joseph one, which widens the search: a camp operating into the 1970s leaves brochures, directory listings, incorporation records and possibly living alumni, none of which an 1890s camp leaves. Chase the Quebec association's camp directories for the 1960s and 1970s, Saint-Donat-de-Montcalm municipal and parish records, and the Powter family.

priorities.description: PATCH THE RESIDUE FROM THE CATALOGUE CROSS-CHECK. scripts/reread/catalogue_check.py screens every dated entry in W. E. Yard's 1949-1963 index of Canadian Camping against this pass's own block for that issue; kb/reread/cc_catalogue_check.txt holds the output. Of 299 entries in issues 1-60, 55 did not match. Most are artefacts: the index is OCR of small type set in columns, so it mangles titles past matching and misaligns dates ("Closed Oceans -- Rev. Wilbur Howard" is filed under Dec. 1951 when the article read in this pass is Dec. 1961; "Pioneers Go Camping" appears under two different years). Others are advertisements, poems and short notices that the terser early blocks summarise without naming. The clearest genuine candidate is "An Experiment in Handi-crafts -- Gisella Commanda" (Dec. 1949, issue 4), which matters because Commanda turns up later in the same run hiring Indian regalia to camps -- a 1949 signed article by her would be an early and direct source on how that material reached Canadian camps. Work the flagged list against the cached OCR issue by issue, patch any real holes in place in cc_findings.md and say so, and re-run the screen. The screen reports candidates; it does not certify the blocks.

priorities.description: FIND THE CAMP COUNSELOR'S BOOK (Northway and Lowes, Longmans Canada, Spring 1963). Announced in Canadian Camping Vol. 15 No. 3 (April 1963) and advertised with its full contributor list in Vol. 15 No. 4 (June 1963), $1.95 paper / $3.50 cloth: edited by Dr Mary L. Northway of the Institute of Child Study and Barry G. Lowes of Camp Timberlane, with Joyce Bertram (Camp Ouareau), Margaret Govan (Camp Onawa), Flora Morrison (Camp Windy Pine Point), David and Elsie Palter (Camp Kawagama), Elizabeth Raymer (Camp Tanamakoon) and Kirk Wipper (Camp Kandalore). Ten chapters, listed in the KB. Endorsed by the CCA president; reviewed by Catherine T. Hammett as the replacement for the out-of-print American Charting the Counselor's Course. This is the single most likely printed source for what a Canadian camp counsellor in the 1960s was told to do, which is the decade of Kanawana's own CIT/LIT programme and of the counsellor research done there. TWO SIDE BENEFITS: it identifies "Mrs David Palter" -- one of only two people who answered the CCA's own "History of Canadian Camping" enquiry -- as Elsie Palter of Camp Kawagama, making her a locatable person; and it confirms Joyce Bertram, this magazine's editor for four issues, as director of Camp Ouareau, which camp-ouareau.md should carry. WHERE TO LOOK: Library and Archives Canada; university education libraries; AbeBooks and the used trade.

priorities.description: REWRITE THE ACQ'S DESCENT IN canadian-camping-movement.md. That article says "The modern successor to the QCA is the Association des camps du Quebec (ACQ)", which makes the ACQ a renamed Quebec Camping Association. Tony Shorgan -- who did the organising -- gives a different descent in Canadian Camping Vol. 17 No. 3 (April 1965), with dates: 1957, he asks at a conference planning meeting whether a few sessions could be held in French, and calls a meeting on twenty-four hours' notice at which, "Despite one of the worst blizzards we have ever had, there were some 18 French-speaking Camp Directors attending"; 12 April 1958, a special session at the Windsor Hotel strikes a committee for a year's trial under his presidency, which adopts the name "Association des Camps Canadiens Francais"; 17 July 1958, a meeting at the Crippled Children's Camp, St-Alphonse, under the honorary presidency of Monsignor J. A. Papineau, Bishop of Joliette, resolves to apply to join the QCA; 15 November 1958, permanent officers elected in the Mont St-Louis gymnasium; 1959, a bi-monthly newsletter and inter-camp visits; 1960, the name changes to "Association des Camps du Quebec (Section Francaise)"; then merger with the English-section QCA Inc. So the body Kanawana is accredited by today carries the FRENCH SECTION'S name, not a renamed QCA. Rewrite with Shorgan's dates, and spawn a Shorgan stub -- this article alone supplies well over the five-fact threshold, and he is separately documented as director of the Province of Quebec Society for Crippled Children's camp and first president of the section. | LARGELY DONE 2026-09-05, IN TWO PARTS. FIRST, THE PREMISE HAD ALREADY MOVED: a later pass had removed 'the modern successor to the QCA' framing and the article already said 'the ACQ was never simply the QCA renamed', with the 1958 founding and 1961 joining. SECOND, WHAT WAS MISSING IS NOW THERE: Shorgan's own April 1965 account, read in full and written in with his dates -- 1957 the office meeting through one of the worst blizzards with some eighteen French-speaking directors; 12 April 1958 the Windsor Hotel session and the committee named Association des Camps Canadiens Francais; 17 July 1958 at his own Crippled Children's Camp under Monsignor Papineau, resolving to apply to the QCA; 15 November 1958 permanent officers in the Mont St-Louis gymnasium; 1959 the bi-monthly newsletter and inter-camp visits; 1960 THE NAME CHANGE TO 'ASSOCIATION DES CAMPS DU QUEBEC (SECTION FRANCAISE)' (f_4863). The naming point the priority asked for is now stated: the body that accredits Kanawana carries the FRENCH SECTION'S name, adopted by that section for itself before the merger (f_4864). Three founding dates are set side by side as answers to different questions -- QCA 1937, French section 1958 named 1960, and the ACQ's own 'Fondee en 1961' from its current website (f_4859). Two discrepancies against the contemporaneous 1958 report are recorded and left standing: eighteen directors against 'some fifteen', and the office meeting of 1957 against an undated meeting chaired by Rene St-Onge; compatible if they are different events, which the 1958 report does not say (f_4865). Also noted: the surname is SHORGAN in his own byline and SHORGUN in Winter 1987. STILL TO DO: the Tony Shorgan stub. The material clears the threshold several times over -- Executive Secretary of the Quebec Society for Crippled Children, Camp Director of the Crippled Children's Camp at St. Alphonse, QCA member from about 1943, first president of the French section, QCA vice-president by 1959 -- and 23 facts in this KB already mention him. It needs its own pass, not a paragraph. | STUB DONE TOO, 2026-09-05, and as a DRAFT rather than a stub: six sources, his own dated chronology, and a career across three decades of the provincial association. wiki/people/tony-shorgan.md. NO KANAWANA CONNECTION IS ASSERTED and Open Question 3 says so plainly -- he and Kanawana's directors sat in the same association for twenty years and appear in the same officer lists, and no source puts them in a room together. He is in people/ because the association he built accredits Kanawana and because this wiki's account of that association's descent now rests on his testimony. Linked from canadian-camping-movement.md and directors-index.md. ONE PROCESS FAILURE RECORDED IN f_4863: I read the April 1965 article without first searching the KB, which had already extracted it as f_3146, f_3147, f_3148 and f_3149. The duplicate is kept, cross-linked in both directions, and says what it adds; the lesson written into it is that the KB is the index to the corpus and a source should be searched for in it BEFORE being read.

priorities.description:
FIND KANAWANA'S CENTENARY JOURNEY TRIP LOG. John Scott, Chairman of the Ontario section of the Cross-Canada Centenary Canoe Journey, closes his June 1965 briefing to participating camps: "don't forget that your Provincial Centennial Committee wants a detailed log of your encounters en route!" So a log of the 1967 Kanawana paddle was expected to exist and to have been submitted to the Quebec Camping Association, not merely kept at camp. Two supporting facts narrow the search: Robert Lazanik, QCA president, wrote in March 1965 that Quebec "already ha[d] our route marked and ha[d] begun to line up member camps who will be taking part in the trip" -- so a QCA committee file exists from 1965 -- and Margaret Govan chaired the national Cross-Canada Centenary Journey Committee from at least December 1964. WHERE TO LOOK: the Association des camps du Quebec's own archives; the CCA/ACC fonds at Trent; the Canadian Centennial Commission records at Library and Archives Canada; and the YMCA of Montreal fonds at Concordia for the camp's own copy. This would be the fullest surviving account of the 1967 trip and is the strongest single archival lead in the 1965 issues.

AMENDMENT (extraction pass, issues 90-91): THE NATIONAL VOLUME IS NOW IDENTIFIED AND DATED. Canadian Camping Vol. 23 No. 3 (Spring 1971), "For Your Bookshelf": "The Centenary Journey Committee of the Canadian Camping Association is pleased to announce that the 'Journal' which tells the story of the project is now available. It includes 'their story' which relates the historical significance of each segment of the journey and 'our story' of the experiences of Young Canadians in 1967. Maps are provided to show the route taken," at $1.50 plus 25c from the CCA, 102 Eglinton Street East, Suite 203, Toronto. Vol. 23 No. 4 (Summer 1971) confirms distribution a second time -- "Kirk Wipper and his committee are very pleased with the response to the Centenary Journey Journal" -- and records that copies went to the organizational leaders of the cross-Canada foot trail project, so the book circulated beyond the camping movement. This is a findable 1971 volume with a publisher, a price, a committee chair (Kirk Wipper) and a structure, and it is the top of the log chain: camp log -> provincial log -> national book. Search library catalogues under Canadian Camping Association and under Centenary Journey; check the OCA fonds at Trent (p_348), Library and Archives Canada, and the Canadian Canoe Museum, which descends from Wipper's own collection. || A ROUTE LOCATED 2026-09-06 (f_5209). **TRENT, QCA FONDS 85-013, BOX 2, FOLDER 22: 'Q.C.A. Centennial Commission'.** That is the provincial committee file the trip log would have been submitted into, if it was. A SUMMARIZING FETCH OF THAT FINDING AID REPORTED THE CENTENNIAL RECORDS ABSENT; the raw page has them at Box 2 Folder 22 -- do not trust a summarizer's negative about a finding aid. Finding aid cached. Not digitized. The other named routes (LAC's Centennial Commission records, Concordia for the camp's own copy) are untouched. || A MUCH BIGGER ROUTE, 2026-09-06 (f_5210). history/centennial-1967.md names 'OCA fonds 72-007, Box 6, files 12-13'. THE FINDING AID HAS TWELVE FOLDERS, NOT TWO: Box 6 Folders 12-19 and Box 7 Folders 1-4 at least, and TRIP LOGS ARE NAMED IN THREE OF THEM -- F12 'personnel data sheets, TRIP LOGS, area histories and trip reports', F13 'personnel lists, correspondence, TRIP LOGS', F15 'routes, schedules, LOGS, etc.' Also F17 'photographs; articles on Quetico and the Peterborough canoe', F19 'historical essays on canoe routes (See also ROLLED MAP OF CENTENARY ROUTE IN MAP COLLECTION)'. Plus BOX 9 FOLDER 1, "'Agency Liaison' material, FROM THE QUEBEC SECTION, Canadian Camping Association - correspondence, papers, 1960-1962". The finding aid is cached whole. Not digitized.

priorities.description: ESTABLISH WHETHER KANAWANA RAN AN INTERCULTURAL CAMPING PROJECT IN 1965. May Brown's president's report, Canadian Camping Vol. 18 No. 1 (December 1965), records "Intercultural or Intergroup Camping projects" run by "a number of our member camps" over the summer of 1965, with the CCA executive gathering information and exploring an Evaluation and Training Seminar. Kanawana was a member camp, and the movement is the same one Hedley Dimock reported on from Goldeye Lake, Alberta in April 1965 -- Dimock being the man who had run counsellor research at Kanawana five years earlier and who by then chaired the Applied Social Science Division at Sir George Williams. Check the YMCA of Montreal annual reports for 1965 and 1966 and the CCA's own files for the list of participating camps.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 65-68, converted to KB facts

priorities.description:
FIND THE QCA'S 1965 INSPECTION REPORT ON KANAWANA. Canadian Camping Vol. 18 No. 3 (April 1966), "From the Provinces": "Quebec's concern for standards resulted in their securing the services of Mr. Murray McFarlane who visited twenty-seven camps during the summer months, and completed an exhaustive report on each camp. The camps were charged $25.00 for the visit, said visit to be made one every three years. A detailed report was submitted to the Standards Committee, and letters of accreditation were then forwarded to twenty-five camps which passed. Notices went to the two who did not meet the standards." That is the Quebec Camping Association's first documented accreditation round: a paid inspector, twenty-seven camps, an individual written report on each, a three-year cycle. Kanawana was a QCA member camp of exactly this size and type, so an exhaustive written 1965 report on the camp -- site, sanitation, waterfront, programme, staff -- was very probably produced and filed. This is the most specific and most promising archival lead the whole word-for-word read has produced for this wiki's own subject. WHERE TO LOOK: the Association des camps du Quebec's own records; the CCA/ACC fonds at Trent; the YMCA of Montreal fonds at Concordia for the camp's own copy and for the $25 payment in the accounts. NAME CAUTION: the inspector is very likely the P. M. McFarlane who wrote the Montreal MacKay Centre camp article in April 1965 -- a former camp director, therefore qualified to inspect -- but the given names differ in the two notices; record both and do not merge without a third source.

AMENDMENT (extraction pass, issue 100): QUEBEC ACCREDITATION IS OLDER THAN 1965. The tribute read when the QCA English Section made Mrs. Alta R. Kahn its first Honorary President on 23 May 1973 records that she was Co-Chairman of the QCA Standards Committee in 1959-60, 'when inspection of camps and accreditation were in the pioneer stage.' So the machinery predates the 1965 McFarlane round by five or six years, and the search window for a written Kanawana accreditation report opens correspondingly earlier. The same tribute dates the association's Provincial Charter to 1961 -- a corporate record Quebec's register of enterprises should hold, and the most concrete handle yet on where the association's own papers went.

FURTHER AMENDMENT (extraction pass, issue 103): QUEBEC RE-ACCREDITED EVERY CAMP ANNUALLY. John Hasell, chairman of the CCA National Standards Committee, in the January 1975 Directory Issue: other provinces required 'a visit every two or three years, but Quebec has developed its programme to the point where every camp is re-accredited annually' -- printed in both languages. So what is missing is not one report but a SERIES: an annual, itemised, externally written assessment of Kanawana's administration, personnel practices, site, programme, health and safety, running from about 1960 (Kahn's 'pioneer stage', 1959-60) to whenever the camp's accreditation lapsed. Two named handles for the request: the QCA English Section had an ARCHIVES chairman in 1975, Mr. Joseph A. Hood, so the Section was actively keeping records; and its Executive Secretary, Miss Frances M. Kelly, ran a STAFF PLACEMENT BUREAU from 2233 Belgrave Avenue, which would have generated its own record of who worked at which Quebec camp. Ask for both by name. || LOCATED 2026-09-06 (f_5209). **TRENT UNIVERSITY ARCHIVES, QUEBEC CAMPING ASSOCIATION FONDS 85-013, BOX 1, FOLDER 1: 'Camp visitation reports and related correspondence, 1962-1968'.** The 1965 McFarlane round falls inside that range. The finding aid is cached verbatim at sources/cache/trent-archives/2026-09-06-qca-fonds-85-013-finding-aid.txt. NOT DIGITIZED -- this is a reading-room visit or a paid retrieval, and it is now specified to the folder rather than to the repository. NOTE FOR THE RECORD: this fonds has been in sources.json since 2026-03-15 and its notes already named the visitation reports and their date ranges; this priority was raised afterwards and pointed at the building without picking up the shelf. || A SECOND ROUTE AND A YEAR-MATCHED DOCUMENT, 2026-09-06 (f_5212). Besides 85-013 Box 1 Folder 1, the OCA's 78-006 BOX 21 FOLDER 10 holds 'Quebec Camping Association, 1966-1975 ... QCA Reports; 1970 Standards; QCA ANNUAL REPORT, 1966' -- the annual report of the year the inspection round was reported in Canadian Camping. And 92-005 holds **'Camp Sights: Desirable Practices for Canadian YMCA Camps', 1965**, a YMCA camping standard of exactly that year.

priorities.description:
SPAWN A STUB FOR DAIS L. GASS, and one for Camp Memphremagog. Gass appears on every masthead in this read as a Montreal past president of the Canadian Camping Association with nothing else attached. Five tributes printed in Vol. 18 No. 4 (June 1966), after her death on 14 February 1966, give her a life: born in Nova Scotia, a graduate of Mount Allison University; to Montreal as a teacher at Trafalgar Girls' School; later personnel worker for the T. Eaton Company; a CGIT leader and YWCA camp volunteer; founder of Camp Memphremagog for Girls in the Eastern Townships in 1946, where campers called her "Kolali", "Friend"; second President of the CCA, 1946-49, succeeding Taylor Statten; chair of the meetings in Montreal, Toronto and Kingston that produced "the first official charter of the Canadian Camping Association"; and Past-President of the Quebec Camping Association. Camp Memphremagog was sold to the United Church in 1959 and run thereafter as a boys' camp. She is one of very few women among the movement's founders and a Montreal figure this project has been listing without knowing anything about. NOTE A DISCREPANCY TO CARRY, NOT RESOLVE: Mary Edgar's tribute says "During her twenty-three years as Director," which does not square with 1946-59 and may count her whole camping career.

AMENDMENT (extraction pass, issue 92): DAIS L. GASS IS NOW IDENTIFIED WELL ENOUGH TO WRITE. Charles Plewman's founding history of the magazine (Vol. 24 No. 1, Fall 1971) names "Miss Dais L. Gass, president of the C.C.A. in 1946" as the author of Canadian Camping's first editorial, and quotes it in full: "Now it starts in its humble way -- may it grow like the acorn and the oak, but most of all may it prove a tie between all of us in Canada... May Canadian Camping weave a bond of understanding, of mutual helpfulness and good will from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the end of the earth." With W. E. Yard's 1966 tribute, which credits her with chairing the Montreal, Toronto and Kingston meetings that produced the CCA's first official charter, she is now a Montreal woman who presided over the national association at its formation and wrote the first words of its magazine, and still has no KB fact of her own beyond this read. That is enough for a stub. Search: Montreal YWCA records, Camp Memphremagog, McGill and Sir George Williams alumni records, and Gazette obituaries.

FURTHER AMENDMENT (extraction pass, issue 94): A BOUND ON HER DEATH. The CCA past-presidents list in Vol. 24 No. 3 (Spring 1972) marks Taylor Statten of Toronto and Dais L. Gass of Montreal with asterisks as deceased, while Anne I. Vail, F. M. Van Wagner and Kenneth H. Murray, also Montreal, carry none. So Gass died before Spring 1972 -- the first bound this read has produced -- and the three unasterisked Montreal past presidents were living in 1972. That narrows an obituary search considerably.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 69-71, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: SEARCH THE SAINT-SAUVEUR AND MONTREAL PRESS OF SUMMER 1967 FOR KANAWANA'S CENTENARY JOURNEY DEPARTURE. John Latimer, chairman of the CCA's Centenary Journey Committee, wrote in Vol. 18 No. 4 (June 1966) that "the administration in Ottawa is not convinced that we deserve their support" and asked every director to contact local radio, TV and newspaper editors when a trip left camp. That is a direct instruction to generate local press coverage of departing trips, which makes the local papers a much better bet for a Kanawana notice than this project has assumed. The same article describes the NATIONAL CENTENARY CAMPFIRE -- "hundreds and hundreds of Campfires, lit at exactly the same time, on the same day in the summer of 1967 ... with the same opening and closing used by everyone who participates," in every camp in Canada and on every canoe trip. voyageur-canoe-pageant.md records that a National Campfire was held on 9 August 1967; this is the plan behind it, and it means Kanawana almost certainly lit one, from a prescribed text that is itself a specific thing to look for. Also findable: the minutes of the March 1966 Toronto conference of all ten provincial Centenary chairmen, at which "the final and official routes were mapped ... safety standards were developed ... Rendezvous Points were established" -- which would fix Kanawana's leg exactly.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 69-71, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: ANSWER OPEN QUESTION 8 IN camp-oolahwan.md. That article records as a confirmed dead end -- "Confirmed dead end across Trent, McCord, and LAC catalog descriptions -- no successor-director name found online" -- the question of who directed Camp Oolahwan after Mary Edgar left in 1919. Faye Ecclestone's profile of the Canadian Camping Association's national president, Canadian Camping Vol. 19 No. 1 (December 1966), supplies a name: "she went east to Montreal where she joined the staff of the Y.W.C.A. in that city. Her responsibilities included directing Camp Oolawahn and she also took the opportunity of completing her B.Sc. in Physical Education at McGill University." That is Mrs. Lorne E. (May) Brown, CCA president 1964-67 and later a Vancouver Parks Board figure. Internal dating from the same profile -- UBC teaching after graduation, marriage, children born about 1950 and 1955, an M.P.E. in 1961, Camp Deka founded about 1961 -- puts the Oolahwan directorship in the 1940s, most plausibly the later 1940s. WRITE IT UP WITH THE CAVEAT: the exact years still need a second source, and the LAC series that article already flags, "Camp Oolahwan committee minutes, reports and training programmes, 1916-1974," should settle them. Note also that Camp Deka, Brown's own camp, is already recorded in voyageur-canoe-pageant.md as a Centenary Journey participant -- so the national president's camp paddled the journey Kanawana paddled.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 72-74, converted to KB facts
priorities.resolution: ALREADY DONE, AND THE ARTICLE HAD OVERTAKEN IT. Camp Oolahwan's article named May Brown on 2026-09-04 and since then acquired two FIRST-HAND accounts that date her better than Ecclestone's undated 1966 profile could: her 1976 interview printed in 1982 ("In 1945 I went back to Montreal... began to work for the YWCA at Camp Oolahwan as programme director and then as Director after a few summers", leaving in the autumn of 1947) and her 1988 interview about her husband ("I had directed Camp Oolawhan out of the Montreal YWCA", the summer after her 1947 McGill degree). So the years are 1945-1947, not "probably the 1940s". What this pass actually fixed on 2026-09-06 is that TWO PLACES IN THE ARTICLE WERE LEFT BEHIND BY ITS OWN BODY: the paragraph built on Ecclestone still said the dating was inference that "should be confirmed before being stated as fact", and Open Question 8 still said her exact years were unfixed. Both now point to the first-hand accounts, and Open Question 8 also names Marjorie A. Booth as the second dated successor and states the two spans that are still blank, 1919-1945 and 1948-1979.

priorities.description: FIND THE MARY S. EDGAR POEM WRITTEN FOR THE NATIONAL CENTENARY CAMPFIRE. The OCA's "OCAsional News" of December 1966, quoted in Canadian Camping Vol. 19 No. 2 (February 1967): "The biggest of these activities is the National Campfire to be held Wednesday, August 9, 1967. On this night each camp will be provided with ideas for suitable programmes, centering around the Voyageur theme. It is hoped that a common opening and closing can be written including a poem for the occasion by Miss Mary Edgar. At the pre-set time every camp across the country will light its campfire!... There may even be a programme on a coast to coast radio network to coincide with the lighting of the campfires." Edgar founded and first edited this magazine and wrote "God Who Touchest Earth With Beauty." A poem written for a single simultaneous national campfire is a findable text, and if Kanawana lit a fire that night its campers heard it. WHERE TO LOOK: Edgar's collections A Christmas Wreath of Verse (1965) and Once There Was a Camper (1970); her fonds at Trent and Queen's; the OCA archive founded in 1966 under Margaret Govan; and the prepared programme packet camps were sent, which is itself a distributable document to hunt for. ALSO FIND: the 1967 Canadian Camping Conference "Digest," sold at three dollars, which Bruno Morawetz calls "that encyclopedia of camping" -- the fullest single record of Canadian camping thinking in the Centennial year.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 72-74, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: PATCH THE NATIONAL CENTENARY CAMPFIRE INTO centennial-1967.md, AND UPDATE a-ross-seaman.md. Canadian Camping Vol. 19 No. 4 (June 1967) prints the complete National Campfire ceremony distributed to every camp in Canada: the timing ("at varying times from 7 p.m. in the Yukon to 12:30 a.m. in Newfoundland," so about 11 p.m. EDT in Quebec on Wednesday 9 August 1967, with a warning to allow for Daylight time); the Fire-lighter call; the oration; the "Indian prayer" from the Centennial Anthology of Prayer; the thirteen-song list, including "Land of the Silver Birch"; the closing torch-light circle and Taps; and the suggestion of a birthday cake baked in a reflector oven. And it prints Mary S. Edgar's commissioned text, "Canada's Our Country," words by Edgar to the hymn tune Hermas, performed by a Toronto boys' choir at the annual meeting of 1 March 1967. NOTE WHAT THIS DEMONSTRATES: the A. Ross Seaman profile in the SAME issue has already been mined -- a-ross-seaman.md quotes it as its footnote 9 -- while the campfire script beside it appears nowhere in the wiki or the KB. Somebody went to this document looking for Seaman, found him, and stopped. Separately, that article should gain from this stretch of the run: Seaman as CCA vice-president for Quebec from December 1966; as president of the QCA English Section to September 1967, stepping down to a vice-presidency at the board elected at Expo on 23 September 1967; and as the resource person the Maritimes brought in to teach "Methods of Measurement in Camping" and "Methods of Evaluation" at the first Atlantic Provinces seminar, Moncton, 17-19 November 1967. [DONE 2026-09-05. Part (a), the National Campfire ceremony, was already written into history/centennial-1967.md by the read pass -- section 'The National Campfire, 9 August 1967', with the Fire-lighter call, the timing across time zones, Mary Edgar's 'Canada's Our Country' to the tune Hermas, and footnote 22 noting explicitly that an earlier pass took the Seaman profile from this same issue and left the ceremony untouched. Part (b) is done here: a-ross-seaman.md now dates his CCA vice-presidency for Quebec to December 1966 - spring 1968 and his QCA presidency to roughly 1966 - 23 September 1967, when the Provincial Board elected at Expo moved him to a vice-presidency; and records the Moncton seminar of 17-19 November 1967 where he taught 'Methods of Measurement in Camping' and 'Methods of Evaluation'. The last of those bears on how Kanawana's own staff-assessment paperwork of the period should be read.]
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 75-77, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: SPAWN A STUB FOR WALLACE FORGIE. He is now one of the most connected figures in the whole word-for-word read, and his signed obituary in Canadian Camping Vol. 20 No. 2 (Winter 1968), by J. H. Ebbs, M.D. -- his nephew by marriage -- supplies the frame: born 1883, died 1 December 1967; "known as 'Commodore' by the many young leaders who came under his influence in Canada from 1908 until 1927"; five years overseas with the YMCA in the First World War; boys' work in Western Canada "during which he conducted many canoe trips into the north-west"; "an associate of the late Dr. Hedley Dimock who was succeeded by Professor Charles E. Hendry"; and Camp Tonakela near Madras, built 1935, followed by "thirty-two years of voluntary service," where the Indian children called him "Tah-Tah" and the head of the Child Health Institute of Madras said he "will be remembered in this part of the world as an Albert Schweitzer." To that the read adds: he photographed C. F. Plewman at the Lake Couchiching YMCA camp in 1903; he built the foundations of Camp On-Da-Da-Waks and moved the Ottawa camp to Golden Lake in 1908; he held the Alberta YMCA boys'-work post that Hendry took over when he left in 1927; he worked in South India and Ceylon from 1927 to 1936; and he was Adele Statten Ebbs's uncle, taking her on her first canoe trip through Temagami at ten -- which makes him kin to Taylor Statten, either Ethel Statten's brother or the husband of Statten's sister Bolina. Settling which is a specific genealogical question worth answering, and taylor-statten.md should say so once it is.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 75-77, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: RECOVER THE QUEBEC CAMP ACCREDITATION STANDARDS THROUGH THEIR FRENCH TRANSLATION. Lionel Perras, president of l'Association des camps du Quebec, writing in Canadian Camping Vol. 22 No. 3 (April 1970): "L'Association fournit aux camps avec le texte des normes actuelles dernierement traduites de la QCA" -- the ACQ's standards are a recent translation of the Quebec Camping Association's. So if the English QCA text Kanawana was measured against is lost, the French version recovers its content. Perras also points directly at where to look: accreditation "fut l'une des premieres preoccupations des fondateurs de l'ACQ en 1958... il suffit de relire les proces-verbaux des assemblees" -- the ACQ's own minutes from 1958 onward. His article sets out the eleven characteristics assessed and the six-heading self-critique in full, so even without the standards text the shape of a camp's accreditation file is now known: administration (including "Y a-t-il un Coutumier du camp?", a book of the camp's own customs, required by the accreditation process); programme; resources; la vie des campeurs; finances; and hygiene, health and safety. He refers besides to "des camps visites au cours de l'ete 1966" -- a second Quebec visiting round, the year after Murray McFarlane's twenty-seven-camp round of 1965 (p_339). Chase both rounds together. NOTE ALSO the mandatory national standards implemented in 1970 under Ron Johnstone as National Chairman of Standards, "Over 20 items are mandatory for a Camp to be an accredited member" -- which is the regime Kanawana operated under from that year. || LOCATED 2026-09-06 (f_5209). **TRENT, QCA FONDS 85-013, BOX 1, FOLDER 21: 'Q.C.A. Standards, correspondence, 1953-1973'**, with Box 1 Folders 7-10 the Provincial Standards Committee under Miss F. M. Kelly (1975-1977). Finding aid cached. Not digitized. || A THIRD LOCATION, 2026-09-06 (f_5212): **78-006, BOX 21, FOLDER 11, 'QUEBEC CAMPING ASSOCIATION MINIMUM STANDARDS, 1970; Program outlines; By-laws'** -- the standards themselves, in the Ontario association's copy. Folder 12 alongside it holds **QCA DIRECTORIES for 1967 and 1969-1973**, which would list Kanawana as a member camp.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 84-86, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: READ THE FRENCH-LANGUAGE CONTENT OF CANADIAN CAMPING FROM APRIL 1970. The magazine went bilingual with Vol. 22 No. 3 (April 1970): cover, masthead, the Prime Minister's editorial and Elsie Palter's article all in both languages, and Lionel Perras contributing a full-length article IN FRENCH ONLY. That is a fact about the source as much as about the movement: from April 1970 the run carries French-language material that an English-only search would never surface, and the word-for-word read has been catching it only because it is a word-for-word read. When the remaining issues are extracted, the French content needs the same attention as the English -- and any earlier pass over this corpus that used English keyword search should be assumed to have missed it entirely. The provincial offices list from that issue gives two addresses to chase separately: Quebec Camping Association, 2233 Belgrave Ave., Montreal 261, and L'Association des camps de Quebec, 952 Cherrier Ave., Montreal.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 84-86, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: QUERY TRENT UNIVERSITY ARCHIVES FOR THE ONTARIO CAMPING ASSOCIATION FONDS -- AND SPECIFICALLY FOR ITS TAPED INTERVIEWS. Mary Northway's account in Canadian Camping, November 1970, dates the deposit exactly: 22 October 1970, past president John Latimer handing the archives to Dr. T. H. B. Symons at Trent, six years' work by a committee chaired successively by Adele Ebbs, Margaret Govan and Northway herself, catalogued at the OCA office by Mrs. Shirley Hall. Contents as she lists them: early brochures, photographs, programmes and schedules, films, financial accounts, diaries, AND TAPED INTERVIEWS OF PROMINENT CAMP PERSONALITIES. The collecting policy was 'everything. Let the archivist decide what is not important' -- so the fonds should contain national and inter-provincial material, not only Ontario. Three specific asks: (a) the taped interviews, and whether any interviewee had Quebec or YMCA connections; (b) the minute David Palter quotes from the Legislative Committee meeting of 7 March 1957, which should be in these papers; (c) whether the fonds includes CCA material from the years the national office was at 102 Eglinton Ave. East inside the OCA office (from 1971). A duplicate file was kept at the camping office; the originals went to Trent. || WORKED 2026-09-06 (f_5210), AND ASK (a) IS ANSWERED. THE TAPES ARE NOT IN THE OCA FONDS. 72-007's own general note: 'The audio tapes have been physically removed from this fonds and been placed within a new fonds titled CANADIAN CAMPING ASSOCIATION FONDS : SOUND TAPE RECORDINGS (83-002).' That accession returned ZERO hits across this project before today. It has an ITEM-LEVEL finding aid -- subject, speaker, interviewer, date, medium, permission -- and searching it for Kanawana, Otoreke, YMCA, Montreal and Quebec returns EXACTLY ONE Quebec item: 83-002/011/008, MARJORIE BOOTH, interviewed by ELEANOR KAY, 12 NOVEMBER 1991, 'Involvement with New Brunswick and Quebec Camping Associations. Involvement as Executive Director of Canadian Camping Association', cassette, with a worksheet and two colour photographs. Booth is already in this wiki as CCA executive director and as a director of the Montreal YWCA's Camp Oolahwan. NO KANAWANA, NO OTOREKE, NO YMCA, NO MONTREAL anywhere else in that collection. ACCESS CAVEAT, the fonds' own words: 'In some cases, interviewers have not secured copyright releases from the interviewees ... All questions of copyright remain the responsibility of the researcher.' ASKS (b) THE 7 MARCH 1957 LEGISLATIVE COMMITTEE MINUTE AND (c) THE POST-1971 CCA MATERIAL ARE STILL OPEN; the 72-007 finding aid is now cached whole at sources/cache/trent-archives/2026-09-06-oca-fonds-72-007-finding-aid.txt, 39,000 characters, and should be read for both before anyone writes to Trent. || ASKS (b) AND (c) ANSWERED FROM THE CACHED AID, no second fetch needed. (b) THE 1957 LEGISLATION COMMITTEE PAPERS ARE **BOX 2, FOLDER 14** -- 'Executive Committee - minutes, 1954-1959; Legislation Committee - minutes, reports 1957, 1969-1973; Nominating Committee...'. (c) POST-1971 CCA MATERIAL IS NOT IN 72-007 AS CATALOGUED: 'Eglinton' and 'national office' return nothing across 39,000 characters, and the fonds' CCA holding (Box 9 Folder 5) stops at 1967. Look instead at OCA 88-006, THE 1988 ADDITIONS, whose Boxes 41-42 this project's QCA source note already flags as 'QCA English Section, 1972-1979'. THAT ACCESSION HAS NOT BEEN FETCHED and is the next thing to do here. ALSO NOTED IN PASSING: Box 9 Folder 5 holds Mary L. Northway's 'Canadian Camping: Its Foundation and Its Future', 1946, and the fonds points at 80-022, THE M. L. NORTHWAY FONDS, also unfetched. SO p_348 IS NOW: one ask answered (the tapes, 83-002), two located to the folder, and two further Trent accessions named and untouched. || 88-006 AND 80-022 NOW FETCHED (f_5211). **88-006, BOX 2, FOLDER 41: 'Quebec Camping Association (English Section) - minutes, reports, some correspondence, 1972-1977'; FOLDER 42: same, 'correspondence, minutes, reports, constitution, 1978-1979'.** That is the section an anglophone YMCA camp in Quebec would appear in, across the years of the Order of Owens' founding and the post-coeducation period. Also BOX 2 FOLDER 20, 'French Language Conference - Quebec, 1976'; BOX 2 FOLDER 22, 'Oral History project, 1976-1977 - financial record' (a SECOND oral-history undertaking, distinct from the tapes in 83-002); and a Box 3 YMCA run holding a 'letter re YMCA camping in Canada, 1968'. Finding aid cached. **80-022, THE NORTHWAY FONDS, IS A NULL** -- household records, genealogy tapes, property, her OCA/CCA participation and the winding-up of the Northway Company; no Kanawana, Otoreke, Quebec, YMCA or Montreal in its description. EIGHT MORE ADDITIONS TO 72-007 REMAIN UNFETCHED: 78-006, 82-009, 84-019, 85-011, 86-018, 89-015, 92-005, 93-021. || SWEEP COMPLETED 2026-09-06 (f_5212). All nine additions to 72-007 fetched raw, plus 82-016. **84-019 BOX 2 FOLDER 4 HOLDS TRANSCRIPTS** -- 'Transcripts of some interview tapes previously recorded': Omer Stringer, Stephen Lewis, Jean Foster, Penny Miall, Tony Fry, Camp Philosophy (CCA meeting 1975), Pat Scollard, and two CCA Directors Conference sessions of 1975. TRANSCRIPTS ARE READABLE WHERE TAPES ARE NOT -- ask for this folder before the tapes. **84-019 BOX 1 FOLDER 10 IS TITLED 'YMCA - MONTREAL'** with no further description. NULLS: 85-011, 86-018, 89-015, 93-021, 82-016, 80-022. THIS PRIORITY IS NOW ANSWERED as far as finding aids can answer it.

priorities.description: FIND MARY S. EDGAR'S 'ONCE THERE WAS A CAMPER' (G. R. Welch, Toronto, 1970) AND RECORD 'HYMN FOR THE SPACE-AGE'. Canadian Camping, November 1970, announces the book as 'a little book of 23 delightful rhymes on kids at camp' with the author's own line drawings, and prints in the same issue Edgar's 'Hymn for the Space-Age' (Tune: Forest Green), an explicitly environmental hymn by the CCA's honorary president -- the third Edgar hymn this read has found, after 'Canada's Our Country' (June 1967) and 'This Fair Land, Our Canada' (1969). Search: Library and Archives Canada, Toronto Public Library, University of Toronto, Trent (the OCA fonds), AbeBooks and Internet Archive. The hymn text belongs in environmental-and-ecological-history and alongside the Edgar material in centennial-1967.md.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 87-89, converted to KB facts
priorities.resolution: THE HYMN HALF IS DONE; THE BOOK HALF IS NOT. 'Hymn for the Space-Age' is written into environmental-history.md as the earliest environmental statement in the national camping press this project holds -- November 1970, eight months before Kanawana's own erosion confession and nine years before 'No Trace Camping', by the movement's Honorary President, then eighty-one. Two verses quoted, the space frame noted (the hymn opens on 'Infinity of space' and turns from there to the planet, which is the argument the Apollo photographs were making everywhere that year), and the honest limit stated: no source says any Kanawana camper ever sang it. Cross-referenced from centennial-1967.md, where 'Canada's Our Country' already sat, with the point that the Centennial hymn form outlived the Centennial by three years and turned into an environmental one. Facts f_3453, f_3454 and f_3343 already existed. STILL OPEN: 'Once There Was a Camper' (G. R. Welch, Toronto, 1970), the book of 23 rhymes with her own line drawings. That needs Library and Archives Canada, Toronto Public Library, Trent's OCA fonds, AbeBooks or the Internet Archive, and none of those catalogue surfaces has been tried from here for this title.
priorities.notes: 2026-09-06: hymn written up; book search untried.

priorities.description: DID KANAWANA SEND A DELEGATE TO THE CCA NATIONAL CONFERENCE ON CAMPING STANDARDS AND RESEARCH, HALIFAX, 22-23 FEBRUARY 1971? The conference was one delegate per member camp, with the CCA board meeting 20-21 February and the annual meeting on the evening of the 21st; delegates were asked to propose topics under standards and accreditation, health and safety, leadership development, and pollution and conservation. A delegate list, if it was printed in a later issue of Canadian Camping, would place a named Kanawana staff member at a national meeting on a precise date. Check the Spring and Summer 1971 issues in the cached run when the read reaches them, and the YMCA of Montreal's own 1971 records.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 87-89, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: READ KANAWANA'S SONG RECORD AGAINST JACK PEARSE'S 'SONG LEADING' (Canadian Camping, June 1970) -- the p_048 comparator the read was looking for. Pearse, director of Camp Tawingo, sets out the period's own five-category taxonomy (novelty numbers, action songs, rounds, spirituals and folk songs, quiet songs) with a named repertoire under each, plus the rule that all sing-songs end quietly and the advice that leaders should make up songs for their own groups. This does three things for the Kanawana song question: it dates the common stock (so a Kanawana song found in Pearse's lists is movement-wide, not camp-specific); it supplies the vocabulary the period actually used for its own singing; and it establishes that camp-specific songs were an advised practice, not an accident. Any traditions article on Kanawana singing should distinguish the common stock from the camp's own on this basis, and say which it is doing. | DONE 2026-09-05. Pearse's five categories are now a table in camp-songs-cheers.md with his named repertoire under each, his eight-step method for teaching a round, and the rule he prints in capitals: ALL SING SONGS SHOULD END WITH QUIET SINGING (f_4869). THE COMPARISON THE PRIORITY WANTED, and it cuts both ways as it should. TWO KANAWANA SONGS ARE IN HIS LISTS: Kum Bah Yah, which he classes under spirituals and folk songs, and 'My Old Kentucky Home' -- sung solo by a twelve-year-old in the 1938 broadcast -- which is a Stephen Foster song, the first entry in his quiet category. Neither is Kanawana property; both are the movement's common stock, and the article says so, so no later pass reads either as evidence of anything local. AND THE CAMP'S OWN SONGS ARE WHAT THE MOVEMENT TOLD LEADERS TO MAKE: 'On My Way to Kanawana', the Marching Song, 'Dear Old Kanawana' to the Battle Hymn, the Alabama Jubilee adaptation -- all fall under Pearse's novelty category, whose instruction is not a description but an order, 'Find some novelty numbers. Invent some.' Camp-specific songs were ADVISED PRACTICE, taught as technique in the association's own magazine. That is better founded than either 'Kanawana's songs are unusual' or 'Kanawana's songs are borrowed' (f_4870). Pearse's closing rule also matches Kay McClelland's 1956 campfire structure already held here (f_2725). camp-songs-cheers.md 23 -> 24 sources.

priorities.description: REVISE THE CHOPSY LINE OF ENQUIRY (p_045) IN LIGHT OF DAVID HARTRY'S 'SNARK HUNTING' (Canadian Camping, Winter 1971). Hartry, then CCA president, documents his own camp's legend from the inside: invented for the first official hunt in 1968 at the Anglican Youth Camp near Halifax, staged by setting campers' watches ahead, the creature built by campers who had been let in on the secret the year before, given a spurious documentary pedigree by a book found in the camp library, and within three years expected annually and already being elaborated in campers' own vocabulary. It tells us nothing about Chopsy. It tells us what kind of evidence a legend like Chopsy leaves: the staging is remembered, the invention is not, and apparent corroboration may be part of the hoax. The DRAFT_ORAL_HISTORY_INSTRUMENT should therefore ask about staging, about who was let in on it and when, and about whether anyone was ever shown 'proof' -- not only about the story as told.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 87-89, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: SPAWN STUBS FOR THE THREE FOUNDERS' NAMES NOW DOCUMENTED FROM CANADIAN CAMPING: Charles Plewman (owner-director of Kilcoo Camp, past president of the OCA, camping from 1909, made an Honorary Member at the Society of Camp Directors' Founders' Meeting, wrote Ethel Statten's obituary); W. Bertram Danson (Camp Winnebagoe, present at the 7 March 1957 OCA Legislative Committee meeting, author of the June 1970 'Do's and Don'ts for Counsellors' with its ban on physical punishment); and David Palter, B.Sc., P.Eng., camp consultant, appointed OCA Standards Committee chairman 29 April 1957 and the man who started Canadian camp accreditation. NOTE FOR THE STUB ON PALTER: he is not David Paltiel, the Kanawana name on the Knights of Kanawana roll, the 1975 board and the 1976 staff list. Different names, no evidence of any link; the stub must say so.

priorities.description: CHECK BRITISH COLUMBIA'S SUMMER CAMP LICENSING AGAINST GERTRUDE 'DINTY' MOORE'S STANDARDS. Her obituary in Canadian Camping, November 1970, states that she founded the BC Camping Association in 1939, was its first president, and that during her ten years in executive office the association drew up standards for camping in the province with the provincial government, 'Later this research and study was used as a basis for Government licensing of summer camps in B.C.' If that holds, British Columbia licensed camps on standards a camp director wrote -- the outcome David Palter was still arguing for in Ontario in 1969, achieved a generation earlier. A checkable claim: search BC statutes and regulations on summer camps, the BC Camping Association's own history, and Moorecroft (the United Church site near Nanoose Bay she sold on retirement). Bears on how to read Quebec's own accreditation arrangements, which never became licensing.

priorities.description: FIND THE PAPERS OF THE QUEBEC ASSOCIATION'S 1971 SEMINAR ON STAFF POLICY AND CAMP FINANCING. Huguette Dagenais reports in Canadian Camping, Summer 1971, that the merged A.C.Q.-Q.C.A. held a seminar for camp directors and their principal colleagues attended by 115 people, on 'politiques de personnel et des questions de financement dans les camps,' run bilingually without simultaneous translation with bilingual animateurs linking the two language groups. A weekend gathering of 115 Quebec camp directors on staff policy and camp financing in 1971 is exactly the forum a Kanawana director would have attended, and its working papers -- if they survive with the association's records -- bear directly on the p_307 staff-assessment thread and on how Quebec camps were financed in the period. Chase: the successor body to the ACQ-QCA and its archives, the Haut-Commissariat a la Jeunesse, aux Loisirs et aux Sports fonds at BAnQ (the association's $30,000 provincial grant means it reported to a ministry), and the association's own newsletter. Dagenais also records that thirteen people represented Quebec at the CCA congress in Halifax that year.

priorities.description: TRACE YVES BEAUREGARD, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR OF THE MERGED QUEBEC CAMPING ASSOCIATION UNTIL 1 FEBRUARY 1971. Dagenais's 'Nouvelles du Quebec' (Spring 1971) records his departure on that date and gives him the title directeur-executif of the A.C.Q.-Q.C.A. -- so the merged Quebec association had a paid professional staff, and this is the first named holder of the post the read has found. A paid executive director keeps files: correspondence, membership records, accreditation reports. Finding him, or his successor, is the most direct route to the written accreditation record the p_339 thread is looking for. Search: Quebec recreation and youth-service directories of the period, BAnQ, Le Devoir and La Presse for the association's announcements, and LinkedIn or obituary sources for a man in a professional post in Montreal in the late 1960s.

priorities.description: RECORD THE CCA'S 1971 REGIONAL RESTRUCTURING IN canadian-camping-movement.md, AND THE QUEBEC SUCCESSION WITH IT. Two things settle in 1971 that this read has been tracking through address changes since issue 80. (a) John Latimer's first president's letter (Summer 1971): 'since the Association was founded, the Executive moved from province to province every two years. Now there are five Vice-Presidents on the Executive of C.C.A. who represent various regions' -- Tom Creighton (Atlantic), Bob Lazanik (Quebec), Jack Pearse (Ontario), Eileen Mayotte (Prairie), Tanya Krisman (BC) -- ending the rotating provincial executive that had moved the national office Winnipeg to Halifax to Toronto. (b) David Hartry's 'C.C.A. -- New National Office' of 14 December 1970 gives the reason the federally funded Ottawa office closed after less than two years: project grants remained available but administrative grants did not, so the CCA moved into the OCA's office at $45 a month and operated from its own income. On the Quebec side, Perras hands the merged association's presidency to Robert Lazanik in 1971 and receives its insignia; the two-section structure with one president over it, printed at issue 89, holds.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 90-91, converted to KB facts
priorities.resolution: Written into canadian-camping-movement.md ahead of the 1985 'money stops' section, because it corrects that section. Both halves verified against the cached issues: Latimer's summer 1971 president's letter with the five regional vice-presidents and the masthead officer list behind it, and Hartry's 'C.C.A. -- New National Office' dated 14 December 1970 with the $45.00 a month OCA arrangement and the sentence that project grants remained and administrative grants did not. New source note 8bs; facts f_3334, f_3525, f_3542 already existed. TWO THINGS BEYOND THE PRIORITY. First, the priority said the Ottawa office was 'federally funded' and closed 'after less than two years' -- I doubted the first half on Hartry's memo alone, which only rejects a PROPOSED Ottawa office, and the Summer 1969 issue settles it: the office opened on a grant from the Fitness and Amateur Sports Branch, announced at the annual meeting of 28 February 1969, with a paid Executive Secretary, Barry Bryant, at Box 2773 Station D. February 1969 to January 1971 is under two years. The priority was right and my doubt was wrong. Second, this CONTRADICTS the article's own paragraph from Jocelyn Palm's winter 1985 editorial, which says the national office with paid staff and a permanent address dates from 1971 and that Fitness Canada funded it from 1971. On the contemporaneous record the office is two years older and federal administrative money stopped rather than started around 1971. Raised as conflict c_064 -- two documented sources, so a human decision point -- and both are now printed beside each other in the article. Also written: what the 1971 restructuring means for this wiki, that Quebec's standing regional vice-presidency, the seat followed through Lazanik, Walsh, Belanger and Willis, exists because the travelling provincial executive ended, and that the same travelling executive is why Seaman could be national secretary from a house in Lachine in 1962.

priorities.description: CHECK KANAWANA'S OWN RECORD AGAINST THE 1971 QUEBEC BUS-TRANSPORT PROCEDURE AND FIRE-SAFETY STANDARD. Two operations documents in the Summer 1971 issue set out what a well-run Quebec camp was expected to do, and both leave paper. Huguette Dagenais's 'Le camp de jour et son transport' requires tendering four months before opening, commercial permits and an insurance policy verified per vehicle by serial number, a monitor on every bus, and written camp rules for drivers. Deputy Chief Bryan Mitchell's 'Fire-Safe Camping' sets out fire permits from the Department of Lands and Forests, flammable-liquid storage, extinguisher placement with staff instructed in their use, and annual servicing of cooking, refrigeration and heating equipment by a qualified serviceman. If the YMCA of Montreal kept insurance schedules, bus contracts, or fire-inspection certificates for Kanawana, they would answer to these. Worth an explicit ask of the YMCA of Montreal's records alongside the accreditation request in p_339.

priorities.description: WRITE THE CANADIAN CAMPING SECTION OF meta/sources-index.md. The 164-issue run is the largest single body of source material this project holds and meta/sources-index.md still has no section on it at all. Charles Plewman's 'The Canadian Camping Magazine and How We Came By It' (Vol. 24 No. 1, Fall 1971) is the founding document and should anchor the section: the OCA formed 1933; Plewman drafted into its presidency autumn 1944; the T. Eaton Company financing the first edition; Mary Edgar as first editor; the Ontario Bulletin closed out in 1947 in favour of a mimeographed quarterly called Canadian Camping; and 'The first real Canadian Camping magazine was published in February of 1949 when for the first time it appeared in print' -- which is exactly where this project's cached run begins, so the run is complete from the first printed issue and the 1947-48 mimeographed bulletin is a separate body of material the project does not hold. Fred Haiblen of Toronto assumed the financial responsibility for going to print; Edgar edited five more years and was succeeded by Mrs. G. W. Flynn. THE SECTION'S FIRST STATEMENT MUST BE THE 1988 FUNDING CUT-OFF as the explanation of the run's end date. Other anchor facts already extracted: Jay Haddad's editorship mid-1981 to Winter 1986; the magazine passing to a Camp Tawingo group from Spring 1986; the 1967 publisher change to Town Talk Publications under Eanswythe Flynn; the December 1969 change to Broydon Printers and Groff's 'From mimeograph to letterpress to offset'; the April 1970 turn to bilingual publication (and with it the French-only content an English keyword search never surfaces -- see p_347); subscription rates ($3/year and $8/three in 1970, a $2 staff rate from 1971, $1.00 a single copy from Winter 1972, $8/$2 to 1987 and $10/$3 from 1987; ISSN 0834325); and the Fall 1971 statement that 'CANADIAN CAMPING is a 100% Canadian magazine and is not subsidized in any way. It is supported solely by advertisements.' [DONE 2026-09-05: written as the '*Canadian Camping* Magazine, February 1949 - Winter 1988' section of meta/sources-index.md. Leads with the 1988 Fitness Canada cut-off as the explanation of the run's end date; carries Plewman's founding history, the production/format/price table, the two warnings about the French text, the statement of what the run does and does not contain about Kanawana, and the register of known scan defects. The Edgar-vs-Plewman 'founder' discrepancy is recorded there unresolved.]

priorities.description: FIND OUT WHAT HAPPENED AT THE CHATEAU LAURIER IN 1946. Charles Plewman, first-hand, in Fall 1971: 'Before very long, I think it was in 1946, the Canadian Camping Association was formed at a meeting held in the Chateau Laurier in Ottawa' -- nearly all members representatives of the Ontario and Quebec associations, no other province then having one, and the body having 'no corporate existence' at that point. That is a second independent first-hand source for a 1946 event, against this project's documented 1936 founding at the Central YMCA, Toronto, and it corroborates the Camp Stephens claim that Nelson McEwen founded the CCA in 1946 (see c_035). The question is now concrete and checkable. Search: the CCA's own minutes, which by Mary Northway's account should be in the OCA archives deposited at Trent in October 1970 (p_348); Chateau Laurier function records; Ottawa press for 1946; and the incorporation file behind the 1949 charter, which Dais L. Gass chaired the meetings for.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 92-93, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: CHECK WHETHER KANAWANA APPEARS AT THE CCA'S MONTREAL MEETINGS OF APRIL 1972. John Latimer's Winter 1972 newsletter gives the dates and the venue: the CCA Board meeting at the Queen Elizabeth Hotel, Montreal, 19-20 April 1972, the Annual Meeting the night of 20 April, and the QCA-ACQ Conference 20-22 April at the same hotel, with a separate Quebec Camping Association annual meeting on 24 May. A national camping conference held in Montreal, hosted by the Quebec association Kanawana belonged to, is the single most likely occasion in the whole run for the camp to appear by name -- as a host, a tour stop, a delegate, or an exhibitor. Read the Spring and Summer 1972 issues of the run for the conference report with this specifically in mind, and search Montreal press for 19-24 April 1972.
