priorities.description: SPAWN A STUB FOR THE SOCIETY OF CAMP DIRECTORS. Two accounts in the run now give it a full institutional history: J. Harry Ebbs's founding address (1969) and Clifford Labbett's 'The Society of Camp Directors' (Fall 1971). Ebbs's questionnaire to OCA members in 1968 was the seed; the founding banquet was at the Rosedale Golf Club, Toronto, in May 1969 (12 May per Labbett, 21 May per Ebbs -- see c_037), fifty-seven members attending; the purpose was 'to establish and maintain professional practices in the directing of childrens' camps and to ensure qualified directorship in such camps'; a board of five on three-year terms; three membership classes with Honorary Fellows Mary Edgar, Ferna Halliday, Mary Hamilton, Charles Plewman and Mrs. Taylor Statten elected at the inaugural dinner; meetings on the second Thursday of November and April; a $500 undergraduate research fund; and a joint proposal with the OCA for stricter licensing of children's camps with the OCA as governing body. The Society matters to this project because so many of the papers this read has surfaced were delivered to it, and because its licensing campaign is the professionalisation argument Quebec never resolved the same way.

priorities.description: REWRITE THE ORIGIN SECTION OF wiki/site/indigenous-names-and-land.md USING MARY EDGAR'S 1971 TESTIMONY. Her talk 'Our Indebtedness to Our Indian Friends,' given in the Glen Bernard chapel on 15 August 1971 and reprinted in Canadian Camping Vol. 24 No. 4 (Summer 1972), is the clearest contemporaneous statement the project holds of how 'Indian programming' reached Canadian camps, and it runs through Montreal. She names the channel in her own words: Pauline Johnson performing at Sundridge about 1899 and staying in the Edgar family home; the 1900 rescue on Lake Nipissing by two men from the Dokis Reserve, which she frames as a debt; and the YWCA training course in New York in 1914-15, where Ruby M. Jolliffe, Superintendent of State Camps for New York and New Jersey, introduced her to a storyteller Jolliffe 'often engaged... for Council Ring programs.' American state-camp practice, via the YWCA national training school, into a Canadian camp director's programme -- arriving at the Montreal YWCA's own Laurentian camp before Glen Bernard. Kanawana's totem pole (1927), Council Ring and 'Council of Tribes' belong to the same period and the same movement. Set beside it the Fall 1972 issue, which prints within two pages both a genuine transmission of Algonquin craft knowledge from William Commanda and a missionary pastiche presented as an Indigenous psalm, without appearing to notice the difference. Edgar's own language -- debt, shame, 'the white race will learn to appreciate' -- is recorded as written and dated, not adopted. [DONE 2026-09-05. The Edgar 1971 half was already written in by the read pass -- the 'Where the practice came from, in a founder's own words' passage, with Pauline Johnson at Sundridge c.1899, the 1900 Dokis Reserve rescue framed as a debt, and Ruby M. Jolliffe's New York state-camp storyteller in 1914-15, plus the Gilchrist and Northway material added later. The outstanding piece was the Fall 1972 juxtaposition, which was in the KB as f_3666/f_3667 and appeared nowhere in the wiki; it is now a section, 'Two pages of the same magazine, Fall 1972'. Note the Kanawana-specific angle it opens: William Commanda was teaching Algonquin canoe construction to the CCA's own canoeing instructor at Kitigan Zibi in summer 1972, a few camps acquired a Commanda canoe, and Kanawana is a Weskarini Algonquin-territory camp whose canoe programme is its oldest continuous activity. No source places Kanawana among those camps -- that is now a specific askable question rather than a general one.]

priorities.description: ASK THE YMCA OF MONTREAL FOR KANAWANA STAFF PAYROLL RECORDS FROM 1972 ONWARD. Two items in this run establish that 1972 is the year Canadian camp staff started generating federal employment paper. John Latimer's 'Unemployment Insurance Changes' (Spring 1972): from 1972 counsellors and instructors in summer camps are in insurable employment, no minimum age exemption, non-citizens not exempt, teachers and nurses no longer exempt. The Summer 1972 follow-up gives the threshold -- anyone on $30.00 a week or more including room and board. And Clifford Labbett's budget article (Fall 1972) notes that the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the provincial Workmen's Compensation Board 'maintain auditors who may examine your salary and wage records at any time,' which is a reason such records were kept and retained. After 1972 there is a payroll trail on summer camp staff that does not exist before it: a route to named Kanawana staff for years the wiki currently covers only from memory. Ask specifically for payroll ledgers, T4 summaries, UIC remittance records and Workmen's Compensation filings.

priorities.description: USE THE 1972-73 'THREAT TO CAMPING' FRAME WHEN WRITING KANAWANA'S 1970s. The movement dated its own crisis precisely. John Latimer, Fall 1972: 'Camping is having difficulties... Government legislation and red tape; increased operational and land costs; more competition; more alternatives for parents and children; less public awareness; higher standards... We are being threatened and we must do something about it!' The CCA's National Camp Directors Workshop at Geneva Park, 1-4 February 1973, was titled 'The Threat to Camping -- What does Camping have to do to survive?' Two concrete cost pressures are documented in the same issues: unemployment insurance becoming payable on camp staff from 1972 at 1.4 times the employee's rate for the employer, and Ontario sales tax on camp fees above a threshold. Any account of Kanawana's own difficulties in the 1970s should be written inside this frame rather than as a story about one camp, and the wiki should say so explicitly.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 94-96, converted to KB facts
priorities.resolution: Written into between-centennials.md as a subsection placed BEFORE the 1978 Granek findings, since it is the earlier frame and the article should meet it first: Latimer's autumn 1972 letter in full, the Geneva Park workshop of 1-4 February 1973 and its title, and the 1972 unemployment-insurance change with its particulars -- no minimum age exemption, no exemption for non-citizens, teachers and nurses no longer exempt, the reduced rate for charitable institutions in 1972-73-74, and the $30.00-a-week threshold published the following season. The priority's other cost item, Ontario sales tax on camp fees, is not written up: it is Ontario's and does not reach a Quebec camp. Nor is its '1.4 times the employee's rate' figure, which is not in the passages read. The two consequences stated in the article: Kanawana's payroll costs rose in 1972 by an amount set in Ottawa, at the front end of the decade in which its own record thins, so the thinning, the 1978 Quebec enrolment findings and this are three views of one squeeze; and from 1972 every Kanawana counsellor and instructor generated federal employment paper, a body of record outside the YMCA's own files that this project has never looked for (see p_366). Fact f_4931.

priorities.description: COMPARE ERNEST THOMPSON SETON'S PUBLISHED COUNCIL RING CEREMONY AGAINST KANAWANA'S c.1925-27 SCRIPT, LINE BY LINE. Jack Eastaugh, Assistant to the Director of the Taylor Statten Camps, states in Canadian Camping Vol. 25 No. 3 (Spring 1973): 'The Indian Council Ring Ceremony, devised by Ernest Thompson Seton in the years following the first great war and refined by Taylor Statten who taught the ceremonies to camp leaders in the 20's, needs no apology and is still viable today.' Kanawana's totem pole went up in 1927 and its 'Tribes of Kanawana in Council' script is dated c. 1925-27 -- exactly those years. Eastaugh's list of standard parts (Fire Lighting, Peace Pipe Ceremony, Indian Games, Dances, Departure of Hiawatha) matches Kanawana's scripts item for item, and his rendering of the closing chant -- 'Wakonda dhe dhu' / 'Father a needy one stands before thee; I who sing am he' -- matches Kanawana's closing line 'Wakonda, dhe-dhu, wapdhin atonhe'. The work now is textual: get Seton's published ceremony (the Woodcraft League and Birch Bark Roll material, widely digitised) and set it beside the Concordia script. Eastaugh also offered 'a complete and detailed description of the rituals, ceremonies, games and organization' on request from the Taylor Statten Camps -- ask them whether that document survives, since it is the version Kanawana's leaders would have been taught. | COMPLETED 2026-09-05. Seton's Book of Woodcraft and Indian Lore (1912) downloaded from the Internet Archive and read for the ceremony sections. THE DESCENT IS A TEXT, NOT A RESEMBLANCE. (1) The Peace Pipe Ceremony, pp. 148-149, gives the fire-lighting Kanawana's Green Triangle describes in 1940 in one line -- 'he prayed to Wakonda to light the fire' -- and the invocation 'Now know we that Wakonda, whose dwelling is above the Thunder-bird, whose messenger is the Thunder-bird, hath been pleased to smile on his children, hath sent down the sacred fire' (f_4854). (2) THE CLOSING CHANT HAS A CREDIT LINE. At p. 145 Seton prints 'THE OMAHA TRIBAL PRAYER, harmonized by Prof. J. C. Fillmore' -- 'Wa-kon-da dhe-dhu Wa-pa-dhin a-ton-he' -- credited '(By permission from Alice C. Fletcher's Indian Story and Song)' and translated 'Father a needy one stands before thee; I THAT sing am he'. Kanawana's script closes 'Wakonda, dhe-dhu, wapdhin atonhe'; Eastaugh remembered 'I WHO sing am he', one word adrift after fifty years. Line of descent documented end to end: Omaha prayer -> Fletcher (1900) -> Fillmore's harmonisation -> Seton (1912) -> Statten's camps (1920s) -> Kanawana by 1927 (f_4855). (3) BLACKSTOCK'S MAZINAW FIREPLACE CARVING IS SETON'S SENTENCE WITH THE TENSES CHANGED -- which settles that the three camps' shared Wakonda material is one text, not three borrowings (f_4856). (4) WHAT THE RITE IS MADE OF: Seton's own ceremony mixes Lakota address and pipe invocations with an Omaha song from another nation, and the 'Departure of Hiawatha' in Eastaugh's list of standard parts is neither -- it is Longfellow, 1855, absent from the Book of Woodcraft (f_4857). CHANGED: council-ring.md gains a section 'The source text, read at last' and the Mazinaw finding (18 -> 19 sources, one RALPH loop); indigenous-names-and-land.md gains the five-hands provenance and the composite point (30 -> 31 sources). STILL OPEN, and the part only a person can do: Eastaugh offered 'a complete and detailed description of the rituals, ceremonies, games and organization' on request from the Taylor Statten Camps -- ask whether that document survives, since it is the version Kanawana's leaders were actually taught. Queued as p_421.

priorities.description: TEST EASTAUGH'S CLAIM ABOUT INDIGENOUS PARTICIPATION IN YMCA CAMP PROGRAMMES. Jack Eastaugh writes in Spring 1973 that 'the Y.M.C.A. camps in Eastern and Western Canada for years have welcomed the participation of, and appreciated the contribution of local Indians in their programs,' naming people from the Golden Lake, Couchiching, Georgian Bay, Brantford and Moosonee reserves working in Ontario camps. That is a claim about Kanawana's own movement which no Kanawana source has confirmed or denied. Search the YMCA of Montreal records and Kanawana staff lists for Indigenous staff or invited participants; check whether any Kanawana source names a person from Kanesatake, Kahnawake or another Quebec community. A null result is worth recording as a null result -- the article should be able to say whether Kanawana did this, not merely that the movement claimed to. || ANSWERED 2026-09-06 (f_5230), IN THE NEGATIVE, AND WRITTEN INTO indigenous-names-and-land.md as its own subsection. The sweep this priority asked for was run across every cached document -- community names (Kahnawake, Caughnawaga, Kanesatake, Odanak, Wendake, Maniwaki, Restigouche) and Indian/Native/Autochtone/Amerindien/Mohawk/Cree/Algonquin/Montagnais/Iroquois in the same line as a word for employment or attendance. NOT ONE HIT IS ABOUT A PERSON AT KANAWANA; 'Caughnawaga' occurs exactly once in the whole cache, in McMorris, about the camp's name. THE NULL IS CALIBRATED rather than merely asserted: the same magazine printed, four years before Eastaugh and unprompted, that at the N.W.T. Camping Association's camps 'approximately one-half of the camping personnel is Indian: no segregation here' -- so the literature reported this when it happened. THE LIMIT IS STATED IN THE ARTICLE: it is silence in a partial record, and Concordia's staff files, payroll and camp committee minutes could still hold a name. Reopen only if those are read.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 97-99, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: WRITE THE HOAX ARGUMENT INTO wiki/traditions/myths-and-legends.md AS AN ARGUMENT, NOT A VERDICT. Within eighteen months Canadian Camping printed three positions: Bob Attfield's how-to for the camp hoax (Spring 1972), Walter Greenway naming 'a hoax' among the traditions deliberately taught to new staff at pre-camp (Spring 1972), and Mary L. Northway -- co-author of The Camp Counsellor's Book, the standard Canadian text -- writing that 'Supernatural fears from spooky stories and myths about malicious ghosts have no place in the young camper's life, nor have unnecessary fears of night raids or hazing' (Summer 1973). Hartry and Attfield both volunteered the same caution about frightening children; Northway states it as a rule. A camp running a Chopsy in the 1970s was doing something the profession was actively arguing about. That is a better documented and more interesting claim than either approval or disapproval alone, and the article should say so and cite all three. | ALREADY DONE, VERIFIED 2026-09-05. myths-and-legends.md carries all three positions and carries them AS AN ARGUMENT, which is what the priority asked for: a section headed 'The camp hoax as a documented practice', Hartry's snark hunt and Attfield's how-to and Greenway's pre-camp list, then 'And the profession was not agreed about it' introducing Northway, then the summary sentence that within a year and a half the national magazine carried a how-to, a director teaching it, and the country's leading authority saying it had no place. It also carries the restraint the priority did not ask for and should have: 'None of this is evidence about Chopsy specifically. No item in the 1949-1988 run mentions Kanawana in this connection, or the name Chopsy.' Sources 24 and 25. The priority was stale, not open; closed on reading rather than on rewriting.

A richly deserved honour will be bestowed on her by Q.C.A. in May and our fall edition will feature an article about her.' priorities.description: SEARCH FOR THE OCA'S 'IT'S WISE TO SUPERVISE' (1973). Advertised at $1.25 in Canadian Camping, Summer 1973, as 'An authoritative discussion on Staff Supervision in Summer Camps,' endorsed by the Ontario Camping Association and ordered from its office. It is the fifth period document on Canadian camp staff practice this read has found, after Moon's 1968 piece, the 1969 CIT study, the OCA job-negotiation guidelines (1972) and Blackstock's model contract and staff-manual outline (1973), and it is the only one specifically about supervision -- which is the act that produces a written staff assessment. Directly relevant to p_307. Search library catalogues, the OCA's successor body and the Trent archives.

priorities.description: FIND HEDLEY G. DIMOCK'S ADDRESS 'CANADIAN CAMPING -- ITS RESISTANCE TO CHANGE,' delivered to the Canadian Camping Association meeting of 2-4 March 1967. Al Knox names and dates it in Canadian Camping (Winter/Spring 1974) and recommends it for its treatment of camper development and of 'the function and influence of the camp director.' The magazine's own April 1967 conference report describes Dimock 'urging them to change from repressive to participative methods of programming,' and a Manitoba director wrote that autumn that his camp was 'heavily impressed by Hedley Dimock at the Canadian Camping Association Conference' and introducing participatory camping. The man who spent 1960-61 studying counsellor effectiveness AT KANAWANA gave the address that put 'participative camping' into the working vocabulary of Canadian camp directors, and camps were still citing it by name seven years later. Search: the OCA Conference Digests for 1966-68 (sold at cost by the association and listed in its own publications catalogue); the CCA material at Trent; Sir George Williams / Concordia's Dimock papers; and the Centre for Human Relations and Community Studies. This is a first-order lead for hedley-dimock.md and for any account of what Kanawana's own director would have been hearing in 1967. | SEARCHED AND NULL 2026-09-05 (f_4858), and note that hedley-dimock.md already carried both contemporaneous references before this pass -- the April 1967 keynote report and the autumn 1967 Manitoba director's letter. TWO SURFACES ADDED TO THE NULL: the complete cached run of Canadian Camping, 164 issues, in which 'resistance to change' occurs in ONE issue, Knox's own 1974 article -- the magazine reported the address twice and printed it never; and the Internet Archive's 22 items under creator 'Dimock, Hedley', 1931 to 2011, none of which is the address. A CAUTION NOW IN THE ARTICLE: 'Canadian Camping -- Its Resistance to Change' is Knox's wording seven years after the fact, while the contemporaneous report calls it a keynote 'on the Individual' from 'Springboard No. 1'. They may be one address or two, and the title should not be treated as the document's own until someone sees it. WHAT IS LEFT is archival: the OCA Conference Digests for 1966-68, the CCA archive the association resolved in 1973 to deposit at the University of Waterloo, the OCA fonds at Trent (p_348), and Dimock's own papers -- he taught at Sir George Williams, so Concordia is the first place to ask (add to the p_282 letter).

priorities.description: TRACE THE QUEBEC CAMPING ASSOCIATION'S PROVINCIAL CHARTER OF 1961 AND THE PAPERS THAT GO WITH IT. The Alta Kahn tribute (Canadian Camping, Fall 1973) states: 'It was through Mrs. Kahn's efforts that the Quebec Camping Association finally secured its Provincial Charter in 1961.' An incorporation is a public record: search Quebec's Registraire des entreprises for the QCA and for l'Association des camps du Quebec, and follow the charter to the directors named on it, the registered address, and any dissolution or continuance filing. That last is the practical point -- when an incorporated association winds up or merges, its records go somewhere, and this is the most concrete handle the project has yet had on where the Quebec association's accreditation files went. Related dates from the same tribute: the association's twenty-first birthday in 1958 (founding 1937), the Provincial Board co-ordinating the English and French sections with Kahn as its second president 1963-65, and Kahn still chairing the English Section's Standards Committee in 1973. | ATTEMPTED 2026-09-05, BLOCKED, AND THE BLOCK IS ABOUT THIS ENVIRONMENT (f_4859). The Registraire des entreprises search page returns HTTP 403 with 'L'acces a nos services vous est temporairement interdit en raison d'une utilisation excessive' -- tried twice, with browser headers and French language preferences. BAnQ numerique answers 200 and renders its results in JavaScript, so the HTML carries no results. NEITHER IS EVIDENCE ABOUT THE CHARTER. WHAT WAS OBTAINED: the ACQ's own about page says 'Fondee en 1961 a l'initiative de directeurs de camps de vacances' -- crediting camp directors collectively, in the same year the Alta Kahn tribute credits her efforts for the QCA's provincial charter. Compatible statements, NOT to be merged: an incorporation and a founding are different events, and whether the 1961 charter is the ACQ's legal birth is the question. BEST UNTRIED ROUTE, and it is documentary rather than a registry lookup: THE GAZETTE OFFICIELLE DU QUEBEC FOR 1961, which publishes letters patent for non-profit corporations and would give the charter's date, the corporate name it was granted under, and the petitioners' names. BAnQ holds the run. Then: the Registraire from an ordinary Quebec browser, where the same search is free and takes a minute; and the Registre des entreprises bulk dataset on Donnees Quebec.

priorities.description: SPAWN A STUB FOR ALTA R. KAHN. The tribute read on 23 May 1973, when the Quebec Camping Association English Section made her the first Honorary President in its history, gives a full and dated life: 1908 the first Jewish teacher to graduate from Macdonald College; 1918 a founder of Montreal Hadassah; 1920 organiser of the first Junior Hadassah chapter in Canada; 1936-45 Executive Director of the Young Women's Hebrew Association; 1946-49 Executive Secretary of the Jewish Community Camps (B'nai B'rith, Jewish Laurentian Fresh Air, and Wooden Acres), where she 'instituted many new projects, including the first Pre-Camp Training Programs for Staff'; with the QCA from 1946; chairing the 1958 joint conference; QCA Standards Committee co-chair 1959-60; English Section president 1960-62; Provincial Board president 1963-65; and still on the CCA National Standards Committee in 1973. She belongs in core people/ rather than notable-alumni: her enduring significance is Quebec camping itself, and she is the person who connects Montreal Jewish community camping in the Laurentians to the standards committee that wrote what Kanawana was measured against. Search the Canadian Jewish Congress archives, Hadassah-WIZO Canada, the Gazette and the Canadian Jewish Review for an obituary.

priorities.description: WRITE THE QUEBEC STANDARDS VISITATION INTO THE KANAWANA ARTICLES USING MADELENE ALLEN'S 1974 ACCOUNT. The Director of Camp Ouareau, a member of the QCA Standards Committee, describes the provincial standards from inside an accredited Quebec camp: 'We view this tome in different lights depending on the time of year... we view it with slight trepidation as we leaf through its pages the night before the visitor is expected.' She then gave the standards AND THE MARKING SCHEME to her five CITs at the six-week point, in pairs, a week each on different sections: they interviewed the director with pencil and notebook, shadowed senior staff, were given the records of programmes and staff lists, and 'inspected the waterfront, examined the canoes, counted the toilets, and checked the outlets of the septic tanks after a heavy rain.' That is what a Quebec standards visitation covered in 1974, and it confirms a written marking scheme as well as a standards document -- two record classes to name explicitly when asking after Kanawana's accreditation file (p_339). | DONE 2026-09-05, into cit-lit-program.md rather than the article the priority named, and the placement is the argument. Madelene Allen's account is two things at once: a description of what a Quebec standards visitation covered in 1974 -- waterfront, craft, sanitation, programme records, personnel records and the director under questioning -- and a CIT TRAINING EXERCISE, since she handed her five CITs the standards AND the marking scheme at the six-week point and had them audit the camp in pairs. The second is the part no Kanawana record has an equivalent for, so it sits in the CIT article, three sections before the 1977 statement of what a CIT was owed nationally, which it precedes and outdoes. The record-shape point the priority wanted is stated there too: a written marking scheme AND a standards document, two classes to name when asking Concordia (p_339), and if Quebec re-accredited annually then what is missing is a SERIES rather than a document. The article ends the section with the honest pair of sentences: no source says Kanawana ever did anything of the kind, and no source says it did not. cit-lit-program.md 10 -> 11 sources. ONE MECHANICAL SLIP CAUGHT BY THE HARNESS: the new footnote was inserted after the first string match for the preceding entry, which was inside the article's own Research Notes comment rather than in the Sources list -- verify_harness.py failed A1 (header says 11, 10 entries present) and the entry was moved. The lesson is the same one as the 8t footnote collision earlier today: locate by structure, not by first string match.

priorities.description: MINE THE JANUARY 1975 DIRECTORY ISSUE FOR KANAWANA -- AND FOR ITS QUEBEC NEIGHBOURS. Canadian Camping Vol. 27 No. 2 (January 1975) is a Directory Issue listing all CCA member camps in each province, 20,000 copies printed, and it is in the cache as issue 103 of this read. A targeted check has already confirmed the line 'KANAWANA (1894) (YMCA)' with St. Sauveur des Monts. This is the first direct Kanawana appearance in the 1970s stretch of the read, and a national directory entry should carry founding date, sponsor, location, ages, capacity, season, fees and director's name as the association held them in 1974-75 -- a period for which this project's Kanawana record is thin. Extract the Kanawana entry in full, field by field, and extract the whole Quebec section as a snapshot of the camps Kanawana sat among. Note also that the directory prints the camp's founding year as 1894, so the association's own national listing corroborates the date. | DONE 2026-09-05. KANAWANA'S ENTRY, field by field: 'KANAWANA (1894) (YMCA)'; director Derek V. Walsh; P.O. Box 310, St. Sauveur des Monts (514-227-2414); winter office 1441 Drummond St., Montreal (514-849-5331); activities tripping, swimming, sailing, arts & crafts, C.I.T. program; capacity 90 BOYS 8-15 AND 90 GIRLS 8-15 -- an even ninety and ninety, seven years after coeducation, in a year this project's Kanawana record is otherwise thin for (f_4866). THREE UNLABELLED COLUMNS reading 'X X C' follow the address in every Quebec entry; the header row is not recoverable from this OCR, so they are left uninterpreted rather than guessed at -- C plausibly marks co-ed or 'camp' against R for resident, but no page this read can reconstruct says so. THE WHOLE QUEBEC SECTION EXTRACTED: 64 member camps with the founding year printed beside each. Sorted, KANAWANA'S 1894 IS THE EARLIEST IN THE PROVINCE BY TWELVE YEARS -- next is Brewery Mission 1906, then Oolahwan 1917, Lewis 1918, B'nai B'rith 1921, Ouareau 1922 (f_4867). The directory prints it as a plain fact of the listing rather than a contested claim, which is worth having, though it is the association's compilation of what member camps told it and not an independent test, and it covers members only. Six of the 64 were founded after 1970 and about a quarter before 1940; francophone and anglophone camps are interleaved in one alphabetical list, fifteen years after the French section formed (f_4868). quebec-camp-landscape.md 25 -> 26 sources, with the entry, the earliest-ten table, and the long tail of camps this wiki does not otherwise follow.

priorities.description: RECORD LES VOYAGEURS DE LA VERENDRYE AS A SEPARATELY ACCREDITED CAMP IN canoe-trips.md AND THE VOYAGEUR MATERIAL. The January 1975 national directory lists it in its own right, not as a Kanawana programme: 'LES VOYAGEURS DE LA VERENDRYE (YMCA); Director Derek V. Walsh; c/o Kamp Kanawana, P.O. Box 310, St. Sauveur des Monts; Activities: Wilderness, Canoe Trips, Fishing, Campcraft; Accommodation: 15 boys 13-17 / 5 girls 13-17.' Two things follow that the wiki does not currently say. First, the Quebec Camping Association treated the trip programme as a distinct wilderness camp operating out of the Kanawana site, which means it was separately accredited and would have generated its own annual visitation report. Second, the project now has a number for its scale and its gender composition in 1975: twenty places, fifteen boys' and five girls', ages 13 to 17 -- the girls' places existed but were a quarter of the boys'. Kanawana's own entry in the same directory gives 90 boys and 90 girls aged 8-15 at exactly equal capacity, so the trip programme's imbalance is not explained by the main camp's.

priorities.description: CHASE THE 1975 CONFERENCE TAPES ON STAFF SUPERVISION AND EVALUATION. The CCA's publications catalogue (April 1975) sells seventeen cassette tapes of the January 1975 Geneva Park national conference at $4.00 each, ten of them Canadian sessions: 'Recruiting, Hiring, Interviewing' (Bruce Harris), 'Evaluating Your Camp' (Barry Lowes), 'Staff Training' (John Boutin), 'Staff Supervision' (Brian Law), 'Develop Staff From Within Your Camp' (Al Knox), plus budget, recruiting and PR, camp philosophy and committees. A recorded, purchasable 1975 seminar on camp staff supervision and evaluation is directly relevant to p_307, and cassettes sold in quantity to member camps sometimes survive where paper does not. Ask the CCA's successor body and the Trent holdings. The same catalogue lists two new Canadian titles to find: the Camp Counsellor's Handbook by Blackstock and Latimer (1975, 128 pp.) and Tolbitt's Counsellor's Guide to Camp Singing (44 pp.), the nearest thing yet found to the national camp songbook p_311 is chasing.

priorities.description: RECORD THE 1976 YMCA LIFESAVING CHANGEOVER IN THE WATERFRONT MATERIAL. Doug Dent, Canadian Camping, January 1976: 'First of all, the YMCA lifesaving program was revamped, and in its place the RLSS program (Bronze Medallion and upwards) has been adopted.' So by 1976 the YMCA had dropped its own lifesaving programme for the Royal Life Saving Society's. The same article prints a three-column equivalence chart -- YMCA Pre-Beginner, Beginner and Star I-VI against Red Cross Pre-Beginner, Beginner, Junior, Intermediate and Senior, and RLSS Survival and Life Saving I, II and III (the RLSS having just replaced its Elementary and Intermediate levels). This matters for reading any Kanawana swimming record: the YMCA 'Star' levels are the system a Kanawana swimmer of the period would have been graded on, and an award named in a camper's memory or a staff list can now be placed against a national scale and dated either side of the 1976 changeover.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 106-109, converted to KB facts
priorities.resolution: Written into wiki/traditions/programs-activities.md as a new subsection under Coeducation and Reorganization: the changeover sentence, the division of labour between the three bodies, the full three-column YMCA / Red Cross / RLSS chart, and the age floors (Senior RC 12, Bronze Medallion and Bronze Cross 14, RC Leaders / Assistant Instructor (Y) / Award of Merit 15). Fact f_4929. The point the priority was after -- that an award named in a camper's memory or a staff list can be placed on a national scale and dated either side of 1976 -- is stated, with the sharper version: a Star level dates a swimmer to the YMCA scheme, a Life Saving I/II/III dates them after the RLSS renumbering. ONE THING THE PRIORITY DID NOT ANTICIPATE: this article already recorded that Kanawana's own top water award of 1923, the KLS, was keyed to the RLSS AWARD OF MERIT -- half a century before the YMCA nationally handed lifesaving to the same society. Written up with the caveat that it shows nothing about what the camp taught in between, and is not evidence Kanawana was ahead of its parent body.

priorities.description: WRITE THE THREE STRUCTURAL BREAKS IN THE CANADIAN CAMPING RUN INTO meta/sources-index.md (see p_359). The run has three dated interruptions in three years, and each explains an apparent hole: publication was SUSPENDED in February 1974 on financial grounds by the CCA Board and resumed only in November 1974 (Vol. 26 No. 2 is a combined Winter/Spring 1974 number, then nothing until Vol. 27 No. 1); the November 1975 number is a FOUR-PAGE NEWSLETTER because the Canadian postal strike left the editor short of advertisements and of the French-language content; and the June 1976 issue announces itself as the LAST -- 'The decision was made by the CCA Board at the recent meetings in Quebec City and was one based wholely on financial considerations' -- after which the title continues from October 1976 as a typewritten eight-page newsletter, five or six numbers a year instead of quarterly. So the format and depth change sharply at issue 109 of this read, and nothing is missing from the project's holdings at any of the three points. The section should say all of this before it says anything about content.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 106-109, converted to KB facts
priorities.resolution: Written into the Canadian Camping section of meta/sources-index.md as 'Three structural breaks, 1974-1976, and why none of them is a hole', placed before the production table so it is read before anything about content. All three verified against the cached issues rather than taken from the priority: the February 1974 suspension in the November 1974 issue's own words, the November 1975 four-page newsletter and the mail strike in Helen E. Stewart's page-one note, and the June 1976 'this issue is its last' editorial. TWO THINGS THE PRIORITY DID NOT HAVE. First, the November 1974 explanation goes on to give the Task Force's recommendation that THE JANUARY ISSUE BECOME A DIRECTORY ISSUE -- so the January 1975 and 1976 directories, which are this project's source for Kanawana's capacity, director, activities and the separate accreditation of Les Voyageurs de la Verendrye, exist because of the 1974 financial crisis. Second, the June 1976 editorial mentions an April issue, which invites the inference that a number is missing; it is not. Vol. 28 is numbered 1, 2, 3, 4 consecutively (Nov 1975, Jan 1976, Jun 1976, Oct 1976), so nothing is absent from the cache, and on the numbering the April 1976 issue was planned rather than published. Earlier volumes did carry an April number, which is what makes it look like a gap. Fact f_4930.

priorities.description: CHECK QUEBEC'S STATUTORY RECORD FOR CAMP WATERFRONT AND SAFETY REGULATION FROM 1976 -- AND FOR A GOVERNMENT INSPECTION FILE ON KANAWANA. Canadian Camping's Quebec column, December 1976: 'A somewhat scary proposal is now being made by the Department of Labour...Waterfronts in camps may not be deeper than six feet!!!' The exclamation marks are the association's. In the same months the High Commission of Leisure and Sports was paying for a full-time provincial camp training post and, by February 1977, giving the association $300,000 for its spring training programme -- so the Quebec government was funding the accrediting body and drafting rules of its own at the same time. Two questions follow. Was the six-foot rule ever enacted, in any form? A depth limit is not something a camp on a natural lake can comply with by adjusting anything, so if it passed it would have forced visible changes at every Laurentian camp. And if a ministry was regulating camp waterfronts from 1976-77, there may be a GOVERNMENTAL inspection file on Kanawana distinct from the association's annual accreditation reports (p_314). Search: Quebec's Gazette officielle and statutory instruments for 1976-80; the Haut-Commissariat a la Jeunesse, aux Loisirs et aux Sports fonds and the ministere du Travail fonds at BAnQ. || ADVANCED 2026-09-06 (f_5229) AND A DATE FOR THE RULE NOW EXISTS. Ka-News of 29 March 1978 tells the Kanawana staff that "il existe maintenant une nouvelle loi qui exige que tout personnel aquatique possede son certificat de sauveteur", with the next National Lifeguard Service course starting 22 April 1978 at the Westmount YMCA (f_5223). So the requirement was NEW to camp staff in the spring of 1978, which brackets it more tightly than this priority's own 1976 starting point. THE CITATION CHAIN IS NOW ESTABLISHED: Code de securite, chapitre IX, Lieux de baignade <- Reglement sur la securite dans les bains publics, B-1.1, r. 11 <- formerly S-3, r. 3 <- Loi sur la securite dans les edifices publics (S-3). WHAT IS MISSING IS THE ORIGINAL ADOPTION DATE AND TEXT, and it is missing because of a host block: legisquebec.gouv.qc.ca answers 403 through an AWS CloudFront edge block on both its document paths, and canlii.org answers 403 behind a JS wall. Both are new failure modes for this project and both are in one-afternoon-with-a-browser.md as item 9. A person with a browser gets the historical note in one click; failing that, the Gazette officielle du Quebec for 1977-78 carries the decree, and BAnQ numerique has the Gazette.

priorities.description: SPAWN A STUB FOR CHARLES F. PLEWMAN. The read has justified it four times over and the biography is now fully dated: born about 1889-90 (he was 87 in February 1977); first at camp as a camper in 1903; ran his first short-term camp in 1909; Director of Camp On-Da-Da-Waks 1913-1916, then three years at Camp Stephens, then Inter-Church camps; eight years YMCA Boys' Work Secretary at Ottawa and Winnipeg and eleven years Secretary for the Ontario Boys' Work Board -- the same office Roy Locke and Nelson McEwen held at Montreal; founded Kilcoo Camp in 1932 and owned it to 1955; OCA president from 1945; Secretary of the Toronto branch of the Canadian Red Cross in the Second World War, where he instituted the Toronto Mobile Blood Donor Service; Honorary Fellow of the Society of Camp Directors at its 1969 inaugural dinner; Honorary Member of the CCA at the Montreal annual meeting of October 1974. He matters to this project for three separate reasons: he founded the magazine that is this project's largest single source and wrote its founding history; he is a first-hand witness on the CCA's own founding (c_035), on both 1936 and 1946; and he published an eyewitness account of Tom Thomson's burial fifty-five years after the event. Place in core people/ only if the wider-lens test is met -- otherwise connections/institutional-lineage/.

priorities.description: SPAWN A STUB FOR FRANCES M. KELLY. She appears across twenty-five years of this run in the same office: secretary at the Quebec Camping Association English Section in the early 1950s, Executive Secretary through the 1960s and 1970s at 2233 Belgrave Avenue, chairman of its Staff Placement Bureau in 1975, author of the F. M. Van Wagner tribute in 1975 that gave this project the QCA's founding date and the 1955 Manual of Standards, and singled out at the fortieth anniversary conference in March 1977 for "special recognition" as "the backbone of the English section of Q.C.A." She is the person who would have handled Kanawana's membership, its accreditation correspondence and its staff placement listings for a quarter-century, which makes her the most likely single custodian of the records p_314 is looking for -- and a person to trace for surviving papers or family. Search Montreal directories, the Gazette, and the association's successor body.

priorities.description: SPAWN A STUB FOR EILEEN MAYOTTE -- and note the Quebec connection. Her CCA executive profile of February 1978: 'During her illustrious career in camping, Eileen has had responsibility for camps and campers in four provinces -- Ontario, Quebec, Saskatchewan, and B.C. Her camping endeavors have lead her into church camping, YWCA and camps for underprivileged children. In the distant past she was the Secretary of the Quebec Camping Association. She was one of the founders of the Saskatchewan Camping Association, and for many years was its President.' She appears through this run as Saskatchewan president from 1970, as the author of the clearest statement of camper agency in it (Responsibility, 1976, on Ginott: 'the selecting belongs to the administration -- the choosing should be the right of the camper'), as CCA Secretary from April 1977 and Vice-President from November 1977. The Quebec secretaryship is undated and is the thing to pin down: she held the office A. Ross Seaman held from about 1949, at some earlier point, which would put her in Kanawana's own provincial association. Search Quebec Camping Association records, YWCA Montreal, and Saskatchewan press.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 114-117, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: GET A QUEBEC DELEGATE LIST FOR THE GENEVA PARK NATIONAL CONFERENCES. Delegates to the CCA's national conferences were SELECTED BY EACH PROVINCIAL ASSOCIATION rather than by application -- the October 1977 announcement of the third conference (19-22 January 1978, theme 'Keys to Success', $75 per delegate with return air fare covered from outside Ontario by Recreation Canada) says so explicitly. So a Quebec delegate list for January 1978 is a short, checkable document naming who the association sent, and Kanawana's own director was that association's English-section president at the time. The same applies to the January 1975 and February 1973 conferences. Ask the Quebec association's successor body and Trent; the 1973 conference also produced a written resume of every session (p_372) and seventeen cassette tapes.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 114-117, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: ASK CONCORDIA FOR KANAWANA'S PER-BUILDING MAINTENANCE RECORDS BY NAME. Wilfred A. Jackson, Director of Camps and Conference Centre for Catholic Community Services in Montreal and chairman of the QCA English Section's fortieth anniversary conference, set out in Canadian Camping (April 1978) exactly what a Montreal camp administrator of the period was told to keep: a MASTERPLAN showing all buildings present and future; a loose-leaf MAINTENANCE MANUAL with check lists, directions and 'a schedule arranged by seasons, including specific details on opening and closing procedures'; and 'A record of each building should be kept showing floor plans, type of construction, history, inventory, and required repairs', with plans of the water, electrical and sewage systems and manufacturers' instructions on file. He adds a large master map, a portfolio of buildings with photographs and floor plans, a LOG OF IMPROVEMENTS, a list of local suppliers kept in the maintenance building, and tagged keys with spares held by the maintenance head. If Kanawana kept any of this, site/the-kanawana-site.md and meta/plaque-audit.md have an unexploited source class -- a per-building file with floor plans and repair history, which is precisely what a plaque audit needs. Ask by these names; a request for 'building records' will not find them.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 118-122, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: SEARCH THE QUEBEC HEALTH DEPARTMENT'S RECORD FOR LAKE KANAWANA WATER SAMPLES. Eanswythe Flynn's checklist tells directors, in May and again in June of every year covered by this run, to 'Send water samples (both drinking and swimming) regularly to Provincial Health Department.' For an accredited camp this was not optional -- water tested before camp and re-tested weekly is item after item in the printed standards. A routine of that kind, kept up over decades, generates a dated series in the provincial health record: sample dates, results, and the name and address of the submitting camp. That would independently date Kanawana's operating seasons, and a failed sample would date a problem. Search: the ministere de la Sante fonds and its predecessors at BAnQ, the regional health unit for the Laurentians, and any municipal record for Saint-Sauveur. Pair this with p_388, which asks the same question of the labour ministry's camp waterfront rule.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 118-122, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: WRITE THE 1979 REBUILDING OF THE TRIPPING ETHIC INTO canoe-trips.md AND environmental-history.md AS A SEQUENCE. Three separate statements of leave-no-trace ethics appear in Canadian Camping within seven months: Kevin Redmond's 'No Trace Camping' (March 1979), with its group-size rule -- 'The organization of trips with more than 20 people is bound to leave its mark on the ecology' -- and its fire and latrine specifics; the twenty Environmental Maintenance Standards from a Conference of Canadian Interpreters (June 1979), which open on exactly Kanawana's own 1970 erosion problem and which question permanent out-trip sites, motor boats and even flush toilets; and 'Canoe Tripping in the Twentieth Century' (October 1979), which abandons four techniques standard in camping manuals -- trenches, bough beds, tables and garbage pits. Taken with the November 1975 flotation regulation and the association's reckoning after the 1978 Quebec fatality, the whole safety-and-ethics framework around a Quebec camp's wilderness tripping was rebuilt between 1975 and 1979, and none of it originated at Kanawana. The articles should say so and date it, so that later Kanawana environmental commitments are read as joining a movement rather than leading one. | DONE 2026-09-05, and HALF OF IT WAS ALREADY DONE. environmental-history.md already carried Redmond's March 1979 'No Trace Camping' and the June 1979 Environmental Maintenance Standards, read against Kanawana's own 1970 erosion confession. What was missing was canoe-trips.md, where the gap was exactly at 1979 -- its chronology ran '1978: a fatal wilderness trip in Quebec' straight into 'What the movement decided, 1980'. A section '1979: the tripping ethic itself is rebuilt' now sits between them, carrying all three statements with their specifics: Redmond's warning to 'beware of the traditions -- axes, saws, elaborate latrines, garbage pits and material shelters, all of which can be found in camping texts' and his test ('Will the next traveller, be he a couple of hours or years away, know that you have been there?'); the twenty standards, cross-linked to the environmental article rather than repeated; and the October 1979 canoe-tripping rules, ending on the four abandoned techniques -- trenches, bough beds, tables and garbage pits. THE POINT THE PRIORITY ASKED FOR IS STATED IN THE ARTICLE: those four were not lapses but TECHNIQUE, printed in the manuals and taught to counsellors, and within seven months the national magazine told camps to stop all of them. And the framing the priority wanted: Kanawana's later environmental commitments read differently depending on whether the movement got there first, and it did -- the whole safety-and-ethics framework around a Quebec camp's wilderness tripping was rebuilt between 1975 and 1979 by people at other camps. The article says Kanawana joined a movement rather than led one, and adds the honest qualifier that no source shows it dissenting either. canoe-trips.md 22 -> 23 sources.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 123-127, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: IDENTIFY THE FORMER LAURENTIAN BOYS' CAMP ADVERTISED FOR RENT IN OCTOBER 1979. The classified reads: 'Property for rent -- to clubs, community, religious, company or other groups for adult, children, or family camping; 75 acres, 3 lakes, large wharf, diving board and tower, playing field, buildings, electricity, central water system, FORMER BOYS' CAMP; weekly, monthly or season: 70 miles from Montreal near Lachute, Quebec.' Only a Montreal telephone number is given. A 75-acre three-lake site with a diving tower near Lachute is specific enough to identify from municipal assessment rolls, the Argenteuil regional county records, or the Quebec association's own membership directories for the 1960s and 1970s -- a camp that had closed by 1979 but was still standing. Match against connections/related-camps/quebec-camp-landscape.md, which is the register of camps Kanawana sat among; a closure in the 1970s is also a datum for the shrinking market Granek documented (p_321).
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 123-127, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: FIND THE QUEBEC ASSOCIATION'S OWN NEWSLETTER. Marjorie Booth, as the CCA's first Executive Director, wrote in February 1980: 'Many times I've come across great articles in provincial newsletters. If each province can continue (or begin?) to include C.C.A. on their mailing list for a few copies of newsletters, conference programs, etc., "Canadian Camping" will be able to carry articles from all parts of the country.' Much of what the national run prints from 1980 onward is reprinted from provincial newsletters -- which means the PROVINCIAL newsletters are a parallel body of material this project has never touched, and the Quebec one is the one to want. It would carry exactly what the national newsletter thins out: Quebec camp news, Quebec officer changes, Quebec conference programmes, and quite possibly Kanawana by name. The read has already shown the Quebec association producing substantial documents of its own -- the 1976 Director Education Program, the standards manual and its marking scheme, the Semaine des camps campaigns. Search: the ACQ's successor body; Trent, which received provincial as well as national camping papers; BAnQ; and the Quebec ministry fonds that funded the association's training programmes.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 128-132, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: SPAWN A STUB FOR MARJORIE A. BOOTH -- and use it to fix a hole in camp-oolahwan.md. She was the Canadian Camping Association's first Executive Director, appointed in November 1979 on a Fitness and Amateur Sport grant, and came to it directly from being 'the director of Camp Oolahwan, the Montreal Y.W.C.A. camp, located north of Montreal.' A native of Toronto, honours degree in Recreation from the University of Waterloo, several years full-time with the Saint John YWCA, Fellow of the Society of Camp Directors since 1977. She is only the SECOND named director of Oolahwan this project holds -- camp-oolahwan.md names nobody in charge between Mary Edgar's departure in 1919 and the final season in 2004 -- and her appointment shows Oolahwan was an operating YWCA residential camp in the late 1970s with a professional director recruited from another province. Search: YWCA Montreal records, YWCA Canada, the University of Waterloo Recreation alumni record, and Canadian Camping's own later issues, which the read will reach.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 128-132, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: ASK CONCORDIA FOR A KANAWANA STAFF MANUAL BY NAME. Canadian Camping's Camp Staff Issue of February 1981 specifies exactly what one contained, in seven parts, and the specification is what makes this worth a targeted request rather than a general one. Part II, Facts About Camp: a directional map, 'a sketch of site showing trails, program areas, buildings', a description of the setting's special features and 'SPECIAL PROBLEMS WHICH SITE GIVES RISE TO'; statements of traditions and philosophy; 'a brief historical sketch of the camp'; and 'explanation of role that camping plays in the total program of the sponsoring organization' -- for Kanawana, the YMCA of Montreal. Personnel Policies: 'sickness allowance; employment and dismissal procedures; salary scales and payment procedures.' Part IV, the blank forms. Part V, job analyses for every post including the CIT programme. A single surviving Kanawana manual would carry all of that in one binder, and it would be the camp's own history as told to nineteen-year-olds, which is a franker document than a brochure. This also explains something the project already holds: the 'Kamp Kanawana History' presented at a staff training course in 1951 is precisely the 'brief historical sketch' the specification prescribes, so it was probably written for, or extracted from, a manual of this kind -- and others may exist for other years. Ask for staff manuals, counsellor manuals and camp manuals by all three names, and for the 1980 national training outline's Camp History session material.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 133-137, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: SOURCE OR DROP THE CAMP KEEWAYDIN 1893 CLAIM. traditions/myths-and-legends.md has said since it was written that 'Camp Keewaydin in Ontario, founded in 1893, also predates Kanawana by one year.' The sentence cited f_0412, which says nothing about Keewaydin, and the KB holds no Keewaydin fact at all -- the citation was wrong and the claim is unsupported. It is now marked in the article as an unverified carry-over. Keewaydin's Canadian operation (Devil's Gap / Temagami) has a documented history and the date should be easy to establish or refute; Keewaydin Temagami is usually given as 1893 but the camp's origin is Vermont, 1893 or earlier, which may be what the original claim confused. Resolve it and either cite it properly or remove the sentence. Found while withdrawing the 'Canada's second-oldest' ranking after the Camp Stephens finding (c_031).
priorities.source: citation audit of myths-and-legends.md during the c_031 ranking withdrawal

priorities.description: TRIAGE THE CITATION-AIM BACK CATALOGUE AND MAKE THE CHECK BLOCKING. scripts/verify/citation_aim.py is advisory and currently reports two thin citations: (1) places-and-locations.md:223 cites f_0226 ('A 1928 Kanawana map and a 1962 Kanawana map were analyzed in the McMorris thesis') for the claim that an 'Indian Grave' marking existed on the camp map -- the fact establishes the maps but says nothing about the marking, so the specific claim is uncited; (2) myths-and-legends.md:108 cites f_0536 (a list of Cropsey name variants) for 'Both films derive from the same campfire tradition', which the fact does not state. Resolve both by finding the right fact or rewording the claim, then flip the script to exit 1 and move its workflow step above the embargo step. NOTE the check is a deliberately weak heuristic -- it compares distinctive tokens and passes any citation sharing one -- so a clean run is not proof of correct aim, only absence of the grossest shape. | COMPLETED 2026-09-05. citation_aim.py is now BLOCKING (exits 1) and its workflow step already sat above the embargo step. Four findings cleared, not two: the two in the queue plus two that surfaced behind them. (1) places-and-locations.md cited f_0226 ('a 1928 and a 1962 map were analyzed in the McMorris thesis') for the 'Indian Grave' marking; f_0228 states that claim exactly, same source, so the pointer was simply wrong and is corrected -- kb_facts_used updated with it. (2) myths-and-legends.md said 'Both films derive from the same campfire tradition [f_0536]', which f_0536 does not say; the sentence now states what the fact carries -- that Madman renamed its killer once The Burning was found to be using the Cropsey concept -- and an uncited Madman Marz backstory that appears in no KB fact went with it. Recorded in that article's Revision History. (3) and (4) oldest-camp-question.md:200 and :293 were both correctly aimed and tripped the heuristic because the distinctive name sat in the PREVIOUS sentence; both citing sentences now name Ottawa 1893 and Big Cove's four-summer gap respectively. That is the general remedy and it is printed in the failure message: a sentence carrying a citation should be checkable on its own. The check remains a weak heuristic -- one shared token passes it -- so a clean run is absence of the grossest shape, not proof of aim.
priorities.source: built after mis-citing fact ids three times in one session; the check found two more pre-existing

priorities.description: FOLD THE REMAINING ORPHANED MOVEMENT FIGURES INTO canadian-camping-movement.md -- DO NOT SPAWN STUBS FOR THEM. A coverage analysis on 2026-09-05 (facts.json entities vs. full-text search of every wiki article) found nine named individuals holding >=8 KB facts each whose names appear in NO wiki article at all: Margaret Govan (32 facts), Wallace Forgie (15), Elsie Palter (14), Keith Cleverdon (12), John Hoyle (11), Elizabeth Wardley Raymer (11), Doug Dent (11), David Palter (10), M. C. MacCulloch (8). Eleven more appear in exactly one article: Anne I. Vail (30), Joyce Bertram (28), Eileen Mayotte (15), Tony Shorgan (14), Paul Belanger (12), Janet Adamson (12), Sam Hambly (10), Dorothy Percival (9), Irwin Haladner (9), Gerard Bachand (9), Colette Pouliot-Marier (8). JUDGEMENT MADE AND RECORDED: these are Ontario and national camping-movement figures, not Kanawana people. Under the hub-and-spoke placement rules in CLAUDE.md, core people/ is for those who built and ran Kanawana, so none of these warrants its own article on present evidence and spawning nine to twenty stubs would bury the camp's own people. The right home is connections/institutional-lineage/canadian-camping-movement.md, plus the topic articles where a given figure is actually load-bearing. EXCEPTIONS worth revisiting if more turns up: Eileen Mayotte and Tony Shorgan are QUEBEC association figures with long runs (Mayotte QCA secretary in the 1940s through a national committee seat in 1987; Shorgan founded the French section in 1958 and was assembling the 1988 fiftieth-anniversary of Quebec camping, per p_319) -- either could earn a stub if a biography can be assembled. ALREADY ACTIONED: Govan's February 1958 'Stop Me If You've Heard This One' and McClelland's June 1956 'set a background whether true or fictitious' are written into traditions/myths-and-legends.md, because they date the deliberate manufacture of camp lore to within a decade of the year the Chopsy story claims for itself. | COUNTS REFRESHED 2026-09-05, AND THE METHOD BEHIND THEM QUALIFIED. Current state by exact-string search: Wallace Forgie 10 facts / 0 articles; Elsie Palter 14/0; John Hoyle 12/0; David Palter 14/0; Doug Dent 8/0; M. C. MacCulloch 7/0; Sam Hambly 6/0; Keith Cleverdon 4/0; Elizabeth Wardley Raymer 3/0. Margaret Govan has moved to 1 article (32 facts). TONY SHORGAN IS OFF THE LIST -- he now has his own article (p_336), which also means the 'appears in exactly one article' half of this priority is one name shorter. THE CAVEAT THAT MATTERS: this analysis matches exact strings, and people in this corpus appear under variant forms. 'Anne I. Vail' now scores 0 articles while the same woman appears throughout the wiki as NAN VAIL and ANN VAIL -- including in the Shorgan article written today. So both lists are approximations, the orphan list may name people who are in the wiki under another form, and any pass acting on this should search the variants before concluding a person is absent. The name_variants.py check in scripts/verify is the place that knowledge belongs. | DONE 2026-09-05, as instructed: FOLDED IN, NO STUBS SPAWNED. canadian-camping-movement.md gains a section, 'The people this article's sources keep naming', covering all nine -- Wallace Forgie (the 'Commodore', 1908-1927 in Canada, and Adele Ebbs's uncle, who took her on her first big canoe trip at ten); Elsie K. and David Palter of Camp Kawagama, on the editorial team of The Camp Counselor's Book, with Elsie Palter's own 1964 use of Maslow -- probably its earliest appearance in Canadian camping literature -- and her 1970 taxonomy of why children steal at camp; John Hoyle, who chaired the standards committee 1947-1950 and wrote the frankest ethics gloss in the run; Keith Cleverdon, who wrote that committee's documentary history in 1955; M. C. MacCulloch of Bolton Camp, whose 1969 discipline policy says 'In no instance may justice at camp take the form of physical punishment. We are not parents and these are not our children'; Elizabeth Wardley Raymer, whose 1958 account of a fouled canoe-trip site is a leave-no-trace argument twenty years early; Doug Dent of the 1974 Task Force; and Sam Hambly, whose composting pamphlet opened the association's HOW TO series. The section states why they are folded rather than spawned: none is documented as having any contact with Kanawana, and what they have is a claim on THIS article as the people whose written work the movement ran on. It also carries the name-variant caution, with Nan/Ann/Anne I. Vail as the worked example. All nine now appear in exactly one article, which is what the priority asked for.
priorities.source: coverage analysis of orphan facts after the Canadian Camping extraction pass

priorities.description: CLOSE THE ATTENDANCE-SERIES GAPS THAT THE '126 CONSECUTIVE SEASONS' CLAIM RESTS ON. canadian-camping-movement.md now states that Kanawana's longest unbroken run is 126 seasons (1894-2019), which beats Camp Stephens (~102) and Big Cove (~87) and is the one superlative that survives the continuity test. It depends on the camp having missed NO season in that span. No source records a missed season and the dangerous years are documented as operating (both wars, 1918 specifically, the 1946 polio outbreak), but meta/attendance-series.md has no figure at all for 1900, 1902-03, 1905-08, 1911, 1914, 1920, 1950-51, 1960-62, 1970-71, 1973, 1975-79, 1981-87, 1989-93, 1995, 1997, 2002-04 and 2006-19. Absence of a figure is not evidence of operation. Before the 126 is used publicly, establish operation (not attendance) for each missing year -- the annual reports carry a Kanawana line most years and the 1970s-80s season reports survive. ALSO OPEN: whether Camp Stephens ran in 2021 (explicit null, f_4747), and the 1917-vs-1918 date of its wartime closure (f_4744). | SUBSTANTIALLY ADVANCED 2026-09-05. Twenty-two seasons closed, and NOT ONE came from a new source: every document behind them was already in this repository, catalogued and marked extracted. The gap was an absence of assembly, not of evidence -- these files had been mined for programme, staff and buildings and their attendance lines never carried across. CLOSED WITH FIGURES: 1900 (45 boys, 28 June-14 July, six tents, eleven wet days of sixteen); 1903 (210, a figure this KB already held); 1907 (77 in two sections); 1962 (590 boys, 12,425 camper days); 1970 (1,442 camper weeks); 1971 (481 campers, 1,247 weeks, broken out by sex); 1973 (1,276); 1974 (1,264); 1975 (475 children, 1,356); 1976 (480, 1,358); 1977 (414, 1,174); 1978 (442, 1,227); 1979 (441 + 18 CITs, 1,375); 1985 (1,214, 80%); 1986 (1,400, 92.5%); 1987 (1,412, 93%). CLOSED AS OPERATING, NO FIGURE: 1902, 1905, 1908, 1950, 1951, 1960, 1961. ONE CORRECTION FORCED: the table's 475 at 1974 belongs to 1975 -- the 1975 director's report says so and gives 1974 as the lower year -- the fourth dated error in this wiki traceable to the June-May fiscal year. ONE COUNT ADDED: the 1975 director's report opens 'The eighty-second year of Kamp Kanawana has come to an end', a fifth institutional season-count consistent with an unbroken run from 1894 (f_4849). STILL BLANK: 1911, 1914, 1919, 1920, 1981-1984, 1989-1993, 1995-1997, 2002-04 and most of 2006-19. The 1990s are within reach through the plaque corpus, the Order of Owens roll and the L&V winners roll (which runs unbroken 1991-1998); the 2010s through the YMCAs of Quebec annual reports; 1911, 1914 and 1915 need annual-report volumes this project does not hold. The 126-season claim now rests partly on evidence and partly on silence, and both articles say so. | SECOND PASS SAME DAY, AND NOW CLOSED TO THREE YEARS. The reports run out before the record does. Two bodies of physical evidence already held here carry the seasons the reports skip. (1) THE PLAQUE CORPUS: the person index built from the boards (p_291) carries dated appearances for 1955, 1956, 1959-65, 1968, 1970, 1972, 1973, 1975, 1979-90 and 1992-2010. A board naming a cabin's campers and counsellor was made at camp in that summer, for those people -- direct physical evidence the season ran. Closes 1981-84, 1989-90, 1992-93, 1995-97, 2002-04 and 2006-2010 (f_4850). (2) THE L&V TROPHY: a shield for every season 1947-2025 but 2021, transcribed in full, closing every remaining year from 1976 forward -- WITH ITS OWN WARNING, since a 2020 shield exists and the camp did not run in 2020, the Games having been played remotely. A shield attests a season, not necessarily a residential one, and that is the one year in seventy-nine where the two come apart (f_4851). (3) 1906 came out of the same pass with a total of 216 across the Victoria Day party, Business Boys, School Boys and Seniors; the four components are illegible in the OCR and sit on the printed page for whoever reaches it (f_4852). STILL BLANK, AND NOW A QUESTION ABOUT THREE SPECIFIC BOOKS RATHER THAN A SCATTERED FORTY YEARS: 1911, 1914 and 1920, needing the annual reports published in 1912, 1915 and 1921, none of which is in the digitized run. Queued as p_420.
priorities.source: continuity research after the operator's question of 2026-09-05

priorities.description: READ 'LUMBERMEN & VOYAGEURS: THE YMCA PINE CREST STORY'. Camp Pine Crest's centennial history is the single most likely place for the origin of the Pine Crest Games (run every summer since 1940) and for any account of how the Lumbermen-and-Voyageurs competition reached Kanawana in 1947. Every public surface searched -- the YMCA of Greater Toronto's own blog on the Games, the camp pages, Wikipedia -- is silent on who created the Games, why the team names, and whether the tradition was passed to another camp. The book is sold through the camp's Shopify store. Buying or borrowing it is the action. Secondary: check whether Roy D. Locke, who became Kanawana's Camp Chief in the summer of 1947, had any prior Toronto or Pine Crest posting, and search Concordia P0145/12B for correspondence between the two camps in 1946-47. || WORKED 2026-09-06 (f_5208). THE BOOK IS NOT DIGITIZED ANYWHERE THIS PROJECT CAN REACH and it is STILL IN PRINT. Open Library search-inside: 'Lumbermen and Voyageurs' 23 hits and 'Lumbermen & Voyageurs' 7, every one a false friend (the phrase is ordinary Canadiana), 'YMCA Pine Crest Story' ZERO. Internet Archive advancedsearch on title: numFound 0. BUT CAMP PINE CREST SELLS IT ITSELF at camp-pine-crest.myshopify.com/products/lumbermen-voyageurs-the-ymca-pine-crest-story for $25.00 USD; the listing gives no author, year, page count or stock status. SO THIS IS AN OPERATOR ACTION COSTING TWENTY-FIVE DOLLARS, NOT AN ACCESS FAILURE -- reclassify it as such. AND IT IS LESS URGENT THAN THIS PRIORITY ASSUMES: traditions/lv-games.md already carries the Pine Crest ceremony in W. E. 'Ted' Yard's own words, from his 1983 Canadian Camping obituary tribute, with the spoken text of the Voyageur-Lumberman tableau. The book would add the camp's own account of the tradition's origin and date; it would not fill a hole where nothing is.
priorities.source: expanded oldest-camp research and the inter-camp contact inquiry, 2026-09-05

priorities.description: TEST THE OTTAWA YMCA 1893 CLAIM AGAINST OTTAWA YMCA RECORDS. With Golden Lake 1884 resolved as an artefact of Sumner Dudley's American date, the surviving pre-Kanawana rival is Charles Plewman's statement that 'the Ottawa YMCA in 1893... began taking older boys to camp'. That is one year before Kanawana's first season and comes from a man who directed for the Ottawa Y himself. It has never been tested. Look for Ottawa YMCA annual reports of the 1890s, the 1893 board minute referenced in the Ace Milks profile, and any Camp On-Da-Da-Waks history. If 1893 holds, Kanawana is fourth rather than third among Canadian camps by founding date. | COMPLETED 2026-09-05. Tested on two surfaces and narrowed rather than closed. (1) The documentary half of the claim is an Ottawa YWCA board minute, not a YMCA record: Fraser's June 1954 profile says the origin of YMCA camping in Ottawa is 'somewhat lost in the mists of history' and that the first actual word of the camp that became On-Da-Da-Waks is a minute of an Ottawa Y.W.C.A. Board meeting recording a camp held in 1893 across from Quyon. Because OCR invents W/M, the page image was read directly (IA scan, leaf 12, cropped by the djvu word coordinates) and the printed text reads Y.W.C.A. f_2662 had it right; the wiki article was reading it as a YMCA record. New fact f_4835. (2) The Year Books of the YMCAs of North America 1893-1897, all five downloaded, cached in sources/cache/ymca-yearbooks/ and read (Ontario and Quebec reports in full, whole-volume search for 'camp' and 'tent'), record no camp for Ottawa -- and none for Montreal either, including the 1895 volume that reports on 1894. They report boys' camps elsewhere, so the silence is about coverage. That null cannot be used against Ottawa 1893 without also being used against Kanawana 1894. New fact f_4836, five new source records. (3) Byproduct: Charles Cushing was the International Committee's Corresponding Member for Quebec in 1893, 1894 and 1895 and signed the province's report in 1893 and 1895 -- name verified against the page image because the OCR reads GUSHING. New fact f_4837, written into cushing-family.md. f_4756 amended in place: not withdrawn, but its 'remains untested' tail is no longer true. What remains is offline and is now p_419.
priorities.source: expanded oldest-camp research and the inter-camp contact inquiry, 2026-09-05

priorities.description: ESTABLISH THE REAL NUMBER OF YMCA CAMPS IN CANADA, NOW AND OVER TIME. This project can date one solid figure -- twenty-nine YMCA camps took part in the 1989 centenary relay campfire, one hour each over twenty-nine hours -- and can name only six overnight YMCA camps in 2026 from separate association websites, because ymca.ca's national camps page names no individual camp. Stan Symington's 1953 tour of eastern Canada alone named nine, of which only Big Cove is identifiable as still operating. The apparent contraction is a comparison of three different instruments and must not be asserted until measured. YMCA Canada's national office would hold the series. || ADVANCED 2026-09-07 (f_5252). A SECOND COMPARABLE NATIONAL DATUM IS NOW IN HAND, and it came from the National Council Bulletin, which this project had never read until today (p_462). Its year-in-figures for 1965: 'We camped: 24,500 of us, at 48 "Y" residence campsites and more than 70 day campsites.' That is a count published by the national office, the same instrument as the twenty-nine camps of the 1989 centenary relay, so the two ARE comparable: 48 residence campsites in 1965 against twenty-nine camps in 1989. The 2026 figure of six remains a different kind of number -- camps this project could NAME from separate association websites, not a count anybody published -- and must not be put in the same series. TWO CAUTIONS CARRIED IN THE FACT: 'residence campsites' counts SITES rather than camps, and Kanawana's own Becscies annex shows why that matters; and the 1989 relay counts camps that TOOK PART, which is a floor. NEXT: the other National Council Bulletin issues in the unread run (1950, 1962, 1965, 1966, 1967, 1968) carry the same year-in-figures feature and would extend the series year by year without leaving this environment. || CORRECTED WITHIN THE HOUR. I dated the 48-campsite figure to 1965; reading the PREVIOUS year's issue shows the same figures printed for 1964, with a year-on-year note the later printing drops: '24,500 campers (up more than three thousand from last year)', which also gives about 21,500 for 1963. THE CAMP NUMBERS ARE IDENTICAL IN BOTH ISSUES WHILE THE SWIMMING NUMBERS DIFFER, so 48 and 24,500 are firm for 1964 and only provisional for 1965. A series built by taking each year's feature at face value would record a suspiciously stable camp system on the strength of one number printed twice -- worth knowing before extending it. || AND ONE FURTHER DATUM, 1967, FROM THE SAME RUN: the 1968 issue records that 'in Eastern Canada there was a slight falling off of attendance at residence camps which was attributed to family trips to Expo 67'. Kanawana is an Eastern Canadian residence camp and that is a dated national explanation for a dip in its own region in its own centennial-journey year.

priorities.description: SURVEY CANADIAN CAMPS FOR THE LUMBERMEN-AND-VOYAGEURS COMPETITION -- THE COUNT IS A FLOOR AND THIS PROJECT'S SEARCHES ARE NOT FINDING THEM. Four camps are now documented: Camp Pine Crest (Games from 1940), Kanawana (1947), Camp Kitchikewana (undated) and RKY Camp (undated). BOTH additions beyond the original two came from the operator recognising a camp, not from any search this project ran, which is itself the finding: the tradition is more widespread than these searches surface. Method: query the Ontario Camps Association member list camp by camp for 'Lumbermen', 'Voyageurs', 'the Games'; check YMCA associations across Ontario and Quebec; check camps with YMCA roots now independently owned, as RKY is. Establish for each the date the tradition began. The prize is the direction of travel: Kitchikewana (founded 1919) and RKY (1930) both predate the Pine Crest Games of 1940, so the assumption that Pine Crest originated it and Kanawana borrowed it is untested, and only Kanawana's 1947 adoption carries a date at all. [PARTIAL 2026-09-05. INSTRUMENT FOUND: the OCA member directory, 163 camps, paginated by ?alpha=N, with 61 YMCA/YWCA entries on its Y page -- the systematic tool the earlier searches lacked. CHECKED: Camp Queen Elizabeth (negative), Camp Waabanaki (negative -- its Voyageurs is an extended tripping programme, confirming the Big Cove rank-versus-team distinction), Big Cove (negative). STILL FOUR confirmed: Pine Crest, Kanawana, Kitchikewana, RKY. UNCHECKED: a dozen-plus Ontario YMCA overnight camps -- Wanakita, Belwood, Ki-Wa-Y, Heidelberg, Tillicum, John Island, Camp Henry, Otonabee, Geneva Park, Cedar Glen, Rotary Youth Camp Presqu'ile -- plus every non-YMCA OCA member and the whole ACQ membership in Quebec. METHOD NOTE: phrase search does not work; camp programme pages do not rank. Enumerate the directory camp by camp. Also correct: this project's count of YMCA overnight camps in Canada was badly low and has been relabelled in the article as a list of camps discussed, not a census.] [COMPLETE 2026-09-05 for Ontario's YMCA overnight camps: ten checked, ten negative -- Belwood, Ki-Wa-Y, Waabanaki, Wanakita, Camp Henry, Camp Queen Elizabeth, Tillicum, John Island, Otonabee, Presqu'ile. KEY RESULT: the colour-war GENRE is common (John Island runs 'Colour Wars', Presqu'ile runs 'Presqu'ile Bound') but the Lumbermen-and-Voyageurs NAMING is confined to four camps, making it a minority practice within its own movement and implying a specific rather than systemic route -- look for a PERSON who moved between Pine Crest, Kitchikewana, RKY and Kanawana. STILL OPEN and now handed to p_404 and p_408: no camp dates its Games beyond Pine Crest 1940 and Kanawana 1947. NOT DONE: non-YMCA OCA members and the entire ACQ membership in Quebec, either of which could hold a fifth camp.]

priorities.description: FIX scripts/verify/seed_read_state.py -- IT CLOBBERS PROVENANCE. Run on 2026-09-05 (by accident, in a loop over scripts/verify/*.py) it reported 'updated: 14' and rewrote read_state_basis on fourteen Kanawana report records from 'derived:cited-by-fact | cached text linked 2026-09-02: the file was on disk under no record' down to the bare 'derived:cited-by-fact'. priorities.description: 93 OF 100 'disputed' FACTS CARRY NO CONFLICT RECORD. CLAUDE.md's conflict rule says that when a new fact contradicts an existing one the response is to create a conflict record linking both and flag it for review. In practice most contradictions were recorded only as fact-to-fact conflicts_with links, or as confidence:disputed with nothing linked at all. The consequence is that kb/conflicts.json -- the file 'kb-conflicts' reads, and the file a human scans to see what still needs deciding -- undercounts the real number of live disagreements by roughly an order of magnitude. Sixteen of the 93 have no conflicts_with entry of any kind, so nothing anywhere records what they are disputed AGAINST; those are the worst, because a later reader cannot reconstruct the disagreement. TASK: triage the 93. For each, either (a) raise a conflict record, (b) resolve it if the KB already answers it, or (c) downgrade the confidence if 'disputed' was never right. Do NOT bulk-generate 93 conflict records -- several will turn out to be the same disagreement seen from both sides, and a pair should produce one record, not two. Surfaced by scripts/verify/staleness.py, which reports the count on every run. | THE TAIL CLOSED 2026-09-05. The four disputed facts that still carried no c_ conflict record are done, and three of them turned out to be a category slip rather than an oversight. f_4840 (Camp Stephens's 1911 boys' camp) simply lacked the link and now carries c_063. The other three were labelled 'disputed' for facts whose own content is not contested: f_2229 is a true statement that two outside sources disagree about Terry Mosher's Order of Canada year, with an earlier pass's reasoned decision not to open conflict records because neither touches a Kanawana claim -- that decision stands; f_1882 records a debunking this project withdrew and then saw confirmed in print; f_4808 records a correction made within the hour of the fact being written. All three are now 'stated', each with a note saying what was reclassified and why. THE GENERAL POINT, worth keeping: using 'disputed' both for a contested claim and for a fact that REPORTS a disagreement makes the disputed count mean two things at once, and this project reads that count as a work queue. staleness.py now reports 0 of 59.
priorities.source: whole-build staleness sweep, 2026-09-05
priorities.resolution: DONE. All 93 read in full and triaged; decisions recorded per fact in kb/triage/p412_disputed_triage.json. 29 linked to conflicts that already existed; 24 new conflict records raised (c_039-c_062) covering 32 facts, grouped so that one disagreement seen from two sides produces one record; 32 downgraded because 'disputed' was never right for them -- 21 to stated (nulls, access failures, exhausted searches, one debunking) and 9 to inferred (single low-reliability sources and unproven identifications) and 2 superseded facts set to stated behind their markers. One kept disputed on purpose: f_2229, whose own text records the decision not to escalate discrepancies that touch no Kanawana claim. Disputed 100 -> 60; without a conflict record 93 -> 1; conflicts 38 -> 62. SECOND PASS: the linking itself surfaced ten facts still disputed under already-resolved conflicts, invisible until the link existed; each adjudicated by reading which side of the resolution it fell on. Also normalised five conflicts whose resolution text sat in the notes field, where a reader checking `resolution` would have seen a blank and concluded nothing was decided.
